## Page: `provider-routing.md` — Provider Routing

### Provider Routing  `id: docs-features.provider-routing`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/config.yaml` → `provider_routing:` section. Docs title **"Provider Routing"**, description *"Configure OpenRouter or Nous Portal provider preferences to optimize for cost, speed, or quality."*
- **What it does:** "When using OpenRouter or Nous Portal as your LLM provider, Hermes Agent supports **provider routing** — fine-grained control over which underlying AI providers handle your requests and how they're prioritized." (`provider-routing.md:10`)
- **How it works:** Preferences are "passed to OpenRouter or Nous Portal on agent chat requests and iteration-limit summaries via the `extra_body.provider` field. (`extra_body` is the OpenAI Python SDK argument; it becomes the top-level `provider` object in the JSON request.)" (`provider-routing.md:170`). Code: `_provider_preferences_for_agent()` builds the object at `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:557-573`, mapping `agent.providers_allowed → only`, `providers_ignored → ignore`, `providers_order → order`, validated `provider_sort → sort`, `provider_require_parameters → require_parameters` (only when truthy), `provider_data_collection → data_collection`. Agent attributes are set at `agent/agent_init.py:951-954` from the constructor parameters declared at `agent/agent_init.py:557-560` and documented at `:637-640`. Sort validation: `_validated_openrouter_provider_sort()` (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:540-554`) lower-cases and checks membership in `_OPENROUTER_PROVIDER_SORT_VALUES`, logging `"Ignoring invalid OpenRouter provider.sort value %r (allowed: %s)"` and returning `None` for anything else.
- **Inputs / options:** The documented config block (`provider-routing.md:23-29`), all 6 keys with their inline comments verbatim: `sort: "price"` — "How to rank providers"; `only: []` — "Whitelist: only use these providers"; `ignore: []` — "Blacklist: never use these providers"; `order: []` — "Explicit provider priority order"; `require_parameters: false` — "Only use providers that support all parameters"; `data_collection: null` — "Control data collection (\"allow\" or \"deny\")". Documented parameter mapping (`provider-routing.md:178-183`): `providers_allowed ← provider_routing.only`, `providers_ignored ← provider_routing.ignore`, `providers_order ← provider_routing.order`, `provider_sort ← provider_routing.sort`, `provider_require_parameters ← provider_routing.require_parameters`, `provider_data_collection ← provider_routing.data_collection`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A `provider` object on the outbound request; no local state.
- **Config / env:** `provider_routing.sort|only|ignore|order|require_parameters|data_collection`. Auxiliary tasks are configured independently under `auxiliary.<task>.extra_body` (`provider-routing.md:170`; see also the comment at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1127`: "Each aux task is independent — main-agent provider_routing and …").
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::info Provider routing only applies when using OpenRouter or Nous Portal. It has no effect with direct provider connections (e.g., connecting directly to the Anthropic API)." (`provider-routing.md:32-34`) Invalid `sort` values are dropped with a warning rather than sent. "CLI mode — configured in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`, loaded at startup"; "Gateway mode — same config file, loaded when the gateway starts" (`provider-routing.md:172-173`). Portal tip: "Traffic routed through Nous Portal respects the same provider preferences — and Portal subscribers get 10% off token-billed providers." (`provider-routing.md:15`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Six config keys → one validated request object, only including keys with truthy values so the aggregator's defaults apply otherwise. A better version would validate provider slugs against a fetched catalog and warn on typos.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:557-573` matches the documented mapping exactly, including the "omit when falsy" behavior).

### `provider_routing.sort`  `id: docs-features.provider-routing-sort`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `provider-routing.md` → **"Options" → "`sort`"**.
- **What it does:** "Controls how OpenRouter ranks available providers for your request."
- **How it works:** Value table (`provider-routing.md:42-46`), all 3 values verbatim: `"price"` — "Cheapest provider first"; `"throughput"` — "Fastest tokens-per-second first"; `"latency"` — "Lowest time-to-first-token first". Validated against `_OPENROUTER_PROVIDER_SORT_VALUES` (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:547`).
- **Inputs / options:** `price` | `throughput` | `latency`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `provider.sort` on the request.
- **Config / env:** `provider_routing.sort`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Non-string or unknown values are ignored with a warning (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:549-553`).
- **Rebuild notes:** Enum with case-insensitive normalization and a fail-soft default. A better version would surface the rejected value in the CLI, not only in logs.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `provider_routing.only` (whitelist)  `id: docs-features.provider-routing-only`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `provider-routing.md` → **"`only`"**.
- **What it does:** "Whitelist of provider slugs. When set, **only** these providers will be used. All others are excluded. Use the lowercase slug shown by OpenRouter for each provider." (`provider-routing.md:55`)
- **How it works:** `preferences["only"] = agent.providers_allowed` (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:560-561`).
- **Inputs / options:** YAML list of slugs; documented example `- "anthropic"` / `- "google"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `provider.only`.
- **Config / env:** `provider_routing.only`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Empty list = not sent.
- **Rebuild notes:** Straight passthrough list. A better version would validate slugs.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `provider_routing.ignore` (blacklist)  `id: docs-features.provider-routing-ignore`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `provider-routing.md` → **"`ignore`"**.
- **What it does:** "Blacklist of provider names. These providers will **never** be used, even if they offer the cheapest or fastest option." (`provider-routing.md:66`)
- **How it works:** `preferences["ignore"] = agent.providers_ignored` (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:562-563`).
- **Inputs / options:** YAML list; documented example `- "together"` / `- "deepinfra"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `provider.ignore`.
- **Config / env:** `provider_routing.ignore`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Empty list = not sent.
- **Rebuild notes:** As above.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `provider_routing.order` (priority order)  `id: docs-features.provider-routing-order`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `provider-routing.md` → **"`order`"**.
- **What it does:** "Explicit priority order. Providers listed first are preferred. Unlisted providers are used as fallbacks." (`provider-routing.md:77`)

- **Inputs / options:** YAML list; documented example `- "anthropic"` / `- "google"` / `- "amazon-bedrock"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `provider.order`.
- **Config / env:** `provider_routing.order`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Unlisted providers remain usable (this is a preference, not a whitelist).
- **Rebuild notes:** As above.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `provider_routing.require_parameters`  `id: docs-features.provider-routing-require-parameters`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `provider-routing.md` → **"`require_parameters`"**.
- **What it does:** "When `true`, OpenRouter will only route to providers that support **all** parameters in your request (like `temperature`, `top_p`, `tools`, etc.). This avoids silent parameter drops." (`provider-routing.md:89`)
- **How it works:** `if agent.provider_require_parameters: preferences["require_parameters"] = True` (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:566-569`) — only ever sent as literal `True`.
- **Inputs / options:** `true` | `false` (default `false`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** `provider.require_parameters: true`.
- **Config / env:** `provider_routing.require_parameters`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `false` is omitted entirely rather than sent as `false`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Boolean flag, omit-when-false. A better version would list which parameters caused a provider to be excluded.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

- **Edge cases / guards:** `null` = not sent (aggregator default applies).
- **Rebuild notes:** Enum passthrough. A better version would default to `deny` and require an explicit opt-in.

## Page: `subscription-proxy.md` — Subscription Proxy

### Subscription Proxy (`hermes proxy`)  `id: docs-features.subscription-proxy`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes proxy start` / `status` / `providers`. Docs title **"Subscription Proxy"** (`sidebar_position: 15`), description *"Use your Nous Portal subscription (or other OAuth provider) as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for external apps"*.
- **What it does:** "The subscription proxy is a local HTTP server that lets external apps — OpenViking, Karakeep, Open WebUI, anything that speaks OpenAI-compatible chat completions — use your Hermes-managed provider subscription as their LLM endpoint. The proxy attaches the right credentials (refreshing them automatically) so the app never needs a static API key." (`subscription-proxy.md:9-13`)
- **How it works:** Per-request architecture (`subscription-proxy.md:187-190`), all 4 steps verbatim: "1. Receive `POST /v1/chat/completions` from your app"; "2. Look up the adapter's current credential (refresh if expiring)"; "3. Forward the request body verbatim, with `Authorization: Bearer <minted-key>`"; "4. Stream the response back unchanged (SSE preserved)". "No transformation. No logging of request bodies. No agent loop. The proxy is a credential-attaching pass-through." Code: `hermes_cli/proxy/server.py:51` `DEFAULT_PORT = 8645`; dispatcher `cmd_proxy` at `hermes_cli/proxy/cli.py:109-131`; adapter registry `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/__init__.py` with `base.py`, `nous_portal.py`, `xai.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** Sub-commands and flags, verbatim from the CLI's own help (`hermes_cli/proxy/cli.py:124-128`): `hermes proxy start [--provider nous|xai] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 8645]` — "Run the proxy in the foreground."; `hermes proxy status` — "Show which upstream adapters are ready."; `hermes proxy providers` — "List available upstream providers." (`list` is accepted as an alias of `providers`, `hermes_cli/proxy/cli.py:116`). Client-side config triple (`subscription-proxy.md:60-62`): `Base URL: http://127.0.0.1:8645/v1`, `API key: anything (e.g. "sk-unused")`, `Model: Hermes-4-70B    # or Hermes-4.3-36B, Hermes-4-405B`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Startup banner (`subscription-proxy.md:46-49`): `Starting Hermes proxy for Nous Portal` / `  Listening on:  http://127.0.0.1:8645/v1` / `  Forwarding to: (resolved per-request from your subscription)` / `  Use any bearer token in the client — the proxy attaches your real credential.` Status output (`subscription-proxy.md:86-88`): `Hermes proxy upstream adapters` / `  [nous    ] Nous Portal — ready (bearer expires 2026-05-15T06:43:21Z)`. Providers list prints `Available proxy upstream providers:` then `  <name>  — <display_name>` per adapter (`hermes_cli/proxy/cli.py:102-105`).
- **Config / env:** Credentials in `~/.hermes/auth.json` (written by `hermes portal`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Leave this running in the foreground. Use `tmux`, `nohup`, or a systemd unit if you want it to survive logout." Status errors: `not logged in` → run `hermes portal`; `credentials need attention` → "your refresh token was revoked (rare — happens if you signed out from the Portal web UI) — just re-run `hermes portal`". "The proxy ignores the `Authorization` header from your app and attaches your real Portal credential to the upstream request."
- **Rebuild notes:** An asyncio HTTP server with a per-provider adapter exposing `{name, display_name, allowed_paths, is_authenticated(), credential()}`; forward body verbatim, swap the auth header, stream SSE through. A better version would add its own bearer auth and per-client quotas so LAN exposure is safe by default.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (port, sub-commands, flags and adapter set all confirmed in code).

Closing rule (`subscription-proxy.md:24-25`): "Use the API server when you want the **agent** as a backend. Use the proxy when you just want **the model** through your subscription."

- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a

### Proxy providers (`nous`, `xai`) and the `UpstreamAdapter` interface  `id: docs-features.proxy-providers`
- **Surface:** CLI

More OAuth providers can be added by implementing the `UpstreamAdapter` interface in `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/`." (`subscription-proxy.md:75-77`) Code: exactly two adapters ship — `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/nous_portal.py` (`NousPortalAdapter`, `name = "nous"`, `display_name = "Nous Portal"`, `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/nous_portal.py:45-59`) and `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/xai.py`, plus `base.py` defining `UpstreamAdapter`.
- **Inputs / options:** `--provider nous|xai` on `hermes proxy start`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Adding a new provider (e.g. HuggingFace, GitHub Copilot's chat endpoint, Anthropic via OAuth) requires implementing `UpstreamAdapter` in `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/<provider>.py` and registering it in `adapters/__init__.py`. Providers that aren't OpenAI-compatible at the protocol level (Anthropic Messages API, for example) would need a transformation layer, which is out of scope for the current shape." (`subscription-proxy.md:197-203`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Adapter ABC + a registry dict keyed by short name. A better version would allow adapters to be contributed as plugins rather than in-tree files.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (two adapters in tree, matching the documented names).

### Proxy allowed-path allow-list  `id: docs-features.proxy-allowed-paths`
- **Surface:** API

Code: `_ALLOWED_PATHS = frozenset({"/chat/completions", "/completions", "/embeddings", "/models"})` (`hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/nous_portal.py:35-42`), exposed via the `allowed_paths` property (`:61-63`); comment at `:32-34`: "Endpoints inference-api.nousresearch.com actually serves. Anything else the proxy will reject with 404 — keeps stray clients from leaking weird requests to the upstream."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** "Other paths (`/v1/images/generations`, `/v1/audio/speech`, etc.) return 404 with a clear error pointing at the allowed paths."
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** The allow-list is per adapter, not global.

### Proxy recipe — Karakeep / any OpenAI-compatible client  `id: docs-features.proxy-karakeep`
- **Surface:** Docs

## Page: `tool-search.md` — Tool Search

### Tool Search (progressive tool disclosure)  `id: docs-features.tool-search`
- **Surface:** Tool + Config
- **Where:** Docs title **"Tool Search"** (`sidebar_position: 95`); config `tools.tool_search.*`; model-visible bridge tools `tool_search`, `tool_describe`, `tool_call`.
- **What it does:** "**Tool Search** is Hermes' opt-in progressive-disclosure layer… When activated, MCP and plugin tools are replaced in the model-visible tools array by three bridge tools, and the model loads each specific tool's schema on demand." (`tool-search.md:13-16`) The problem it solves: "When you have many MCP servers or non-core plugin tools attached to a session, their JSON schemas can consume a substantial fraction of the context window on every turn."
- **How it works:** Implementation is `tools/tool_search.py` (named in the docs' See-also, `tool-search.md:204`). Core tools never defer: "Core tools defined in `toolsets._HERMES_CORE_TOOLS` are *never* deferred" (`tools/tool_search.py:10`, import at `:226-227`); session-gated GUI toolsets are handled separately (`tools/tool_search.py:232-241`). Deferral eligibility returns one of `"available" | "not_found" | "not_deferrable"` (`tools/tool_search.py:268-276`). Retrieval is BM25 with Snowball English stemming over tokenized name/source/description/parameter names (`tools/tool_search.py:379-562`), with a literal substring fallback on the tool name "when no query token matches any document (e.g. searching `\"hub\"` where the token is `github`)" (`tools/tool_search.py:558-562`). Empty-result groups carry `available_sources` + `hint` (`tools/tool_search.py:1054`, `:1087`).
- **Inputs / options:** The three bridge tools verbatim (`tool-search.md:33-35`): `tool_search(queries, limit?)` — "search the deferred-tool catalog (one or more queries)"; `tool_describe(names)` — "load the full schemas for one or more tools"; `tool_call(name, arguments)` — "invoke a deferred tool". Worked transcript (`tool-search.md:41-53`): `tool_search(["create a github issue", "send a slack message"])` → `{results: [{query, matches: [...]}, …], tools: {…}}`; `tool_describe(["mcp_github_create_issue", "mcp_slack_post_message"])` → `{tools: {…: {parameters: {…}}}}`; `tool_call("mcp_github_create_issue", {title, body})` → `{ok: true, issue_number: 42}`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** "Each query in a `tool_search` call is searched independently against the same catalog (`limit` applies per query); the per-query groups carry tool names only, while the shared `tools` map holds each matched tool's description and required parameter names once. Queries are stemmed, so \"issues\" finds `create_issue`. Each query group that returns no matches includes an `available_sources` summary of the connected servers so a lexical miss is not mistaken for a missing capability. `tool_describe` resolves every requested name in one call; unknown names are reported in `not_found` without failing the rest of the batch." (`tool-search.md:56-64`)
- **Config / env:** `tools.tool_search.enabled|threshold_pct|search_default_limit|max_search_limit|listing|listing_max_tokens` — see the dedicated config entry.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Bridge unwrapping (`tool-search.md:66-71`): "When the model invokes `tool_call`, Hermes **unwraps the bridge** and dispatches the underlying tool exactly as if the model had called it directly. Pre-tool-call hooks, guardrails, approval prompts, and post-tool-call hooks all run against the real tool name — not against `tool_call`. The activity feed in the CLI and gateway also unwraps so you see the underlying tool, not the bridge." Info admonition **"Built-in Hermes tools never defer"** naming, verbatim, `terminal`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `patch`, `search_files`, `todo`, `memory`, `browser_*`, `web_search`, `web_extract`, `clarify`, `execute_code`, `delegate_task`, `session_search`, "and the rest of `_HERMES_CORE_TOOLS`" (`tool-search.md:18-25`). "Per-call array caps are internal safety bounds, not configuration. Over-cap calls return an error so the model can retry with a smaller batch." (`tool-search.md:112-113`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Replace deferrable tool defs with three bridge defs; keep a stateless per-assembly catalog; BM25 + stemming for retrieval; unwrap at dispatch so all policy runs on the real name. A better version would cache `tool_describe` results in the system-prompt prefix when the catalog is stable, recovering the lost cache benefit.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`tools/tool_search.py` matches every documented mechanism).

### Tool Search tiered disclosure (tiers 0/1/2)  `id: docs-features.tool-search-tiers`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `tool-search.md` → **"When does it activate?"**.
- **What it does:** "Tool Search uses **tiered disclosure**: the presence of *any* deferrable (MCP/plugin) tool activates the bridge; what scales with catalog size is how much of the catalog stays visible, not whether schemas defer." (`tool-search.md:75-77`)
- **How it works:** Complete tier table (`tool-search.md:79-83`): **Tier 0** — Condition "No MCP/plugin tools" — "Every tool eager, no bridge. Pass-through."; **Tier 1** — "Deferred catalog's listing fits the budget" — "Bridge + a skills-style manifest of every deferred tool (name + short description, degrading to names-only when over budget). Degradation is **per server**: when one oversized server (Cloudflare) is attached alongside small ones (Linear), the small servers keep their per-tool listings and only the oversized server collapses to a summary line."; **Tier 2** — "Per-tool listing exceeds the budget even names-only for every server (e.g. Cloudflare's flat API surface alone: ~3,300 tools whose names are ~32K tokens)" — "Bare bridge + a one-line-per-server summary (server name + tool count), so the model knows which domains are reachable; individual tools are discoverable only through `tool_search`." Budget formula: "The listing budget is `min(threshold_pct% of context, listing_max_tokens)`" (`tool-search.md:85`; matches the code comment "Effective budget = min(this % of context, listing_max_tokens)" at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:3011-3014`).
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (automatic).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Different bridge descriptions per tier.
- **Config / env:** `tools.tool_search.threshold_pct`, `tools.tool_search.listing_max_tokens`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "The decision is re-evaluated every time the tools array is built, so adding or removing MCP servers mid-session moves the session between tiers on the next assembly." (`tool-search.md:86-88`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Compute listing cost per server, degrade the biggest offenders first, recompute per assembly. A better version would keep a per-server relevance prior so frequently used servers keep full listings longest.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (budget formula matches the config comment verbatim).

### Tool Search configuration keys  `id: docs-features.tool-search-config`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/config.yaml` → `tools.tool_search:`; `tool-search.md` → **"Configuration"**.
- **What it does:** Six keys controlling activation, budgets and the listing.
- **How it works:** Documented YAML (`tool-search.md:92-101`) plus the key table (`tool-search.md:103-110`), all six verbatim: `enabled` (default `auto`) — "`auto`/`on` activate whenever at least one deferrable tool exists; `off` disables entirely (everything stays eager). `auto` is currently an alias of `on` — it is reserved for a future mode that inlines schemas when they fit the context and defers only when they don't. Pin `on` or `off` if you want today's behavior guaranteed across upgrades."; `threshold_pct` (default `5`) — "Listing budget as a percentage of the active model's context length. Range 0–100."; `search_default_limit` (default `5`) — "Hits returned per query when the model calls `tool_search` without a `limit`."; `max_search_limit` (default `25`) — "Hard upper bound the model can request via `limit` (per query). Range 1–50."; `listing` (default `auto`) — "Embed a skills-style manifest of every deferred tool (name + first sentence of its description, ≤60 chars, grouped by MCP server) in the `tool_search` bridge description. `auto` includes it when it fits the budget (falling back to names-only, then to the tier-2 server summary); `on`/`off` force either way."; `listing_max_tokens` (default `4000`) — "Absolute cap on the embedded listing, regardless of context size. Range 200–60000. Large catalogs degrade to names-only or per-server summaries, keeping full schemas available through search." Legacy shape (`tool-search.md:128-131`): `tools: {tool_search: true}` — "equivalent to `{enabled: auto}`".
- **Inputs / options:** As above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Changes the assembled tools array.
- **Config / env:** `tools.tool_search.*` — all six confirmed with identical defaults and identical prose at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:3005-3033`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Ranges: `threshold_pct` 0–100, `max_search_limit` 1–50, `listing_max_tokens` 200–60000, `search_default_limit` 1..`max_search_limit`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Config-first design with a legacy boolean coercion. A better version would expose a dry-run that prints which tier the current session lands in.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (defaults and prose match the code comments almost word-for-word).

### Why the tool listing exists  `id: docs-features.tool-search-listing-rationale`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `tool-search.md` → **"Why the listing exists"**.
- **What it does:** Explains the empirical reason the catalog manifest is embedded.
- **How it works:** Verbatim (`tool-search.md:117-124`): "Without it, deferred capabilities are *invisible* — live benchmarking showed models substituting visible core tools (running `gh` in the terminal instead of searching for the deferred GitHub tool) or declaring a capability nonexistent instead of calling `tool_search`. The listing applies the skills pattern to tools: every capability stays discoverable by name at all times, while full parameter schemas remain deferred. If the model sees the exact tool name in the listing, it can skip `tool_search` and go straight to `tool_describe`, saving a round trip."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `tools.tool_search.listing`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** Always keep names visible; defer only schemas. This is the single most important design lesson on the page.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### When NOT to use Tool Search  `id: docs-features.tool-search-when-not`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `tool-search.md` → **"When NOT to use it"**.
- **What it does:** States the cost model and the opt-out.
- **How it works:** "Tool Search trades a fixed per-turn token cost (the three bridge tool schemas plus the catalog listing) and at least one extra round trip on cold tools (describe → call) for the savings on the deferred schemas. At tier 1 the listing keeps every capability visible, so the discovery round trip usually disappears — the model goes straight to `tool_describe`. Live benchmarking showed the listing mode matching eager loading's task success while costing less than the bare bridge." (`tool-search.md:135-141`) "If you want the old always-eager behavior for a small toolset, set `enabled: off`."
- **Inputs / options:** `tools.tool_search.enabled: off`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `tools.tool_search.enabled`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Tool Search inherent trade-offs  `id: docs-features.tool-search-tradeoffs`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `tool-search.md` → **"Trade-offs that don't go away"**.
- **What it does:** Names the four costs "inherent to any progressive-disclosure design".
- **How it works:** All four verbatim (`tool-search.md:151-167`): "**One extra round trip on cold tools.** The first time the model needs a deferred tool, it spends one or two extra model calls to find and load the schema."; "**No cache benefit on deferred schemas.** A loaded `tool_describe` result enters the conversation history (so it does get cached on subsequent turns) but it never benefits from the system-prompt cache prefix."; "**Model-quality dependence.** Tool Search assumes the model can write a reasonable search query for the tool it wants. Smaller models do this less well; the published Anthropic numbers (49% → 74% on Opus 4 with vs. without tool search) show the upside but also that ~26 points of accuracy is still retrieval failure."; "**Toolset edits invalidate cache.** Adding or removing a tool mid-session changes the bridge tools' descriptions (which include the count of deferred tools) and the catalog, so the prompt cache is invalidated."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** These come "from the prompt-cache integrity invariant".
- **Rebuild notes:** Publishing the honest failure rate (26 points of retrieval failure) is the right posture; a better version would log retrieval misses so users can see them.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Tool Search implementation details  `id: docs-features.tool-search-implementation`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `tool-search.md` → **"Implementation details"**.
- **What it does:** Five documented internals.
- **How it works:** All five verbatim (`tool-search.md:171-200`): "**Retrieval:** BM25 over tokenized tool name, source name (the MCP server or plugin toolset the tool belongs to, so searching `\"linear\"` finds that server's tools even when a tool's own name doesn't carry the service), description, and parameter names, with Snowball stemming (English) applied to both the index and the query… Falls back to a literal substring match on the tool name when no query token matches any document (e.g. searching `\"hub\"` where the token is `github`)." (code: `tools/tool_search.py:379-562`, tokenizer docstring "Lowercase alphanumeric tokens, Snowball-stemmed (English)" at `:420`, snake_case/dotted name splitting at `:456`); "**Parallel execution unwraps the bridge.** The batch planner decides concurrency on the *underlying* tool of a `tool_call`, not on the literal bridge name — so an MCP server opted in via `supports_parallel_tool_calls: true` keeps its concurrency when its tools are called through the bridge, and `tool_search` / `tool_describe` lookups batch concurrently like any read-only tool."; "**Catalog is stateless across turns.** It rebuilds from the current tool-defs list every assembly — no session-keyed `Map`."; "**The catalog is scoped to the session's toolsets.** … A subagent, kanban worker, or gateway session restricted to a subset of toolsets cannot use the bridge to discover or call a tool outside that subset."; "**No JS sandbox.** Hermes uses the simpler \"structured tools\" mode (search / describe / call as plain functions). The JS-sandbox \"code mode\" some other implementations offer is a large surface area; we skip it."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** MCP server key `supports_parallel_tool_calls`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The toolset-scoping guarantee is a security property, not just an optimization.
- **Rebuild notes:** Stateless catalog + scoped registry + unwrapped dispatch. A better version would add embedding-based retrieval alongside BM25 for semantic queries.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (BM25, Snowball, substring fallback, core-tool exclusion all present in `tools/tool_search.py`).

## Page: `vision.md` — Vision & Image Paste

### Vision & Image Paste  `id: docs-features.vision-paste`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** Docs title **"Vision & Image Paste"** (`sidebar_position: 7`), description *"Paste images from your clipboard into the Hermes CLI for multimodal vision analysis."* Surface: the interactive CLI composer.
- **What it does:** "Hermes Agent supports **multimodal vision** — you can paste images from your clipboard directly into the CLI and ask the agent to analyze, describe, or work with them. Images are sent to the model as base64-encoded content blocks, so any vision-capable model can process them." (`vision.md:10`)
- **How it works:** Five documented steps (`vision.md:18-22`): "1. Copy an image to your clipboard (screenshot, browser image, etc.)"; "2. Attach it using one of the methods below"; "3. Type your question and press Enter"; "4. The image appears as a `[📎 Image #1]` badge above the input"; "5. On submit, the image is sent to the model as a vision content block". Storage: "Images are saved to `~/.hermes/images/` as PNG files with timestamped filenames." (`vision.md:26`) — confirmed as a real home subdirectory in the dashboard's media roots (`hermes_cli/web_server.py:2494` `roots = [home / "images", home / "screenshots", home / "cache"]`, `:2796` `img_dir = Path(home) / "images"`).
- **Inputs / options:** Attach methods (each has its own entry): `/paste`, `Ctrl+V` / `Cmd+V`, `/terminal-setup`. Multi-attach: "You can attach multiple images before sending — each gets its own badge. Press `Ctrl+C` to clear all attached images." (`vision.md:24`)
- **Outputs / side effects:** A `[📎 Image #1]` badge in the composer; a PNG under `~/.hermes/images/`; a vision content block on the request.
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.vision` (for the text-only routing path). Portal tip (`vision.md:12-14`): "Portal subscribers get vision-capable models (Claude, GPT-5, Gemini) in the same catalog — no extra credentials needed."
- **Edge cases / guards:** See the platform-compatibility, SSH and routing entries.
- **Rebuild notes:** Composer-side attachment list + OS clipboard readers + base64 content blocks. A better version would support drag-and-drop and an `/attach <path>` command (the docs say one is "planned for a future release").
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`~/.hermes/images/` is a real, served media root).

### `/paste` command  `id: docs-features.vision-paste-command`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** Type `/paste` and press Enter in the CLI. `vision.md` → **"Paste Methods" → "`/paste` Command"**, headlined "**The most reliable explicit image-attach fallback.**"
- **What it does:** "Hermes checks your clipboard for an image and attaches it. This is the safest option when your terminal rewrites `Cmd+V`/`Ctrl+V`, or when you copied only an image and there is no bracketed-paste text payload to inspect." (`vision.md:40`)
- **How it works:** Calls OS-level clipboard tools via subprocess (`osascript`, `powershell.exe`, `xclip`, `wl-paste`) rather than relying on the terminal paste event (`vision.md:180`).
- **Inputs / options:** No arguments.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A new `[📎 Image #N]` badge; a PNG in `~/.hermes/images/`.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** The only method that works when the clipboard holds an image and no text.
- **Rebuild notes:** One explicit command that shells out to the platform clipboard reader. A better version would report *why* nothing was attached (empty clipboard vs missing tool).
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `Ctrl+V` / `Cmd+V` layered paste  `id: docs-features.vision-ctrl-v`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** Keyboard shortcut in the CLI composer. `vision.md` → **"Ctrl+V / Cmd+V"**.
- **What it does:** "Hermes now treats paste as a layered flow" (`vision.md:44`).
- **How it works:** Three layers verbatim (`vision.md:45-47`): "normal text paste first"; "native clipboard / OSC52 text fallback if the terminal did not deliver text cleanly"; "image attach when the clipboard or pasted payload resolves to an image or image path". "This means pasted macOS screenshot temp paths and `file://...` image URIs can attach immediately instead of sitting in the composer as raw text." (`vision.md:49`)
- **Inputs / options:** `Ctrl+V` (Linux/Windows), `Cmd+V` (macOS).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Either pasted text or an attached image.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::warning If your clipboard has **only an image** (no text), terminals still cannot send binary image bytes directly. Use `/paste` as the explicit image-attach fallback." (`vision.md:51-53`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Try text → OSC52 → clipboard-image → path-resolution, in that order. A better version would show a one-line hint in the composer when a paste resolved to an image path.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Vision platform setup — macOS / X11 / Wayland / WSL2  `id: docs-features.vision-platform-setup`
- **Surface:** Docs + Env
- **Where:** `vision.md` → **"Platform-Specific Setup"** (four sub-sections).
- **What it does:** Names the per-OS clipboard dependency and its install command.
- **How it works:** **macOS** — "**No setup required.** Hermes uses `osascript` (built into macOS) to read the clipboard. For faster performance, optionally install `pngpaste`: `brew install pngpaste`." **Linux (X11)** — install `xclip`: `sudo apt install xclip` / `sudo dnf install xclip` / `sudo pacman -S xclip`. **Linux (Wayland)** — install `wl-clipboard`: `sudo apt install wl-clipboard` / `sudo dnf install wl-clipboard` / `sudo pacman -S wl-clipboard`; detection tip `echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE` with "\"wayland\" = Wayland, \"x11\" = X11, \"tty\" = no display server". **WSL2** — "**No extra setup required.** Hermes detects WSL2 automatically (via `/proc/version`) and uses `powershell.exe` to access the Windows clipboard through .NET's `System.Windows.Forms.Clipboard`… The clipboard data is transferred as base64-encoded PNG over stdout, so no file path conversion or temp files are needed." (`vision.md:83-132`)
- **Inputs / options:** `pngpaste`, `xclip`, `wl-clipboard`, `powershell.exe`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `XDG_SESSION_TYPE` (read for detection guidance).
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::info WSLg Note If you're running WSLg (WSL2 with GUI support), Hermes tries the PowerShell path first, then falls back to `wl-paste`. WSLg's clipboard bridge only supports BMP format for images — Hermes auto-converts BMP to PNG using Pillow (if installed) or ImageMagick's `convert` command." (`vision.md:134-136`) Verification recipe (`vision.md:141-149`): `grep -i microsoft /proc/version`; `which powershell.exe`; `powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command "Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Windows.Forms; [System.Windows.Forms.Clipboard]::ContainsImage()"` — "Should print \"True\"".
- **Rebuild notes:** Per-platform reader chain with a documented fallback per OS. A better version would ship a `hermes doctor` check for the clipboard tool.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Vision over SSH — limits and workarounds  `id: docs-features.vision-ssh`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `vision.md` → **"SSH & Remote Sessions"**.
- **What it does:** States that clipboard image paste does not work over SSH and gives four workarounds.
- **How it works:** "**Clipboard image paste does not fully work over SSH.** … Clipboard tools (`xclip`, `wl-paste`, `powershell.exe`, `osascript`) read the clipboard of the machine they run on — which is the remote server, not your local machine." (`vision.md:154`) "Text can sometimes still bridge through terminal paste or OSC52, but image clipboard access and local screenshot temp paths remain tied to the machine running Hermes."
- **Inputs / options:** All four workarounds verbatim (`vision.md:160-166`): "1. **Upload the image file** — Save the image locally, upload it to the remote server via `scp`, VSCode's file explorer (drag-and-drop), or any file transfer method. Then reference it by path. *(A `/attach <filepath>` command is planned for a future release.)*"; "2. **Use a URL** — If the image is accessible online, just paste the URL in your message. The agent can use `vision_analyze` to look at any image URL directly."; "3. **X11 forwarding** — Connect with `ssh -X` to forward X11. This lets `xclip` on the remote machine access your local X11 clipboard. Requires an X server running locally (XQuartz on macOS, built-in on Linux X11 desktops). Slow for large images."; "4. **Use a messaging platform** — Send images to Hermes via Telegram, Discord, Slack, or WhatsApp. These platforms handle image upload natively and are not affected by clipboard/terminal limitations."
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** `/attach <filepath>` is explicitly documented as **not yet implemented** ("planned for a future release").
- **Rebuild notes:** Accept a local path or URL as a first-class attachment source — that is exactly the missing `/attach`.
- **Verification:** **documented gap** — `/attach` is stated as planned, not shipped.

### Why terminals can't paste images (explainer)  `id: docs-features.vision-why-terminals`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `vision.md` → **"Why Terminals Can't Paste Images"**.
- **What it does:** Explains the bracketed-paste limitation that motivates `/paste`.
- **How it works:** Three steps verbatim (`vision.md:172-176`): "1. Reads the clipboard for **text content**"; "2. Wraps it in bracketed paste escape sequences"; "3. Sends it to the application through the terminal's text stream". "If the clipboard contains only an image (no text), the terminal has nothing to send. There is no standard terminal escape sequence for binary image data. The terminal simply does nothing." "This is why Hermes uses a separate clipboard check — instead of receiving image data through the terminal paste event, it calls OS-level tools (`osascript`, `powershell.exe`, `xclip`, `wl-paste`) directly via subprocess to read the clipboard independently."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Vision content-block format / supported models  `id: docs-features.vision-content-format`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `vision.md` → **"Supported Models"**.
- **What it does:** Documents the wire format images are sent in.
- **How it works:** "The image is sent as a base64-encoded data URL in the OpenAI vision content format" (`vision.md:184`), verbatim JSON (`vision.md:186-193`): `{"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64,..."}}`. "Most modern models support this format, including GPT-4 Vision, Claude (with vision), Gemini, and open-source multimodal models served through OpenRouter."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** Emit OpenAI-shaped image content and let the provider adapter translate. A better version would downscale before encoding to bound token cost.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Image routing (vision-capable vs text-only models)  `id: docs-features.vision-routing`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `vision.md` → **"Image Routing (Vision-Capable vs Text-Only Models)"**.
- **What it does:** "When a user attaches an image — from the CLI clipboard, the gateway (Telegram/Discord photo), or any other entry point — Hermes routes it based on whether your current model actually supports vision." (`vision.md:199`)
- **How it works:** Table verbatim (`vision.md:201-204`): **Vision-capable** (GPT-4V, Claude with vision, Gemini, Qwen-VL, MiMo-VL, etc.) — "Sent as **real pixels** using the provider's native image content format above. No text summary layer."; **Text-only** (DeepSeek V3, smaller open-source models, older chat-only endpoints) — "Routed through the `vision_analyze` auxiliary tool — an auxiliary vision model describes the image, and the text description is injected into the conversation." "You don't configure this — Hermes looks up your current model's capability in the provider metadata and picks the right path automatically." (`vision.md:206`)
- **Inputs / options:** None (automatic).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Either native pixels or an injected description.
- **Config / env:** "Which auxiliary model handles the text-description path is configurable under `auxiliary.vision`" (`vision.md:208`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** "you can switch between vision and non-vision models mid-session and image handling 'just works'… Text-only models get coherent context about the image rather than a broken multimodal payload they'd have to reject."
- **Rebuild notes:** Capability lookup in provider metadata → two delivery paths behind one API. A better version would cache the description per image hash so a model switch does not re-describe.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `vision_analyze` dual behavior  `id: docs-features.vision-analyze-dual`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `vision.md` → **"`vision_analyze` has the same dual behavior"**.
- **What it does:** The `vision_analyze` tool short-circuits the auxiliary describer when the main model and provider can carry images inside tool results.
- **How it works:** "When the active main model is vision-capable **and** its provider supports image content inside tool results (currently the Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure-OpenAI, and Gemini 3.x stacks), `vision_analyze` short-circuits the auxiliary describer and returns the raw image pixels as a multimodal tool-result envelope. The main model sees the image natively on its next turn — no aux call, no text-summary information loss, no extra latency." "For text-only main models (or providers whose tool-result channel doesn't carry images), `vision_analyze` falls back to the legacy path: it asks the configured auxiliary vision model to describe the image and returns the description as plain text. Either way the calling tool signature is the same — the tool decides which path to take at runtime based on the active model." (`vision.md:212-214`)
- **Inputs / options:** Same tool signature in both paths.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Either a multimodal tool-result envelope or a plain-text description.
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.vision`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The four provider stacks that support image-in-tool-result are enumerated: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure-OpenAI, Gemini 3.x.
- **Rebuild notes:** One tool, runtime-selected result envelope based on `(model_vision_capable AND provider_supports_image_tool_results)`. A better version would report which path it took in the result so the model can reason about fidelity.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `tools` shard for `vision_analyze`'s registered schema).

## Page: `tool-gateway.md` — Nous Tool Gateway

### Nous Tool Gateway  `id: docs-features.tool-gateway`
- **Surface:** Config + CLI
- **Where:** Docs title **"Nous Tool Gateway"**, `sidebar_label: "Tool Gateway"` (`sidebar_position: 2`), tagline **"One subscription. Every tool built in."** CTA button label: **"Start or manage subscription →"** linking to `https://portal.nousresearch.com/manage-subscription`.
- **What it does:** "The Tool Gateway is included with every paid Nous Portal subscription. It routes Hermes' tool calls — web search, image generation, text-to-speech, and cloud browser automation — through infrastructure Nous already runs, so you don't have to sign up with Firecrawl, FAL, OpenAI, Browser Use, or anyone else just to make your agent useful." (`tool-gateway.md:12`)
- **How it works:** Per-category selection keys stored in `config.yaml`; picking the **Nous Subscription** row stores the literal value `nous`. "The runtime **always uses the stored selection** — credential presence never selects or reroutes a category." (`tool-gateway.md:157`)
- **Inputs / options:** Three entry commands (`tool-gateway.md:44-54`): `hermes setup --portal` — "Fresh install: Nous OAuth + set Nous as provider + turn on the Tool Gateway in one go"; `hermes model` — "Switch your inference provider to Nous Portal — Hermes then offers to turn on the gateway for all tools"; `hermes tools` — "Enable the gateway per-tool — pick \"Nous Subscription\" for any tool you want". Three status commands (`tool-gateway.md:63-65`): `hermes portal info` — "Portal auth + Tool Gateway routing summary"; `hermes portal tools` — "Gateway catalog with current routing per tool"; `hermes status` — "Full system status (Tool Gateway is one section)".
- **Outputs / side effects:** `hermes portal info` prints (`tool-gateway.md:71-76`): `◆ Nous Tool Gateway` / `  Nous Portal     ✓ managed tools available` / `  Web tools       ✓ active via Nous subscription` / `  Image gen       ✓ active via Nous subscription` / `  TTS             ✓ active via Nous subscription` / `  Browser         ○ active via Browser Use key`. "Tools marked \"active via Nous subscription\" are going through the gateway. Anything else is using your own keys."
- **Config / env:** Selection keys `web.backend`, `image_gen.provider`, `tts.provider`, `stt.provider`, `browser.cloud_provider` (all accept `nous`); decline memory `tool_gateway_declined_tools`; self-hosting env `TOOL_GATEWAY_DOMAIN`, `TOOL_GATEWAY_SCHEME`, `TOOL_GATEWAY_USER_TOKEN`, `FIRECRAWL_GATEWAY_URL`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "**You don't have to log in first.** With `hermes tools`, the Nous-managed backends (Web search, Image, Video, TTS, Browser) are always listed, even if you've never signed into Nous Portal. Select one and Hermes runs the Portal login right there… This path only logs you in and turns on the one tool you picked — it does **not** switch your inference provider, and it does **not** prompt you to enable the gateway for every other tool." (`tool-gateway.md:58`)
- **Rebuild notes:** One selection key per tool category, a login-on-demand picker, and strict "stored selection wins over credential presence". A better version would show live per-tool spend next to each row in the picker.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`tool_gateway_declined_tools` at `hermes_cli/config.py:2238`; all four env vars registered at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:4433-4460` and listed at `hermes_cli/config.py:1368-1369`).

- **Surface:** Tool + Toolset
- **Where:** Docs title **"Tools & Toolsets"** (`sidebar_position: 1`), description *"Overview of Hermes Agent's tools — what's available, how toolsets work, and terminal backends"*.
- **What it does:** "Tools are functions that extend the agent's capabilities. They're organized into logical **toolsets** that can be enabled or disabled per platform." (`tools.md:9`)
- **How it works:** Category table (`tools.md:21-31`), all 9 rows verbatim: **Web** — `web_search`, `web_extract` — "Search the web and extract page content."; **X Search** — `x_search` — "Search X (Twitter) posts and threads via xAI's built-in `x_search` Responses tool — gated on xAI credentials (SuperGrok OAuth or `XAI_API_KEY`); off by default, opt in via `hermes tools` → 🐦 X (Twitter) Search."; **Terminal & Files** — `terminal`, `process`, `read_file`, `patch` — "Execute commands and manipulate files."; **Browser** — `browser_navigate`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_vision` — "Interactive browser automation with text and vision support."; **Media** — `vision_analyze`, `image_generate`, `text_to_speech` — "Multimodal analysis and generation."; **Agent orchestration** — `todo`, `clarify`, `execute_code`, `delegate_task` — "Planning, clarification, code execution, and subagent delegation."; **Memory & recall** — `memory`, `session_search` — "Persistent memory and session search."; **Automation** — `cronjob` — "Scheduled tasks with create/list/update/pause/resume/run/remove actions. Outbound delivery is handled by cron's own delivery, the `hermes send` CLI, and the gateway notifier — not by an agent-callable tool."; **Integrations** — `ha_*`, MCP server tools — "Home Assistant, MCP, and other integrations."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (index page).
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::note **Honcho cross-session memory** is available as a memory provider plugin (`plugins/memory/honcho/`), not as a built-in toolset." (`tools.md:15-17`) ":::tip Nous Tool Gateway Paid Nous Portal subscribers can use web search, image generation, TTS, and browser automation through the **Tool Gateway** — no separate API keys needed." (`tools.md:35-37`) Authoritative registry lives in `/reference/tools-reference` and `/reference/toolsets-reference` (outside this shard — see `## Handoffs`).
- **Rebuild notes:** Group tools into named toolsets that are the unit of enable/disable, per platform. A better version would generate this table from the registry so it cannot drift.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (the live registry holds 83 tools across 59 toolsets — `hermes_inv/tools_full.json`, `hermes_inv/tools_toolsets.json`).

### Using toolsets (`--toolsets`, `hermes tools`)  `id: docs-features.tools-using-toolsets`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Using Toolsets"**.
- **What it does:** Shows how to select toolsets for a run and how to configure them interactively.
- **How it works:** Documented commands verbatim (`tools.md:41-49`): `hermes chat --toolsets "web,terminal"` — "# Use specific toolsets"; `hermes tools` — "# See all available tools"; `hermes tools` — "# Configure tools per platform (interactive)".
- **Inputs / options:** Documented common toolsets, all 22 named (`tools.md:52`): `web`, `search`, `terminal`, `file`, `browser`, `vision`, `image_gen`, `skills`, `tts`, `todo`, `memory`, `session_search`, `cronjob`, `code_execution`, `delegation`, `clarify`, `homeassistant`, `messaging`, `spotify`, `discord`, `discord_admin`, `debugging`, `safe` (23 tokens listed). Also named: platform presets `hermes-cli`, `hermes-telegram`, and "dynamic MCP toolsets like `mcp-<server>`" (`tools.md:54`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Persisted per-platform toolset selection.
- **Config / env:** Per-platform toolset config.
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** A comma-separated CLI flag plus a curses picker writing the same config. A better version would validate unknown toolset names at parse time with a suggestion.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (all named toolsets appear in the live 59-toolset dump).

### Tool result annotations — signal deaths  `id: docs-features.tools-signal-annotations`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Tool result annotations"**, first bullet.
- **What it does:** "**Signal deaths are explained.** When a terminal command is killed by a signal, the result carries a human-readable note instead of a bare numeric code."
- **How it works:** Documented example verbatim (`tools.md:60`): exit `-9`/`137` becomes "terminated by signal 9: SIGKILL — often the kernel OOM killer on memory exhaustion, or an explicit kill -9", "and segfaults, aborts, SIGTERM, broken pipes, and CPU/file-size limits are labeled the same way. Negative codes (subprocess semantics) are stated definitively; the shell's `128+signum` convention is hedged with \"usually\" since an application can legitimately exit with those codes."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** An explanatory note in the terminal tool result.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** The `128+signum` hedge is deliberate — an application may legitimately exit 137.
- **Rebuild notes:** Signal→description map with two confidence levels (negative code = definite, 128+n = "usually"). A better version would also surface the container's OOM counter when available.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `tools` shard for the terminal result formatter).

### Tool result annotations — UTF-16 transcoding  `id: docs-features.tools-utf16`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Tool result annotations"**, second bullet.
- **What it does:** "**UTF-16 text files are transcoded, not refused.**"
- **How it works:** "`read_file` detects UTF-16 (BOM or byte-pattern heuristic, either endianness — common for Windows Notepad files and PowerShell `>` redirects) and transcodes it to UTF-8 for display instead of flagging the file as binary. The result includes a hint disclosing the conversion; edits via `patch`/`write_file` re-encode as UTF-8." (`tools.md:61`)
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** UTF-8 text plus a conversion hint; UTF-8 re-encoding on write.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Files over 10 MB and genuinely binary files still get the binary-file refusal."
- **Rebuild notes:** BOM sniff → byte-pattern heuristic → transcode + disclose. A better version would preserve the original encoding on write unless asked to convert.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Terminal backends table  `id: docs-features.tools-terminal-backends`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Terminal Backends"**; `terminal.backend` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`.
- **What it does:** "The terminal tool can execute commands in different environments."
- **How it works:** Complete table (`tools.md:67-75`), all 7 backends verbatim: `local` — "Run on your machine (default)" — "Development, trusted tasks"; `docker` — "Isolated containers" — "Security, reproducibility"; `ssh` — "Remote server" — "Sandboxing, keep agent away from its own code"; `singularity` — "HPC containers" — "Cluster computing, rootless"; `modal` — "Cloud execution" — "Serverless, scale"; `daytona` — "Cloud sandbox workspace" — "Persistent remote dev environments"; `vercel_sandbox` — "Vercel Sandbox cloud microVM" — "Cloud execution with snapshot-backed filesystem persistence".
- **Inputs / options:** Config block (`tools.md:79-85`): `terminal.backend: local` ("or: docker, ssh, singularity, modal, daytona, vercel_sandbox"), `terminal.cwd: "."` ("Working directory"), `terminal.timeout: 180` ("Command timeout in seconds").
- **Outputs / side effects:** Where commands run.
- **Config / env:** `terminal.backend` (default `"local"`, `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:389`), `terminal.cwd`, `terminal.timeout`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Container resource keys are "ignored for local/ssh" (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:484`).
- **Rebuild notes:** One `backend` key selecting a driver, with a shared command interface. A better version would allow per-task backend overrides without a config edit.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (all 7 backend names present in the config defaults and their comments).

### Shell startup files and non-interactive commands  `id: docs-features.tools-shell-init`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Shell startup files and non-interactive commands"**.
- **What it does:** Explains why heavy shell rc files break agent terminal calls and gives the fix.
- **How it works:** Three documented failure modes (`tools.md:91-93`): "**Slow init (`nvm`, version managers, network-touching prompts):** the classic `nvm.sh` sourcing adds noticeable latency to *every* shell start… Multi-second rc files turn a quick `git status` into a timeout risk."; "**TTY-expecting blocks:** anything in `.bashrc`/`.zshrc` that prompts, runs `tmux`/`screen` attach, calls `read`, or prints a menu will hang a non-interactive shell."; "**Unconditional output:** rc files that `echo` banners pollute every command's output the agent has to parse." The fix, verbatim (`tools.md:98-107`): `case $- in` / `  *i*) ;;      # interactive: continue` / `  *) return;;  # non-interactive: stop here` / `esac` then `export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"` / `[ -s "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" ] && \. "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"`.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, `.zprofile`, `.zshenv`, `PATH`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Zsh users: put login-only setup in `.zprofile` and interactive-only setup in `.zshrc`; keep `.zshenv` minimal, since it runs for every shell including non-interactive ones. If the agent genuinely needs a tool that only your rc file puts on `PATH`, export the `PATH` change *above* the guard (path exports are cheap) or symlink the binary into `~/.local/bin`." "If agent terminal commands hang or time out immediately after working in your own terminal, your shell init is the first suspect." (`tools.md:109-111`)
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a (environment guidance). A better version would detect a slow/hanging rc at first use and warn once with this exact advice.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (guidance only).

### Docker terminal backend (persistent container)  `id: docs-features.tools-docker-backend`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Docker Backend"**.
- **What it does:** "**One persistent container, shared across the whole process.**"
- **How it works:** "Hermes starts a single long-lived container on first use (`docker run -d ... sleep infinity`) and routes every terminal, file, and `execute_code` call through `docker exec` into that same container. Working-directory changes, installed packages, environment tweaks, and files written to `/workspace` all carry over from one tool call to the next, across `/new`, `/reset`, and `delegate_task` subagents, for the lifetime of the Hermes process. The container is stopped and removed on shutdown." (`tools.md:121`)
- **Inputs / options:** `terminal.backend: docker`, `terminal.docker_image: python:3.11-slim`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A long-lived container; `/workspace` state.
- **Config / env:** `terminal.docker_image`, `terminal.container_persistent`, plus (from code) `terminal.docker_volumes` (default `[]`, "Each entry is \"host_path:container_path\"", `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:489-497`) and `terminal.docker_mount_cwd_to_workspace` (default `False`, "Explicit opt-in: mount the host cwd into /workspace for Docker sessions. Default off because passing host directories into a sandbox weakens isolation.", `:498-500`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** "This means the Docker backend behaves like a persistent sandbox VM, not a fresh container per command. If you `pip install foo` once, it's there for the rest of the session." Full lifecycle details live in `../configuration.md#docker-backend` (outside this shard).
- **Rebuild notes:** One container per process, `docker exec` per call, teardown on shutdown. A better version would offer per-session containers with copy-on-write from a warm base.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### SSH terminal backend  `id: docs-features.tools-ssh-backend`
- **Surface:** Config + Env
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"SSH Backend"**.
- **What it does:** "Recommended for security — agent can't modify its own code."
- **How it works:** `terminal.backend: ssh` plus three env vars in `~/.hermes/.env` (`tools.md:135-137`): `TERMINAL_SSH_HOST=my-server.example.com`, `TERMINAL_SSH_USER=myuser`, `TERMINAL_SSH_KEY=~/.ssh/id_rsa`.
- **Inputs / options:** The three env vars above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Commands run on the remote host.
- **Config / env:** `terminal.backend`, `TERMINAL_SSH_HOST`, `TERMINAL_SSH_USER`, `TERMINAL_SSH_KEY`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Container resource keys are ignored for `ssh`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Persistent SSH connection with a shared remote working directory. A better version would support a jump host and agent forwarding options.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Vercel Sandbox terminal backend  `id: docs-features.tools-vercel-backend`
- **Surface:** CLI + Config + Env
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Vercel Sandbox"**.
- **What it does:** Runs terminal commands in a Vercel Sandbox cloud microVM with snapshot-backed persistence.
- **How it works:** Setup verbatim (`tools.md:162-164`): `pip install 'hermes-agent[vercel]'`, `hermes config set terminal.backend vercel_sandbox`, `hermes config set terminal.vercel_runtime node24`. "Authenticate with all three of `VERCEL_TOKEN`, `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID`, and `VERCEL_TEAM_ID`. This access-token setup is the supported path for deployments and normal long-running Hermes processes on Render, Railway, Docker, and similar hosts. Supported runtimes are `node24`, `node22`, and `python3.13`; Hermes defaults to `/vercel/sandbox` as the remote workspace root." (`tools.md:167`)
- **Inputs / options:** `terminal.vercel_runtime` ∈ {`node24`, `node22`, `python3.13`}; env `VERCEL_TOKEN`, `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID`, `VERCEL_TEAM_ID`, `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN`. One-off dev forms (`tools.md:172`, `:178`): `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN="$(vc project token <project-name>)" hermes chat` and, from a linked project directory, `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN="$(vc project token)" hermes chat`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A remote microVM; snapshots when `container_persistent: true`.
- **Config / env:** As above; `terminal.container_disk`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "With `container_persistent: true`, Hermes uses Vercel snapshots to preserve filesystem state across sandbox recreation for the same task. This can include Hermes-synced credentials, skills, and cache files inside the sandbox. Snapshots do not preserve live processes, PID space, or the same live sandbox identity." (`tools.md:181`) "Background terminal commands use Hermes' generic non-local process flow: spawn, poll, wait, log, and kill work through the normal process tool while the sandbox is alive, but Hermes does not provide native Vercel detached-process recovery after cleanup or restart." (`tools.md:183`) "Leave `container_disk` unset or at the shared default `51200`; custom disk sizing is unsupported for Vercel Sandbox and will fail diagnostics/backend creation." (`tools.md:185`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Cloud microVM driver + snapshot save/restore keyed by task. A better version would surface snapshot age and size in `hermes status`.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`terminal.vercel_runtime` present at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:481-482`; `container_disk` default `51200` at `:487`).

### Container resource keys  `id: docs-features.tools-container-resources`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Container Resources"**.
- **What it does:** "Configure CPU, memory, disk, and persistence for all container backends."
- **How it works:** Documented block (`tools.md:192-197`), all 4 keys verbatim: `container_cpu: 1` — "CPU cores (default: 1)"; `container_memory: 5120` — "Memory in MB (default: 5GB)"; `container_disk: 51200` — "Disk in MB (default: 50GB)"; `container_persistent: true` — "Persist filesystem across sessions (default: true)". Code defaults match exactly (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:485-488`), with the scope comment "docker, singularity, modal, daytona, vercel_sandbox — ignored for local/ssh" (`:484`).
- **Inputs / options:** The four keys above; applies to `docker`, `singularity`, `modal`, `daytona`, `vercel_sandbox`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Container creation parameters.
- **Config / env:** `terminal.container_cpu|container_memory|container_disk|container_persistent`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "When `container_persistent: true`, installed packages, files, and config survive across sessions." Ignored for `local` and `ssh`.
- **Rebuild notes:** One resource block shared by every container driver. A better version would validate the request against the backend's real limits before creation.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (defaults byte-identical).

### Container security hardening  `id: docs-features.tools-container-security`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Container Security"**.
- **What it does:** "All container backends run with security hardening."
- **How it works:** All six documented properties (`tools.md:206-211`): "Read-only root filesystem (Docker)"; "All Linux capabilities dropped"; "No privilege escalation"; "PID limits (256 processes)"; "Full namespace isolation"; "Persistent workspace via volumes, not writable root layer".
- **Inputs / options:** `terminal.docker_forward_env` (explicit env allowlist).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Hardened container flags.
- **Config / env:** `terminal.docker_forward_env`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Docker can optionally receive an explicit env allowlist via `terminal.docker_forward_env`, but forwarded variables are visible to commands inside the container and should be treated as exposed to that session." (`tools.md:213`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Drop caps, read-only root, PID cap, no-new-privileges, named volumes. A better version would add seccomp/AppArmor profiles and an egress allowlist by default (the code already has an opt-in egress lockdown, `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:501`).
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Background process management (`process` tool)  `id: docs-features.tools-background-processes`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Background Process Management"**.
- **What it does:** Start background terminal commands and manage them with the `process` tool.
- **How it works:** Documented calls verbatim (`tools.md:220-229`): `terminal(command="pytest -v tests/", background=true)` → `{"session_id": "proc_abc123", "pid": 12345}`; then all six process actions: `process(action="list")` — "Show all running processes"; `process(action="poll", session_id="proc_abc123")` — "Check status"; `process(action="wait", session_id="proc_abc123")` — "Block until done"; `process(action="log", session_id="proc_abc123")` — "Full output"; `process(action="kill", session_id="proc_abc123")` — "Terminate"; `process(action="write", session_id="proc_abc123", data="y")` — "Send input".
- **Inputs / options:** `terminal(background=true)`, `terminal(pty=true)`; `process(action=list|poll|wait|log|kill|write, session_id, data)`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A tracked background session with a pid.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "PTY mode (`pty=true`) enables interactive CLI tools like Codex and Claude Code." (`tools.md:232`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Session registry keyed by `proc_*` id with poll/wait/log/kill/write. A better version would stream logs incrementally rather than returning the full buffer.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `tools` shard for the `process` schema).

### Sudo support  `id: docs-features.tools-sudo`
- **Surface:** CLI + Env
- **Where:** `tools.md` → **"Sudo Support"**.
- **What it does:** "If a command needs sudo, you'll be prompted for your password (cached for the session). Or set `SUDO_PASSWORD` in `~/.hermes/.env`." (`tools.md:236`)
- **How it works:** Interactive prompt with session-scoped caching, or the env var.
- **Inputs / options:** `SUDO_PASSWORD`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Elevated command execution.
- **Config / env:** `SUDO_PASSWORD`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::warning On messaging platforms, if sudo fails, the output includes a tip to add `SUDO_PASSWORD` to `~/.hermes/.env`." (`tools.md:238-240`) — because there is no interactive prompt on those surfaces.
- **Rebuild notes:** Prompt on interactive surfaces, env var elsewhere, cache per session in memory only. A better version would use a per-command approval instead of a cached password.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

## Page: `batch-processing.md` — Batch Processing

### Batch Processing (`batch_runner.py`)  `id: docs-features.batch-processing`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `python batch_runner.py …` from the repo root. Docs title **"Batch Processing"** (`sidebar_position: 12`), description *"Generate agent trajectories at scale — parallel processing, checkpointing, and toolset distributions"*.
- **What it does:** "Batch processing lets you run the Hermes agent across hundreds or thousands of prompts in parallel, generating structured trajectory data. This is primarily used for **training data generation** — producing ShareGPT-format trajectories with tool usage statistics that can be used for fine-tuning or evaluation." (`batch-processing.md:9`)
- **How it works:** "The batch runner (`batch_runner.py`) processes a JSONL dataset of prompts, running each through a full agent session with tool access. Each prompt gets its own isolated environment. The output is structured trajectory data with full conversation history, tool call statistics, and reasoning coverage metrics." (`batch-processing.md:13`) Code: `batch_runner.py` exists at the repo root; its module docstring carries the same three usage examples (`batch_runner.py:14-20`), the runner constructor takes `dataset_file`, `num_workers=4`, `ephemeral_system_prompt=None`, `log_prefix_chars=100`, `max_samples=None` (`batch_runner.py:576-646`), and unknown distributions raise `ValueError(f"Unknown distribution: {distribution}. Available: {list(list_distributions().keys())}")` (`batch_runner.py:650`).
- **Inputs / options:** Three documented invocations verbatim (`batch-processing.md:18-34`): basic — `python batch_runner.py --dataset_file=data/prompts.jsonl --batch_size=10 --run_name=my_first_run --model=anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6 --num_workers=4`; resume — `python batch_runner.py --dataset_file=data/prompts.jsonl --batch_size=10 --run_name=my_first_run --resume`; list distributions — `python batch_runner.py --list_distributions`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `data/<run_name>/` (see the output-format entry).
- **Config / env:** `--api_key` falls back to an env var.
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::tip Predictable cost at scale Batch runs spin up many concurrent agent sessions… A Nous Portal subscription bundles model access plus web search, image gen, TTS, and cloud browsers under one bill… Set up with `hermes setup --portal`, then point `--model` at a Nous model." (`batch-processing.md:37-39`)
- **Rebuild notes:** JSONL in → parallel agent sessions → JSONL trajectories out, with checkpointing between batches. A better version would stream results to a datastore and expose live progress rather than only end-of-run statistics.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`batch_runner.py` present with matching parameter names; note the docstring's default for `log_prefix_chars` says "default: 20" at `batch_runner.py:613` while the signature and the docs both say `100` — a code-comment drift).

### Batch dataset format  `id: docs-features.batch-dataset-format`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `batch-processing.md` → **"Dataset Format"**.
- **What it does:** Defines the JSONL input schema.
- **How it works:** "The input dataset is a JSONL file (one JSON object per line). Each entry must have a `prompt` field" (`batch-processing.md:43`). Example lines verbatim (`batch-processing.md:46-48`): `{"prompt": "Write a Python function that finds the longest palindromic substring"}`; `{"prompt": "Create a REST API endpoint for user authentication using Flask"}`; `{"prompt": "Debug this error: TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable NoneType object"}`.
- **Inputs / options:** Required: `prompt`. Optional (`batch-processing.md:52-53`): "`image` or `docker_image`: A container image to use for this prompt's sandbox (works with Docker, Modal, and Singularity backends)"; "`cwd`: Working directory override for the task's terminal session".
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "The batch runner verifies Docker images are accessible before running each prompt." (`batch-processing.md:230`)
- **Rebuild notes:** One JSON object per line with a required prompt and optional per-task environment overrides. A better version would allow per-entry `toolsets` and expected-answer fields for eval runs.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Batch configuration options (core flags)  `id: docs-features.batch-config-flags`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `batch-processing.md` → **"Configuration Options"**.
- **What it does:** The 12 core CLI flags.
- **How it works:** Complete table (`batch-processing.md:57-71`), all 12 rows verbatim: `--dataset_file` (required) — "Path to JSONL dataset"; `--batch_size` (required) — "Prompts per batch"; `--run_name` (required) — "Name for this run (used for output dir and checkpointing)"; `--distribution` (default `"default"`) — "Toolset distribution to sample from"; `--model` (default `claude-sonnet-4.6`) — "Model to use"; `--base_url` (default `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`) — "API base URL"; `--api_key` (default: env var) — "API key for model"; `--max_turns` (default `10`) — "Maximum tool-calling iterations per prompt"; `--num_workers` (default `4`) — "Parallel worker processes"; `--resume` (default `false`) — "Resume from checkpoint"; `--verbose` (default `false`) — "Enable verbose logging"; `--max_samples` (default: all) — "Only process first N samples from dataset"; `--max_tokens` (default: model default) — "Maximum tokens per model response". (13 rows counting `--max_tokens`.)
- **Inputs / options:** As above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `--api_key` env fallback.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `--max_samples` truncates the dataset before batching (`batch_runner.py:664-666`).
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`num_workers=4`, `max_samples`, `log_prefix_chars=100` confirmed in the runner signature at `batch_runner.py:584-646`).

### Toolset distributions (sampling)  `id: docs-features.batch-distributions`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `batch-processing.md` → **"Toolset Distributions"**; `--distribution`, `--list_distributions`.
- **What it does:** "Each prompt gets a randomly sampled set of toolsets from a **distribution**. This ensures training data covers diverse tool combinations." (`batch-processing.md:99`)
- **How it works:** "In the current implementation, distributions assign a probability to **each individual toolset**. The sampler flips each toolset independently, then guarantees that at least one toolset is enabled. This is different from a hand-authored table of prebuilt combinations." (`batch-processing.md:101`) Code: `list_distributions` is imported at `batch_runner.py:51` and used in the unknown-distribution error at `:650`; the docstring names `--distribution=image_gen` as an example (`batch_runner.py:20`).
- **Inputs / options:** `--distribution <name>` (default `"default"`), `--list_distributions`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Per-prompt toolset selection recorded in `toolsets_used`.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** At least one toolset is always enabled; unknown names raise a `ValueError` listing the available ones.
- **Rebuild notes:** Independent Bernoulli per toolset + a non-empty guarantee. A better version would support explicit combination tables and stratified sampling.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.
