## Page: `curator.md` — Curator

### Curator (background skill maintenance)  `id: docs-features.curator`
- **Surface:** Core + CLI
- **Where:** Automatic background pass; `hermes curator …`; `/curator` slash command. Docs title **"Curator"** (`sidebar_position: 3`), description *"Background maintenance for agent-created skills — usage tracking, staleness, archival, and LLM-driven review"*.
- **What it does:** "The curator is a background maintenance pass for **agent-created skills**. It tracks how often each skill is viewed, used, and patched, moves long-unused skills through `active → stale → archived` states, and periodically spawns a short auxiliary-model review that proposes consolidations or patches drift." (`curator.md:9`)
- **How it works:** Rationale (`curator.md:11`): "Every time the agent solves a novel problem and saves a skill, that skill lands in `~/.hermes/skills/`. Without maintenance, you end up with dozens of narrow near-duplicates that pollute the catalog and waste tokens." Scope (`curator.md:13`): "By default (`prune_builtins: true`) the curator can archive **unused bundled built-in skills** (shipped with the repo) after `archive_after_days` of non-use… Hub-installed skills (from agentskills.io) are always off-limits. Set `curator.prune_builtins: false` to restore the old agent-created-only behavior… The curator also **never auto-deletes** — the worst outcome is archival into `~/.hermes/skills/.archive/`, which is recoverable."
- **Inputs / options:** See the CLI entry (23 documented commands).
- **Outputs / side effects:** State transitions in `.usage.json`; moves into `.archive/`; snapshots; ledger entries; per-run reports.
- **Config / env:** `curator.enabled|interval_hours|min_idle_hours|stale_after_days|archive_after_days|consolidate|prune_builtins|archive_ttl_days|backup.enabled|backup.keep`; `auxiliary.curator.*`; `skills.ledger`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Tracks issue #7816 (`curator.md:15`).
- **Rebuild notes:** Deterministic inactivity pruning (always on) + an opt-in LLM consolidation pass, both fronted by snapshots and an append-only ledger. A better version would rank consolidation candidates by measured token savings.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `skills-core` shard for the curator implementation modules; `agent/curator.py` and `agent/curator_backup.py` exist in the tree).

### Curator trigger conditions and two-phase run  `id: docs-features.curator-run`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"How it runs"**.
- **What it does:** Explains when the curator fires and what a run does.
- **How it works:** "The curator is triggered by an inactivity check, not a cron daemon. On CLI session start, and on a recurring tick inside the gateway's cron-ticker thread, Hermes checks whether: 1. Enough time has passed since the last curator run (`interval_hours`, default **7 days**), and 2. The agent has been idle long enough (`min_idle_hours`, default **2 hours**). If both are true, it spawns a background fork of `AIAgent` — the same pattern used by the memory/skill self-improvement nudges. The fork runs in its own prompt cache and never touches the active conversation." (`curator.md:21-27`) Two phases (`curator.md:35-41`): "1. **Automatic transitions** (deterministic, no LLM). Skills unused for `stale_after_days` (30) become `stale`; skills unused for `archive_after_days` (90) are moved to `~/.hermes/skills/.archive/`. This is the always-on pruning behavior — it runs whenever the curator is enabled, with no aux-model cost."; "2. **LLM consolidation** (single aux-model pass with a high iteration ceiling — a full curation sweep typically takes 50–100 API calls) — **OFF by default**. When `curator.consolidate: true`, the forked agent surveys the agent-created skills, can read any of them with `skill_view`, and decides per-skill whether to keep, patch (via `skill_manage`), consolidate overlapping ones into class-level umbrellas, or archive via the terminal tool."
- **Inputs / options:** `interval_hours`, `min_idle_hours`, `consolidate`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** State transitions; optional LLM-driven edits.
- **Config / env:** As above.
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::info First-run behavior On a brand-new install (or the first time a pre-curator install ticks after `hermes update`), the curator **does not run immediately**. The first observation seeds `last_run_at` to \"now\" and defers the first real pass by one full `interval_hours`. This gives you a full interval to review your skill library, pin anything important, or opt out entirely before the curator ever touches it. If you want to see what the curator *would* do before it runs for real, run `hermes curator run --dry-run`." (`curator.md:29-33`) Auto-transition exemptions (`curator.md:36-38`): "**Pinned skills** and **skills referenced by any cron job** (including paused/disabled jobs) are skipped entirely… Consolidation also rewrites cron skill references when it merges umbrellas."; "**Never-used skills** (`use_count == 0`) get a grace floor: they are not archived until they are at least `stale_after_days` old. Zero uses is absence of evidence, not proof the skill is disposable." Package rule (`curator.md:41`): "Consolidation treats a skill as a full package: if a skill has `references/`, `templates/`, `scripts/`, `assets/`, or relative links to those paths, the curator must either keep it standalone, re-home the needed support files and rewrite paths, or archive the entire package unchanged — not flatten only `SKILL.md` into another skill's `references/` file." ":::info Consolidation is opt-in… Turn it on with `curator.consolidate: true`, or run it once on demand with `hermes curator run --consolidate`." (`curator.md:43-45`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Idle-gated background work with a deferred first run — the deferral is what makes an automatic destructive-ish feature acceptable.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Curator configuration keys  `id: docs-features.curator-config`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `config.yaml` → `curator:`.
- **What it does:** Seven documented top-level keys (plus backup and TTL sub-keys).
- **How it works:** Documented defaults block (`curator.md:53-61`), verbatim: `enabled: true`; `interval_hours: 168` ("7 days"); `min_idle_hours: 2`; `stale_after_days: 30`; `archive_after_days: 90`; `consolidate: false` ("LLM umbrella-building pass — opt-in (prune-only by default)"); `prune_builtins: true` ("archive unused bundled built-in skills too (hub skills always exempt)"). Plus `curator.archive_ttl_days: 180` ("0 (default) = never purge", `curator.md:190-192`) and `curator.backup: {enabled: true, keep: 5}` (`curator.md:139-142`).
- **Inputs / options:** As above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Curator behavior.
- **Config / env:** `curator.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "To disable entirely, set `curator.enabled: false`. To keep the always-on pruning but opt into LLM consolidation, set `curator.consolidate: true`." (`curator.md:63`) "All settings live in `config.yaml` under `curator:` (not `.env` — this isn't a secret)."
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Curator auxiliary model routing (`auxiliary.curator`)  `id: docs-features.curator-aux-model`
- **Surface:** Config + CLI + Web dashboard
- **Where:** `hermes model` → "Auxiliary models — side-task routing" → "Curator"; dashboard **Models** tab; `config.yaml` → `auxiliary.curator`.
- **What it does:** Routes the LLM review pass to a cheaper model.
- **How it works:** "The curator's LLM review pass is a regular auxiliary task slot — `auxiliary.curator` — alongside Vision, Compression, Session Search, etc. \"Auto\" means \"use my main chat model\"; override the slot to pin a specific provider + model for the review pass instead." (`curator.md:67`) CLI path verbatim (`curator.md:71-73`): `hermes model` → "\"Auxiliary models — side-task routing\"" → "pick \"Curator\" → pick provider → pick model". Config equivalent (`curator.md:81-86`): `auxiliary: {curator: {provider: openrouter, model: google/gemini-3-flash-preview, timeout: 600}}` with the comment "generous — reviews can take several minutes".
- **Inputs / options:** `auxiliary.curator.provider|model|timeout|base_url|api_key|extra_body`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Which model runs the review.
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.curator.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::note Legacy config Earlier releases used a one-off `curator.auxiliary.{provider,model}` block. That path still works but emits a deprecation log line — please migrate to `auxiliary.curator` above so the curator shares the same plumbing (`hermes model`, dashboard Models tab, `base_url`, `api_key`, `timeout`, `extra_body`) as every other aux task." (`curator.md:90-92`) "Leaving `provider: auto` (the default) routes the review pass through whatever your main chat model is."
- **Rebuild notes:** Fold one-off task config into a shared aux-task slot system. A better version would auto-migrate the legacy block on write.
- **Verification:** **partial** — implemented as documented, with a legacy path still accepted and deprecation-logged.

### `hermes curator` CLI (23 commands)  `id: docs-features.curator-cli`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"CLI"**; also available as the `/curator` slash command "inside a running session (CLI or gateway platforms)" (`curator.md:148`).
- **What it does:** Every documented curator command.
- **How it works:** Complete list verbatim (`curator.md:94-121`), all 23 lines: `hermes curator status` — "last run, counts, pinned list, LRU top 5"; `hermes curator run` — "trigger a run now (blocks until done). Prune-only unless curator.consolidate: true"; `hermes curator run --consolidate` — "force the LLM consolidation pass on for this run, overriding the config default"; `hermes curator run --background` — "fire-and-forget: start the run in a background thread"; `hermes curator run --dry-run` — "preview only — report without any mutations"; `hermes curator backup` — "take a manual snapshot of ~/.hermes/skills/"; `hermes curator rollback` — "restore from the newest snapshot"; `hermes curator rollback --list` — "list available snapshots"; `hermes curator rollback --id <ts>` — "restore a specific snapshot"; `hermes curator rollback -y` — "skip the confirmation prompt"; `hermes curator pause` — "stop runs until resumed"; `hermes curator resume`; `hermes curator pin <skill>` — "never auto-transition this skill"; `hermes curator unpin <skill>`; `hermes curator adopt <skill>` — "hand an unmanaged skill to the curator"; `hermes curator adopt --all-unmanaged` — "hand over every unmanaged skill"; `hermes curator list-unmanaged` — "itemize skills with no provenance marker"; `hermes curator restore <skill>` — "move an archived skill back to active"; `hermes curator list-archived` — "list skills currently in ~/.hermes/skills/.archive/"; `hermes curator archive <skill>` — "manually archive a single skill now"; `hermes curator prune [--days N]` — "bulk-archive agent-created skills idle >= N days (default 90)"; `hermes curator ledger` — "list the per-mutation audit ledger (all actors)"; `hermes curator ledger --skill <name> --limit 50` — "filter/paginate ledger entries"; `hermes curator rollback <entry-id>` — "undo a single mutation from the ledger"; `hermes curator purge [--days N] [--dry-run]` — "delete archived skills older than the TTL (explicit only)". Also documented separately: `hermes curator backup --reason "before-refactor"`, `hermes curator adopt --all-unmanaged --dry-run`, `hermes curator adopt --all-unmanaged --yes`.
- **Inputs / options:** As above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Snapshots, archive moves, ledger entries.
- **Config / env:** `curator.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `cli-*` shards for the `hermes curator` argparse tree).

### Curator backups and whole-run rollback  `id: docs-features.curator-backups`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"Backups and rollback"**.
- **What it does:** "Before every real curator pass, Hermes takes a tar.gz snapshot of `~/.hermes/skills/` at `~/.hermes/skills/.curator_backups/<utc-iso>/skills.tar.gz`." (`curator.md:125`)
- **How it works:** "If a pass archives or consolidates something you didn't want touched, you can undo the whole run with one command." Commands (`curator.md:128-130`): `hermes curator rollback` ("restore newest snapshot (with confirmation)"), `hermes curator rollback -y` ("skip the prompt"), `hermes curator rollback --list` ("see all snapshots with reason + size"). "The rollback itself is reversible: before replacing the skills tree, Hermes takes another snapshot tagged `pre-rollback to <target-id>`, so a mistaken rollback can be undone by rolling forward to that one with `--id`." (`curator.md:133`)
- **Inputs / options:** `--list`, `--id <ts>`, `-y`, `--reason "<text>"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** tar.gz snapshots under `.curator_backups/`; `manifest.json` per snapshot carrying `--reason`.
- **Config / env:** `curator.backup.enabled` (default true), `curator.backup.keep` (default 5).
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Snapshots are pruned to `curator.backup.keep` (default 5) to keep disk usage bounded." "Set `curator.backup.enabled: false` to disable automatic snapshotting. The manual `hermes curator backup` command still works when backups are disabled only if you set `enabled: true` first — the flag gates both paths symmetrically so there's no way to accidentally skip the pre-run snapshot on mutating runs." (`curator.md:144`) "`hermes curator status` also lists the five least-recently-used skills — a quick way to see what's likely to become stale next." (`curator.md:146`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Snapshot before every mutating pass, make rollback itself snapshotted, and gate both paths with one flag. A near-ideal safety design to copy.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`agent/curator_backup.py` exists).

### Curator audit ledger and single-edit rollback  `id: docs-features.curator-ledger`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"Audit ledger and single-edit rollback"**; `~/.hermes/skills/.curator_ledger.jsonl`.
- **What it does:** "Every skill mutation — curator auto-transitions, agent `skill_manage` calls, and your own CLI archive/restore/purge — appends one entry to the append-only JSONL ledger." (`curator.md:152`)
- **How it works:** Entry fields, all four verbatim (`curator.md:154-157`): "**actor** — `curator` (background review fork / auto-transitions), `agent` (foreground agent tool calls), or `user` (CLI commands)"; "**action** — `create`, `edit`, `patch`, `delete`, `write_file`, `remove_file`, `archive`, `restore`, `purge`, `rollback`"; "**evidence** — delete intent (`absorbed_into` for consolidations, empty for prunes, and whether the recoverable-archive path handled it), triggering session id when available"; "**before/after** — per-file `{path, sha256}` manifests. File contents are stored content-addressed (deduped by hash) under `~/.hermes/.curator_backups/blobs/`, so a hundred entries touching the same unchanged file cost one blob."
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes curator ledger` ("newest 20 entries"), `hermes curator ledger --skill my-skill --limit 50`, `hermes curator rollback <entry-id>` ("restore that one mutation's before-state").
- **Outputs / side effects:** JSONL entries; content-addressed blobs.
- **Config / env:** `skills.ledger: false` to disable.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Single-entry rollback restores exactly the files that mutation touched (and removes files it created) from the blob store — nothing else in the skills tree moves. Like whole-tree rollback, it takes a safety ledger entry of the current state first and **fails closed**: if the safety capture can't be written, nothing is changed. Because foreground deletes are ledgered too, `hermes curator rollback <entry-id>` can resurrect a hard-deleted skill." (`curator.md:165`) "The ledger is telemetry, never a gate — if writing an entry fails, the mutation still goes through." (`curator.md:167`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Content-addressed blobs + per-mutation manifests give cheap single-edit undo. The "telemetry never gates, but rollback fails closed" split is the right asymmetry.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Curator archive TTL purge  `id: docs-features.curator-purge`
- **Surface:** CLI + Config
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"Archive TTL purge"**.
- **What it does:** "Archived skills are kept forever by default. If you want `~/.hermes/skills/.archive/` bounded, set a TTL and purge explicitly — purging never runs automatically, and every purged skill is captured into the ledger (with blobs) first, so even a purge leaves an auditable, recoverable trail." (`curator.md:188`)
- **How it works:** `curator.archive_ttl_days: 180` — "0 (default) = never purge". Commands (`curator.md:195-197`): `hermes curator purge --dry-run` ("preview what would be deleted"), `hermes curator purge` ("delete archives older than the TTL (with confirmation)"), `hermes curator purge --days 90` ("one-off TTL override").
- **Inputs / options:** `--dry-run`, `--days N`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Deletion of archived skills, ledgered first.
- **Config / env:** `curator.archive_ttl_days`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Purge is explicit-only — never automatic.
- **Rebuild notes:** Make the only irreversible operation explicit and still ledgered.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### What "agent-created" means (curator jurisdiction)  `id: docs-features.curator-agent-created`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"What \"agent-created\" means"**.
- **What it does:** Defines exactly which skills the curator may touch.
- **How it works:** "A skill qualifies when ALL of the following are true" — all three verbatim (`curator.md:205-207`): "1. Its name is **not** in `~/.hermes/skills/.bundled_manifest` (bundled skills shipped with the repo)."; "2. Its name is **not** in `~/.hermes/skills/.hub/lock.json` (hub-installed skills)."; "3. Its `.usage.json` entry has `\"created_by\": \"agent\"` or `\"agent_created\": true`." "Currently, only the **background self-improvement review fork** sets this marker — when it creates a new umbrella skill during its periodic review pass (~every 10 agent turns). The background fork runs with a write origin of `\"background_review\"` (via `tools/skill_provenance.py`), which is the only path that triggers the `mark_agent_created()` call in `skill_manage`." (`curator.md:209-213`) "Skills the foreground agent creates via `skill_manage(action=\"create\")` during a conversation are **not** marked as agent-created — they are considered user-directed and the curator intentionally leaves them alone." (`curator.md:215-217`)
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `.usage.json`, `.bundled_manifest`, `.hub/lock.json`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::warning Your hand-written skills are NOT curated If you manually created a `SKILL.md` or pointed Hermes at an external skill directory, that skill will have a `.usage.json` entry with `created_by: null` (or the field absent). The curator will not touch it… **To see which skills the curator actually manages**, run `hermes curator status`. If the agent-created count is 0, no skills are currently in the curator's jurisdiction — the LLM review pass is skipped and the report will show `Model: (not resolved) via (not resolved)` with `Duration: 0s`." (`curator.md:219-227`) Lifecycle summary (`curator.md:289-292`): "`active` → (30d unused) `stale` → (90d unused) `archived`"; "Pinned skills bypass all auto-transitions"; "Archives are recoverable via `hermes curator restore <name>`".
- **Rebuild notes:** Three-condition jurisdiction test based on provenance, with the default being "don't touch". A better version would show the jurisdiction reason per skill in `status`.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`tools/skill_provenance.py` named by the docs).

### Adopting unmanaged skills (`hermes curator adopt`)  `id: docs-features.curator-adopt`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"Adopting unmanaged skills"**.
- **What it does:** Hands skills with no provenance marker over to the curator "by **declaration**".
- **How it works:** `hermes curator status` output shape verbatim (`curator.md:234-244`): `curator-managed skills: 43 total  (agent-created=43  bundled=0)` / `  active     41` / `  stale       2` / `  archived    0` / `unmanaged (no provenance marker): 112 total` / `  pre-dates marker    34` / `  foreground-created  78` / `  never auto-staled or archived — \`hermes curator adopt <name>\` hands one over`. Two documented reasons (`curator.md:249-253`): "**pre-dates marker** — the record was written before `created_by` existed, so it carries no provenance signal at all. Authorship is genuinely unknowable from the record."; "**foreground-created** — a foreground `skill_manage(create)` left the marker unset by design, since skills you ask for belong to you."
- **Inputs / options:** All five forms verbatim (`curator.md:258-262`): `hermes curator list-unmanaged` ("itemize them, with reasons"); `hermes curator adopt <name> [<name> ...]` ("hand specific skills over"); `hermes curator adopt --all-unmanaged --dry-run` ("preview the full list"); `hermes curator adopt --all-unmanaged` ("hand over everything (prompts)"); `hermes curator adopt --all-unmanaged --yes` ("skip the prompt").
- **Outputs / side effects:** Writes `created_by: agent`.
- **Config / env:** `.usage.json`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Adoption writes the same `created_by: agent` marker the background review fork writes. It does **not** reset the inactivity clock — an adopted skill keeps its existing `last_activity_at`, so handing over a library you already stopped using does not buy it a fresh 90-day window. Expect adopted long-idle skills to go `stale` (or `archived`) on the next pass; that is the point." (`curator.md:265-269`) "Adoption is also what unblocks autonomous *improvement*. The background review fork refuses to patch a skill that isn't curator-managed." (`curator.md:271-274`) ":::note `created_by` is a policy flag, not a provenance claim… read it as policy." (`curator.md:277-284`) ":::note Provenance is declared, never inferred Adoption is deliberately manual. Telemetry cannot establish authorship… An automatic \"looks agent-made, adopt it\" heuristic would eventually archive something you hand-wrote. `adopt` refuses bundled, hub-installed, external, and protected built-in skills, which have an owner other than you." (`curator.md:286-293`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Never infer ownership from telemetry; require an explicit declaration. The reasoning here is worth reproducing verbatim in any similar system.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Pinning a skill (`hermes curator pin`)  `id: docs-features.curator-pin`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `curator.md` → **"Pinning a skill"**.
- **What it does:** "Pinning protects a skill from deletion — both the curator's automated archive passes and the agent's `skill_manage(action=\"delete\")` tool call." (`curator.md:301`)
- **How it works:** Two effects verbatim (`curator.md:303-304`): "The **curator** skips it during auto-transitions (`active → stale → archived`), and its LLM review pass is instructed to leave it alone."; "The **agent's `skill_manage` tool** refuses `delete` on it, pointing the user at `hermes curator unpin <name>`. Patches and edits still go through, so the agent can improve a pinned skill's content as pitfalls come up without a pin/unpin/re-pin dance." "The flag is stored as `\"pinned\": true` on the skill's entry in `~/.hermes/skills/.usage.json`, so it survives across sessions." (`curator.md:313`)
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes curator pin <skill>`, `hermes curator unpin <skill>`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `"pinned": true` in `.usage.json`.
- **Config / env:** `.usage.json`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Skills named in any cron job's `skills:` list are protected the same way for **auto-transitions** (the curator never stales/archives them while the reference remains), even when the job is paused or disabled. Prefer an explicit pin when you also want `skill_manage delete` blocked." (`curator.md:315`) "Only **agent-created** skills can be pinned — `hermes curator pin` refuses on bundled and hub-installed skills with an explanatory message if you try. Hub-installed skills are never subject to curator mutation. Bundled built-in skills are only touched when `curator.prune_builtins: true` (the default), and even then only archived after `archive_after_days` of non-use — never patched, consolidated, or deleted." (`curator.md:317`) Protected built-ins (`curator.md:319`): "A small set of **protected built-ins** can be hardcoded as never-archivable and never-consolidatable, regardless of `curator.prune_builtins`, pin state, or LLM judgment… (The set is currently empty — `plan`, its original member, graduated to a built-in `/plan` command with no skill on disk.) Protected built-ins are filtered out of the curator's candidate list entirely." "If you want a stronger guarantee than \"no deletion\" — for instance, freezing a skill's content entirely while the agent still reads it — edit `~/.hermes/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` directly with your editor. The pin guards tool-driven deletion, not your own filesystem access." (`curator.md:321`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Pin blocks deletion but not improvement — a deliberate and useful asymmetry.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (protected-builtins set is documented as currently empty).

### Curator usage telemetry (`.usage.json`)  `id: docs-features.curator-telemetry`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/skills/.usage.json`; `curator.md` → **"Usage telemetry"**.
- **What it does:** "The curator maintains a sidecar at `~/.hermes/skills/.usage.json` with one entry per skill." (`curator.md:325`)
- **How it works:** Complete record shape (`curator.md:328-341`), all 10 fields: `use_count`, `view_count`, `last_used_at`, `last_viewed_at`, `patch_count`, `last_patched_at`, `created_at`, `state`, `pinned`, `archived_at`. Counter rules verbatim (`curator.md:345-347`): "`view_count`: the agent calls `skill_view` on the skill."; "`use_count`: the skill is loaded into a conversation's prompt."; "`patch_count`: `skill_manage patch/edit/write_file/remove_file` runs on the skill."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** `.usage.json` writes.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Bundled and hub-installed skills are explicitly excluded from telemetry writes." (`curator.md:349`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Three distinct counters (view / use / patch) give a much better staleness signal than a single "last touched".
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Curator per-run reports  `id: docs-features.curator-reports`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/logs/curator/<timestamp>/`; `curator.md` → **"Per-run reports"**.
- **What it does:** "Every curator run writes a timestamped directory under `~/.hermes/logs/curator/`."
- **How it works:** Layout verbatim (`curator.md:355-359`): `20260429-111512/` containing `run.json` ("machine-readable: full fidelity, stats, LLM output") and `REPORT.md` ("human-readable summary"). "`REPORT.md` is a quick way to see what a given run did — which skills transitioned, what the LLM reviewer said, which skills it patched. Good for auditing without having to grep `agent.log`." (`curator.md:361`)
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** Two files per run.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::note No candidates? Report shows `(not resolved)` When the curator has **no agent-created skills** to review, the LLM review pass is skipped entirely. The report header will show `Model: (not resolved) via (not resolved)` with `Duration: 0s` — this does **not** indicate a configuration error… The auto-transition phase still runs and reports its counts normally." (`curator.md:363-371`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Machine + human report side by side per run. A better version would diff consecutive reports.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

## Page: `memory.md` — Persistent Memory

### Persistent Memory (MEMORY.md + USER.md)  `id: docs-features.memory`
- **Surface:** Core + Tool
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md` and `USER.md`; the `memory` tool. Docs title **"Persistent Memory"** (`sidebar_position: 3`), description *"How Hermes Agent remembers across sessions — MEMORY.md, USER.md, and session search"*.
- **What it does:** "Hermes Agent has bounded, curated memory that persists across sessions. This lets it remember your preferences, your projects, your environment, and things it has learned." (`memory.md:9`)
- **How it works:** Two files (`memory.md:15-18`), verbatim: **MEMORY.md** — "Agent's personal notes — environment facts, conventions, things learned" — "2,200 chars (~800 tokens)"; **USER.md** — "User profile — your preferences, communication style, expectations" — "1,375 chars (~500 tokens)". "Both are stored in `~/.hermes/memories/` and are injected into the system prompt as a frozen snapshot at session start. The agent manages its own memory via the `memory` tool — it can add, replace, or remove entries." (`memory.md:20`)
- **Inputs / options:** `memory` tool actions `add` / `replace` / `remove`; targets `memory` / `user`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Disk writes; a system-prompt block at next session start.
- **Config / env:** `memory.memory_enabled`, `memory.user_profile_enabled`, `memory.memory_char_limit`, `memory.user_char_limit`, `memory.write_approval`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::caution One agent per Hermes home Don't point two agent processes at the same Hermes home directory. Memory writes are automatic and load back into the system prompt at session start, so two writers sharing one home will compound each other's entries into state neither of them (nor you) authored. Memory is scoped per profile by design — give a second agent its own profile, and if they need shared memory, use an external memory provider instead." (`memory.md:22-24`) ":::info Character limits keep memory focused. Memory does **not** auto-compact: when a write would exceed the limit, the `memory` tool returns an error instead of silently dropping entries. The agent then makes room itself… Note that `replace` is also bound by the limit: swapping an entry for a longer one can still overflow." (`memory.md:26-34`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Two bounded stores, hard limits with an actionable error instead of silent truncation, frozen at session start for cache stability. A better version would let the agent see the live block without breaking the cache (e.g. a tail-injected delta).
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `tools` shard for the `memory` tool schema).

### Memory system-prompt rendering (frozen snapshot)  `id: docs-features.memory-prompt-format`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"How Memory Appears in the System Prompt"**.
- **What it does:** Renders memory entries into a delimited block with capacity metadata.
- **How it works:** Exact rendered shape (`memory.md:41-51`): `══════…` / `MEMORY (your personal notes) [67% — 1,474/2,200 chars]` / `══════…` then entries separated by `§`. Format elements, all four verbatim (`memory.md:54-57`): "A header showing which store (MEMORY or USER PROFILE)"; "Usage percentage and character counts so the agent knows capacity"; "Individual entries separated by `§` (section sign) delimiters"; "Entries can be multiline". "**Frozen snapshot pattern:** The system prompt injection is captured once at session start and never changes mid-session. This is intentional — it preserves the LLM's prefix cache for performance. When the agent adds/removes memory entries during a session, the changes are persisted to disk immediately but won't appear in the system prompt until the next session starts. Tool responses always show the live state." (`memory.md:59`)
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** Disk state and prompt state deliberately diverge within a session.
- **Rebuild notes:** Show the capacity in the prompt so the model can self-manage. That single header is what makes the "consolidate before adding" behavior possible.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `memory` tool actions and substring matching  `id: docs-features.memory-tool`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"Memory Tool Actions"**, **"Substring Matching"**.
- **What it does:** Three actions with substring-based targeting.
- **How it works:** All three verbatim (`memory.md:63-65`): "**add** — Add a new memory entry"; "**replace** — Replace an existing entry with updated content (uses substring matching via `old_text`)"; "**remove** — Remove an entry that's no longer relevant (uses substring matching via `old_text`)". "There is no `read` action — memory content is automatically injected into the system prompt at session start." (`memory.md:67`) Example (`memory.md:74-79`): `memory(action="replace", target="memory", old_text="dark mode", content="User prefers light mode in VS Code, dark mode in terminal")`.
- **Inputs / options:** `action`, `target` (`memory` | `user`), `old_text`, `content`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Disk writes.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "If the substring matches multiple entries, an error is returned asking for a more specific match." (`memory.md:81`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Substring targeting removes the need for entry ids while staying unambiguous by erroring on multi-match.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Memory targets: `memory` vs `user`  `id: docs-features.memory-targets`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"Two Targets Explained"**.
- **What it does:** Says what belongs in each store.
- **How it works:** **`memory`** — "For information the agent needs to remember about the environment, workflows, and lessons learned", five bullets verbatim (`memory.md:88-92`): "Environment facts (OS, tools, project structure)"; "Project conventions and configuration"; "Tool quirks and workarounds discovered"; "Completed task diary entries"; "Skills and techniques that worked". **`user`** — "For information about the user's identity, preferences, and communication style", five bullets (`memory.md:98-102`): "Name, role, timezone"; "Communication preferences (concise vs detailed, format preferences)"; "Pet peeves and things to avoid"; "Workflow habits"; "Technical skill level".
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a

### What to save vs skip  `id: docs-features.memory-save-skip`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"What to Save vs Skip"**.
- **What it does:** Six save categories and five skip categories.
- **How it works:** **Save These (Proactively)** — "The agent saves automatically — you don't need to ask", all six verbatim (`memory.md:110-115`): "**User preferences:** \"I prefer TypeScript over JavaScript\" → save to `user`"; "**Environment facts:** \"This server runs Debian 12 with PostgreSQL 16\" → save to `memory`"; "**Corrections:** \"Don't use `sudo` for Docker commands, user is in docker group\" → save to `memory`"; "**Conventions:** \"Project uses tabs, 120-char line width, Google-style docstrings\" → save to `memory`"; "**Completed work:** \"Migrated database from MySQL to PostgreSQL on 2026-01-15\" → save to `memory`"; "**Explicit requests:** \"Remember that my API key rotation happens monthly\" → save to `memory`". **Skip These**, all five verbatim (`memory.md:119-123`): "**Trivial/obvious info:** \"User asked about Python\" — too vague to be useful"; "**Easily re-discovered facts:** \"Python 3.12 supports f-string nesting\" — can web search this"; "**Raw data dumps:** Large code blocks, log files, data tables — too big for memory"; "**Session-specific ephemera:** Temporary file paths, one-off debugging context"; "**Information already in context files:** SOUL.md and AGENTS.md content".
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Memory capacity management and full-memory error  `id: docs-features.memory-capacity`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"Capacity Management"**, **"What Happens When Memory is Full"**.
- **What it does:** Enforces hard character limits with an instructive error.
- **How it works:** Limits table (`memory.md:129-132`): memory — 2,200 chars — "8-15 entries"; user — 1,375 chars — "5-10 entries". Error payload verbatim (`memory.md:138-145`): `{"success": false, "error": "Memory at 2,100/2,200 chars. Adding this entry (250 chars) would exceed the limit. Consolidate now: use 'replace' to merge overlapping entries into shorter ones or 'remove' stale or less important entries (see current_entries below), then retry this add — all in this turn.", "current_entries": ["..."], "usage": "2,100/2,200"}`. Recovery steps, all four verbatim (`memory.md:148-151`): "1. Read the current entries (shown in the error response)"; "2. Identify entries that can be removed or consolidated"; "3. Use `replace` to merge related entries into shorter versions"; "4. Then `add` the new entry".
- **Inputs / options:** `memory.memory_char_limit`, `memory.user_char_limit`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A structured error carrying the current entries.
- **Config / env:** As above.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "**Best practice:** When memory is above 80% capacity (visible in the system prompt header), consolidate entries before adding new ones." (`memory.md:153`) Good/bad entry examples (`memory.md:160-175`): good — "User runs macOS 14 Sonoma, uses Homebrew, has Docker Desktop and Podman. Shell: zsh with oh-my-zsh. Editor: VS Code with Vim keybindings."; "Project ~/code/api uses Go 1.22, sqlc for DB queries, chi router. Run tests with 'make test'. CI via GitHub Actions."; "The staging server (10.0.1.50) needs SSH port 2222, not 22. Key is at ~/.ssh/staging_ed25519."; bad — "User has a project." (too vague); a verbose dated narrative (too verbose).
- **Rebuild notes:** Return the data needed to fix the error inside the error itself — this is why the agent can self-consolidate in one turn.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Memory duplicate prevention and security scanning  `id: docs-features.memory-safety`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"Duplicate Prevention"**, **"Security Scanning"**.
- **What it does:** Rejects duplicates and blocks injection/exfiltration content.
- **How it works:** "The memory system automatically rejects exact duplicate entries. If you try to add content that already exists, it returns success with a \"no duplicate added\" message." (`memory.md:179`) "Memory entries are scanned for injection and exfiltration patterns before being accepted, since they're injected into the system prompt. Content matching threat patterns (prompt injection, credential exfiltration, SSH backdoors) or containing invisible Unicode characters is blocked." (`memory.md:183`)
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** Rejection messages.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** Duplicate rejection returns *success*, not an error — deliberate so the agent does not retry.
- **Rebuild notes:** Anything that lands in the system prompt must be scanned; memory is a persistent injection vector.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

CLI: `hermes sessions list` — "Browse past sessions".

- **Outputs / side effects:** Read-only.
- **Config / env:** `~/.hermes/state.db`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** FTS5 over the session store gives unlimited recall at zero token cost until queried.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Learning Journey (`/journey`)  `id: docs-features.journey`
- **Surface:** CLI + TUI + Desktop app
- **Where:** `hermes journey` (aliases `hermes learning`, `hermes memory-graph`); `/journey` (aliases `/learning`, `/memory-graph`).
- **What it does:** "The learning journey is a timeline view of everything Hermes has learned — saved skills and memory entries plotted over time (oldest at top, newest at bottom), with a playable \"constellation\" scrubber that replays the build-up." (`memory.md:215`)
- **How it works:** Three surfaces verbatim (`memory.md:217-219`): "**Classic CLI / standalone** — `hermes journey` (aliases: `hermes learning`, `hermes memory-graph`) renders the timeline in the terminal. Flags: `--play` animates the build-up (`--fps` to tune it), `--width`/`--height` override the render size, `--no-color` disables color, and `--json` dumps the raw graph payload."; "**TUI** — `/journey` (aliases: `/learning`, `/memory-graph`) opens the timeline as an overlay."; "**Desktop app** — `/journey` opens the Star Map / memory-graph panel, an interactive visual of the same nodes."
- **Inputs / options:** CLI flags: `--play`, `--fps`, `--width`, `--height`, `--no-color`, `--json`. Management sub-commands (`memory.md:223-227`), all three verbatim: `hermes journey list` — "List node ids — skill names and `memory:<source>:<index>` ids for memory chunks."; `hermes journey delete <node> [-y]` — "Delete a node. Skills are **archived** (restorable), memory chunks are removed. `-y` skips the confirmation."; `hermes journey edit <node>` — "Open the node's content (a skill's `SKILL.md` or the memory chunk) in `$EDITOR`."
- **Outputs / side effects:** Node deletions/edits; JSON graph payload with `--json`.
- **Config / env:** `$EDITOR`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "The same `list` / `delete <id>` / `edit <id>` subcommands work from the in-chat `/journey` command on the CLI, and the desktop panel offers edit/delete on nodes directly." (`memory.md:229`)
- **Rebuild notes:** One graph payload, three renderers, plus prune/correct verbs on the same node ids. A better version would show which nodes were never used since creation.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `cli-*`/`tui`/`desktop-*` shards).

### Memory configuration keys  `id: docs-features.memory-config`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `config.yaml` → `memory:`.
- **What it does:** Five documented keys.
- **How it works:** Block verbatim (`memory.md:233-240`): `memory_enabled: true`; `user_profile_enabled: true`; `memory_char_limit: 2200` ("~800 tokens"); `user_char_limit: 1375` ("~500 tokens"); `write_approval: false` ("false = write freely (default) | true = require approval").
- **Inputs / options:** As above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Tool schema and prompt-block changes.
- **Config / env:** `memory.*`; `agent.disabled_toolsets`; `memory.provider`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Setting **both** `memory_enabled` and `user_profile_enabled` to `false` turns the built-in stores off completely: the `memory` tool is dropped from the schema and its guidance block is dropped from the system prompt, so the model is never told about a tool it cannot use. An external provider set via `memory.provider` (Hindsight, Mem0, Honcho, …) is unaffected and keeps its own tools… Listing `memory` under `agent.disabled_toolsets` is the heavier switch: it hides external provider tools too." (`memory.md:242-249`) "With only `memory_enabled: false` (user profile still on), the tool stays — it backs the profile store — but the system prompt swaps the full memory guidance for a narrower profile-only block. The tool schema advertises only the `user` target, and direct or staged writes to disabled `MEMORY.md` are rejected. The inverse configuration advertises only `memory` and rejects `USER.md` writes." (`memory.md:251-255`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Drop the tool from the schema when it cannot be used — never advertise a disabled capability.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Memory write approval (`memory.write_approval`)  `id: docs-features.memory-write-approval`
- **Surface:** Config + CLI + Gateway/Telegram
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"Controlling memory writes (`write_approval`)"**; `/memory pending|approve|reject|approval`.
- **What it does:** "By default the agent saves memory freely — including from the background self-improvement review that runs after a turn. If you'd rather approve saves first, set `memory.write_approval: true`." (`memory.md:259-262`)
- **How it works:** Behaviour table verbatim (`memory.md:264-267`): `false` (default) — "Write freely — the gate is off (the pre-gate behaviour)."; `true` — "Require approval before anything is saved. In the interactive CLI, foreground writes prompt you inline (entries are small enough to read in full). Everywhere else — messaging platforms, scripts, and the background self-improvement review — writes are **staged** for review with `/memory pending`."
- **Inputs / options:** All four commands verbatim (`memory.md:273-277`): `/memory pending` — "list staged memory writes (auto ones tagged [auto])"; `/memory approve <id>` — "apply one (or 'all')"; `/memory reject <id>` — "drop one (or 'all')"; `/memory approval on` — "turn the gate on (or 'off') and persist it".
- **Outputs / side effects:** Staged writes awaiting approval.
- **Config / env:** `memory.write_approval`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "> To turn memory off entirely (not just gate it), set both `memory_enabled: false` and `user_profile_enabled: false`." (`memory.md:269`) "This is the answer to \"the agent saved a wrong assumption about me\": set `write_approval: true`, and every save — especially the unprompted background ones — waits for your yes/no before it ever enters your profile." (`memory.md:279-281`)
- **Rebuild notes:** One gate covering both foreground and background writes, with a surface-appropriate review UX (inline vs staged).
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Background review notifications (`display.memory_notifications`)  `id: docs-features.memory-notifications`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `config.yaml` → `display.memory_notifications`; per-platform `display.platforms.<platform>.memory_notifications`.
- **What it does:** Controls the chat line shown when the background review writes something.
- **How it works:** "After a turn, the background self-improvement review may quietly save a memory or update a skill. This is Hermes' consent-aware learning loop: repeated corrections and durable workflow lessons become compact memory entries or procedural skills… By default it surfaces a short `💾 Memory updated` line in chat so you know it happened." (`memory.md:285-292`) Value table verbatim (`memory.md:300-303`): `off` — "No chat notification. The review still runs and still writes — you just don't see a line for it."; `on` (default) — "Generic line, e.g. `💾 Memory updated`, `💾 Skill 'foo' patched`."; `verbose` — "Includes a compact preview of what changed, e.g. `💾 Memory ➕ User prefers terse replies` or a `\"old\" → \"new\"` skill diff snippet."
- **Inputs / options:** `off` | `on` | `verbose`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Chat notification lines.
- **Config / env:** `display.memory_notifications`, `display.platforms.<platform>.memory_notifications`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "> This only governs the **gateway** chat notification. The review itself, and writes to your memory/skill stores, are unaffected by this setting." (`memory.md:305-307`)
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Background review model (`auxiliary.background_review`)  `id: docs-features.background-review-model`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `config.yaml` → `auxiliary.background_review`.
- **What it does:** Routes the post-turn self-improvement review to a cheaper model.
- **How it works:** "The review runs on your **main chat model** by default, replaying the conversation — which is already warm in the prompt cache, so it's cheap cache reads." (`memory.md:311-313`) Override (`memory.md:316-320`): `auxiliary: {background_review: {provider: openrouter, model: google/gemini-3-flash-preview}}` — "auto (default) = main chat model". "When you point it at a model **different** from your main one, the review runs there for substantially lower cost (~3–5× in benchmarks). Because a different model can't reuse your main model's prompt cache anyway, the fork automatically replays a compact **digest** of the conversation (recent turns verbatim + a summary of older ones) rather than the full transcript… Capture holds: in testing, memory capture was identical and skill capture near-identical to the main-model review." (`memory.md:322-328`)
- **Inputs / options:** `provider`, `model`, `enabled`, `extra_tools`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** "Fork usage is persisted in `session_model_usage` with `task='background_review'` and a completion line is written to `agent.log` (`Background review complete: thread=bg-review calls=… in=… out=… result=…`)." (`memory.md:348-351`)
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.background_review.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Leave it at `auto` (or set it to your main model) and nothing changes." (`memory.md:330`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Switch the replay strategy (full transcript vs digest) based on whether the cache can be reused. That coupling is the clever part.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (`agent/background_review.py` exists).

### Disabling automatic background reviews (`enabled`)  `id: docs-features.background-review-enabled`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `auxiliary.background_review.enabled`.
- **What it does:** "The review fork can burn a meaningful share of total tokens on busy hosts. Operators can disable it without zeroing nudge intervals." (`memory.md:334-336`)
- **How it works:** `auxiliary: {background_review: {enabled: true}}` — "false = skip automatic post-turn forks". "With `enabled: false`, automatic post-turn forks do not spawn; manual `/refine` still works." (`memory.md:344-346`)
- **Inputs / options:** `true` | `false`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** No automatic forks.
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.background_review.enabled`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `/refine` remains available.
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Background review `extra_tools` allowlist  `id: docs-features.background-review-extra-tools`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `auxiliary.background_review.extra_tools`.
- **What it does:** "Background review can use memory, skill-management, and read-only file tools by default. If a profile provides another tool that is safe for unattended review, opt it in by name." (`memory.md:355-357`)
- **How it works:** Example (`memory.md:359-364`): `auxiliary: {background_review: {extra_tools: [propose_shared_memory]}}`.
- **Inputs / options:** A list of tool names.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A wider review-fork whitelist.
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.background_review.extra_tools` (default empty list).
- **Edge cases / guards:** "The tool must already be available to the parent agent; this setting only adds it to the review fork's runtime whitelist. It does not enable arbitrary tools, and tools not listed here remain denied. Keep the list narrow and prefer tools that stage a proposal for human review rather than applying external or destructive changes directly. The default is an empty list." (`memory.md:366-370`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Default-deny whitelist that can only narrow what the parent already has. A better version would require the tool to declare itself review-safe.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Skill write approval (`skills.write_approval`)  `id: docs-features.skills-write-approval-memorypage`
- **Surface:** Config + CLI
- **Where:** `memory.md` → **"Controlling skill writes (`skills.write_approval`)"**; `/skills pending|diff|approve|reject|approval`.
- **What it does:** "Skills use the same on/off gate, but the review UX differs because a `SKILL.md` is far too large to read in a chat bubble." (`memory.md:374-375`)
- **How it works:** `skills: {write_approval: false}` — "false = write freely (default) | true = require approval". "When `write_approval: true`, skill writes (create / edit / patch / write_file / delete) always **stage** regardless of origin. You review the one-line gist inline, but the full diff stays out-of-band." (`memory.md:381-383`)
- **Inputs / options:** All five commands verbatim (`memory.md:386-390`): `/skills pending` — "list staged skill writes + a one-line gist each"; `/skills diff <id>` — "full unified diff (best viewed in CLI or dashboard)"; `/skills approve <id>` — "apply it (or 'all')"; `/skills reject <id>` — "drop it (or 'all')"; `/skills approval on` — "turn the gate on (or 'off') and persist it".
- **Outputs / side effects:** Staged files at `~/.hermes/pending/skills/<id>.json`.
- **Config / env:** `skills.write_approval`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "On a messaging platform, approve a skill from its gist + metadata, or open `/skills diff` on the CLI / dashboard / the staged file under `~/.hermes/pending/skills/<id>.json` when you want to read the whole change." (`memory.md:392-395`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Match the review UX to the artifact size — inline for small, out-of-band diff for large.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (fuller treatment in `skills.md`).

## Page: `fallback-providers.md` — Fallback Providers

### Three layers of provider resilience  `id: docs-features.fallback-layers`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** `fallback-providers.md` intro (`sidebar_position: 8`), description *"Configure automatic failover to backup LLM providers when your primary model is unavailable."*
- **What it does:** Names the three resilience layers and their order.
- **How it works:** Verbatim (`fallback-providers.md:11-13`): "1. **Credential pools** — rotate across multiple API keys for the *same* provider (tried first)"; "2. **Primary model fallback** — automatically switches to a *different* provider:model when your main model fails"; "3. **Auxiliary task fallback** — independent provider resolution for side tasks like vision and compression". "Credential pools handle same-provider rotation (e.g., multiple OpenRouter keys). This page covers cross-provider fallback. Both are optional and work independently." (`fallback-providers.md:15`)
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Primary model fallback (`fallback_providers`)  `id: docs-features.fallback-primary`
- **Surface:** Config + CLI
- **Where:** `hermes fallback`; `config.yaml` → top-level `fallback_providers:`.
- **What it does:** "When your main LLM provider encounters errors — rate limits, server overload, auth failures, connection drops — Hermes can automatically switch to a backup provider:model pair mid-session without losing your conversation." (`fallback-providers.md:20`)
- **How it works:** Four documented switch steps (`fallback-providers.md:117-120`): "1. Resolves credentials for the fallback provider"; "2. Builds a new API client"; "3. Swaps the model, provider, and client in-place"; "4. Resets the retry counter and continues the conversation". "The switch is seamless — your conversation history, tool calls, and context are preserved."
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes fallback` (interactive) with subcommands "`add`, `list` (alias `ls`), `remove` (alias `rm`), and `clear`" (`fallback-providers.md:31`). YAML shape (`fallback-providers.md:36-38`): `fallback_providers: [{provider: openrouter, model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4}]`. "Each entry requires both `provider` and `model`. Entries missing either field are ignored." (`fallback-providers.md:40`)
- **Outputs / side effects:** Config writes under `fallback_providers:`.
- **Config / env:** `fallback_providers` (list), legacy `fallback_model` (single).
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::note `fallback_model` vs `fallback_providers` `fallback_providers` (plural, list) is the current config shape and supports multiple fallbacks tried in order. `fallback_model` (singular) is the legacy single-fallback key — Hermes still honors it for back-compat, but `hermes fallback` writes the current `fallback_providers` key and migrates legacy config on write. When both are set, `fallback_providers` takes priority." (`fallback-providers.md:42-44`) ":::tip There are no environment variables for the primary fallback chain — configure it exclusively through `config.yaml` or `hermes fallback`. This is intentional: fallback configuration is a deliberate choice, not something a stale shell export should override." (`fallback-providers.md:186-188`)
- **Rebuild notes:** In-place client swap preserving history, with the chain declared only in config (never env). A better version would report the active provider in the transcript when it switches.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Fallback trigger conditions  `id: docs-features.fallback-triggers`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `fallback-providers.md` → **"When Fallback Triggers"**.
- **What it does:** Five documented error classes.
- **How it works:** All five verbatim (`fallback-providers.md:109-113`): "**Rate limits** (HTTP 429) — after exhausting retry attempts"; "**Server errors** (HTTP 500, 502, 503) — after exhausting retry attempts"; "**Auth failures** (HTTP 401, 403) — immediately (no point retrying)"; "**Not found** (HTTP 404) — immediately"; "**Invalid responses** — when the API returns malformed or empty responses repeatedly".
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** Provider switch.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::warning Fallback resets the prompt cache … the next request re-reads the entire history at full input-token price instead of the ~75–90% discounted cached rate. The same applies when the turn ends and the primary is restored — that first request back on the primary is a full re-read too (unless the primary's cache TTL hasn't expired)." (`fallback-providers.md:124-126`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Retry-then-fallback for transient classes, immediate fallback for terminal ones.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Fallback is per-turn and reset-aware  `id: docs-features.fallback-per-turn`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `fallback-providers.md` → the ":::info Per-Turn, Not Per-Session" admonition.
- **What it does:** Scopes fallback to a single turn and skips doomed primary retries.
- **How it works:** Verbatim (`fallback-providers.md:128-132`): "Fallback is **turn-scoped**: each new user message starts with the primary model restored. If the primary fails mid-turn, fallback activates for that turn only. On the next message, Hermes tries the primary again. Within a single turn, fallback activates at most once — if the fallback also fails, normal error handling takes over (retries, then error message). This prevents cascading failover loops within a turn while giving the primary model a fresh chance every turn."; "The per-turn retry is **reset-aware**: when the primary's credentials report a rate-limit reset time that hasn't elapsed yet (subscription windows like Claude Pro/Max's 5-hour blocks or Codex weekly limits report these as hours or days), Hermes skips the doomed retry and stays on the fallback until the reset passes — avoiding two pointless provider switches (and two prompt-cache invalidations) per turn. The moment the reset time elapses, the next turn goes back to the primary automatically. Transient 429s without a reset time keep the existing behavior: a short cooldown, then retry every turn."
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** At most one fallback activation per turn.
- **Rebuild notes:** Honor provider-reported reset times so retries are evidence-based rather than clock-based.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

The top-level `fallback_providers` chain is the same policy the main agent uses, so free-only or same-provider fallback rules apply to auxiliary tasks on `auto` as well." - **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.<task>.provider: auto`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Those built-in chains are a convenience fallback for users who have not declared a task-specific or main fallback policy." (`fallback-providers.md:232`)
- **Rebuild notes:** User policy always beats built-in discovery. A better version would log which chain step served each aux call.

### Auxiliary capacity-error fallback ladder  `id: docs-features.aux-capacity-fallback`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `fallback-providers.md` → **"Auxiliary Capacity-Error Fallback"**.
- **What it does:** Falls back through a ladder when an explicitly configured aux provider hits a capacity error.
- **How it works:** All four layers verbatim (`fallback-providers.md:319-322`): "1. **Primary aux provider** — the one you configured (tried first, always)"; "2. **`auxiliary.<task>.fallback_chain`** — your per-task override list, if you wrote one"; "3. **Main agent provider + model** — last-resort safety net (always tried, even if you didn't write a chain)"; "4. **Warn + re-raise** — if every layer fails, Hermes logs `Auxiliary <task>: ... all fallbacks exhausted` at WARNING level and re-raises the original error". Trigger definition (`fallback-providers.md:317`): "a **capacity error** (HTTP 402 payment required, HTTP 429 daily-quota exhaustion, connection failure)".
- **Inputs / options:** `auxiliary.<task>.fallback_chain`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A WARNING log line and the original error re-raised on total failure.
- **Config / env:** As above.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Transient HTTP 429 rate limits (`Retry-After: ...`) are treated as request constraints, not capacity problems — they respect your explicit provider choice and do **not** trigger the fallback ladder. Only daily/monthly quota exhaustion, payment errors, and connection failures bypass the explicit-provider gate." (`fallback-providers.md:324`) "For users on `provider: auto` (no explicit aux provider), the existing auto-detection chain runs in place of steps 2–3." (`fallback-providers.md:326`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Distinguish "cannot serve at all" from "slow down" — only the former may override an explicit user choice.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Per-task `fallback_chain` (with per-entry timeout)  `id: docs-features.aux-fallback-chain`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `fallback-providers.md` → **"Optional: per-task fallback chain"**.
- **What it does:** Overrides the default "main agent model first" fallback order for one aux task.
- **How it works:** "Each entry needs at least `provider`; `model`, `base_url`, and `api_key` are optional." (`fallback-providers.md:330`) Example (`fallback-providers.md:333-348`): `auxiliary: {vision: {provider: glm, model: glm-4v-flash, fallback_chain: [{provider: openrouter, model: google/gemini-3-flash-preview}, {provider: nous, model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4}]}, compression: {provider: openrouter, fallback_chain: [{provider: openai, model: gpt-4o-mini, timeout: 240}]}}` — `timeout` commented as "optional — this candidate's own deadline (seconds)".
- **Inputs / options:** `provider` (required), `model`, `base_url`, `api_key`, `timeout`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `auxiliary.<task>.fallback_chain`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "You do **not** need to configure `fallback_chain` to get fallback — the main-agent safety net runs regardless." (`fallback-providers.md:350`) "Each `fallback_chain` entry may also declare its own `timeout` (seconds). Without it, a fallback candidate inherits the task-level timeout — which may be tuned for the primary provider. Declaring a per-entry `timeout` lets a slower-but-reliable fallback (e.g. a large-context summarizer) get the budget it actually needs instead of dying on the primary's clock." (`fallback-providers.md:352`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Per-candidate timeouts — a fallback tuned for the primary's clock is a fallback that always fails.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

## Page: `web-search.md` — Web Search & Extract

### `web_search` and `web_extract` tools  `id: docs-features.web-tools`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** Docs title **"Web Search & Extract"** (`sidebar_position: 6`), `sidebar_label: Web Search`, description *"Search the web and extract page content with multiple backend providers — including free self-hosted SearXNG."*
- **What it does:** "Hermes Agent includes two model-callable web tools backed by multiple providers: **`web_search`** — search the web and return ranked results; **`web_extract`** — fetch and extract readable content from one or more URLs." (`web-search.md:10-13`)
- **How it works:** "Both are configured through a single backend selection. Providers are chosen via `hermes tools` or set directly in `config.yaml`." (`web-search.md:15`)
- **Inputs / options:** `web_extract` accepts a per-call `char_limit`; `web_search` accepts a `limit`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Ranked results / extracted markdown, plus disk-cached extracts under `~/.hermes/cache/web/`.
- **Config / env:** `web.backend`, `web.search_backend`, `web.extract_backend`, `web.extract_char_limit`, `web.cache_enabled`, `web.cache_ttl_minutes`, `web.cache_exempt_hosts`, `web.keyless_fallback`, `web.keyless_rescue`, `web.provider_tier.<name>`, `web.xai.*`; plus the provider env vars below.
- **Edge cases / guards:** See truncation, caching and auto-detection entries.
- **Rebuild notes:** Two tools, one backend registry, per-capability routing, deterministic truncation and a shared cache. A better version would attach per-result provenance (which backend served it) to every hit.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `tools` shard for both registered schemas).

### Web backends table (8 providers)  `id: docs-features.web-backends`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `web-search.md` → **"Backends"**.
- **What it does:** The complete provider matrix.
- **How it works:** Complete table (`web-search.md:19-28`), all 8 rows verbatim (provider / env var / search / extract / free tier): **Firecrawl** (default) — "`FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` (optional — keyless when selected)" — ✔ / ✔ — "500 credits/mo · keyless cloud when selected"; **SearXNG** — `SEARXNG_URL` — ✔ / — — "✔ Free (self-hosted)"; **Brave Search (free tier)** — `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY` — ✔ / — — "2 000 queries/mo"; **DDGS (DuckDuckGo)** — "— (no key)" — ✔ / — — "✔ Free"; **Exa** — "`EXA_API_KEY` (optional)" — ✔ / ✔ — "✔ Keyless ring member · 1 000 searches/mo with key"; **Parallel** — "`PARALLEL_API_KEY` (optional)" — ✔ / ✔ — "✔ Keyless ring member · paid with key"; **Keenable** — "`KEENABLE_API_KEY` (optional)" — ✔ / ✔ — "✔ Keyless ring member · paid with key"; **xAI (Grok)** — "`XAI_API_KEY` or `hermes auth add xai-oauth`" — ✔ / — — "Paid (SuperGrok or per-token)".
- **Inputs / options:** `web.backend` values (`web-search.md:404`): `firecrawl | searxng | brave-free | ddgs | keenable | exa | parallel | xai` (plus `nous` for the Tool Gateway).
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** The env vars above.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Brave Search, DDGS, and xAI are **search-only** — pair any of them with Firecrawl/Keenable/Exa/Parallel when you also need `web_extract`. DDGS uses the `ddgs` Python package under the hood; if it isn't already installed, run `pip install ddgs` (or let Hermes lazy-install it on first use). xAI runs Grok's server-side `web_search` tool on the Responses API — results are LLM-generated rather than index-backed." (`web-search.md:30`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Declare per-provider capability (search / extract) so a search-only backend errors clearly rather than silently failing extraction.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Keyless free-tier ring  `id: docs-features.web-keyless-ring`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `web-search.md` → the ":::info Works out of the box — keyless free-tier rotation" admonition and **"Auto-detection"**.
- **What it does:** "A fresh install with **no web credentials at all** gets working `web_search` and `web_extract` out of the box: requests rotate round-robin across the ring vendors' public free tiers — **Exa, Parallel, Firecrawl, and Keenable** — spreading load evenly, and a rate-limited request automatically retries on the next vendor in the ring (multi-hop, until one serves or all are throttled)." (`web-search.md:34-36`)
- **How it works:** "This tier is strictly last-resort — any configured backend or present API key always wins — and requests carry no user identifiers (only a random per-process session id, rotated on restart). For guaranteed, unthrottled service, set up a keyed provider. Disable the keyless tier entirely with `web.keyless_fallback: false`."
- **Inputs / options:** `web.keyless_fallback: false`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Rotating vendor selection.
- **Config / env:** `web.keyless_fallback`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "All free tiers are vendor-rate-limited under burst load; sustained normal usage goes through fine." "with it off and no credentials, web tools are unavailable until a provider is configured." (`web-search.md:440`)
- **Rebuild notes:** A last-resort anonymous ring that never overrides an explicit choice and carries no identifiers. Copy the privacy framing.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Free vs paid tier pinning (`web.provider_tier`)  `id: docs-features.web-provider-tier`
- **Surface:** CLI + Config
- **Where:** `hermes tools` → Web Search & Extract; `web.provider_tier.<name>`.
- **What it does:** "in `hermes tools`, Exa, Parallel, and Keenable each appear as two rows — **Free (keyless)** and **Paid (API key)**." (`web-search.md:40`)
- **How it works:** "Picking Free pins that vendor's anonymous endpoint (even if you later add a key); picking Paid pins the keyed path (a missing key then errors instead of silently downgrading to the free tier). The selection is stored as `web.provider_tier.<name>: free|paid`; leave it unset for auto (key present → paid, otherwise the keyless ring)."
- **Inputs / options:** Picker rows **"Free (keyless)"** and **"Paid (API key)"**; `web.provider_tier.<name>: free | paid`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Config write.
- **Config / env:** `web.provider_tier.<name>`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Missing key on the paid path errors rather than downgrading.
- **Rebuild notes:** Explicit tier pinning avoids a silent, surprising downgrade.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `web_extract` truncation budget  `id: docs-features.web-extract-truncation`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `web-search.md` → **"How `web_extract` handles long pages"**.
- **What it does:** "To keep your context window usable, `web_extract` applies a **deterministic character budget** — no LLM summarization is involved." (`web-search.md:53`)
- **How it works:** Complete table (`web-search.md:55-59`), all 3 rows verbatim: "At or under the budget (default 15 000)" — "Returned whole — full markdown reaches the agent"; "Over the budget" — "Head+tail window (~75% head / ~25% tail, cut on markdown line boundaries) plus an explicit `[TRUNCATED]` footer. The full clean text is stored to disk and the footer tells the agent the file path and the exact `read_file` call to page through the omitted middle"; "Over 2 000 000" — "Stored text is capped at 2 MB".
- **Inputs / options:** `web.extract_char_limit` (default `15000`, "clamped to 2 000–500 000"); per-call `char_limit`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A `[TRUNCATED]` footer plus an on-disk full text file.
- **Config / env:** `web.extract_char_limit`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "If you specifically need the live DOM rather than extracted markdown — for example, a JS-heavy page where extraction returns little content — use `browser_navigate` + `browser_snapshot` instead. The browser tool returns the live accessibility tree (subject to its own snapshot cap on huge pages)." (`web-search.md:60-62`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Deterministic head+tail truncation that names the exact recovery call. The footer telling the agent the precise `read_file` invocation is the key usability detail.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Web result caching  `id: docs-features.web-caching`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `web-search.md` → **"Result caching"**.
- **What it does:** "Repeat web calls within a short window are served from cache instead of the paid backend — this saves credits and latency in the two patterns where duplicates are common: subagent fan-outs… and the agent re-checking a page it read minutes ago." (`web-search.md:68`)
- **How it works:** Cache table (`web-search.md:70-73`), both rows verbatim: "`web_search` — same query (case/whitespace-insensitive), same provider" — "In-memory memo" — "Per process"; "`web_extract` — same URL, same format, same provider" — "Full text stored under `~/.hermes/cache/web/`" — "Shared across CLI, gateway, cron, and subagent processes". "Concurrent identical searches (a parallel subagent fan-out firing the same query at once) are **coalesced into a single backend request** — the first caller pays; the rest share the response. Requested search limits are bucketed up to 10/20/50/100 so near-identical requests (`limit=5` vs `limit=8`) share one entry, with each caller receiving its requested count." (`web-search.md:75`)
- **Inputs / options:** `web.cache_enabled` (default true), `web.cache_ttl_minutes` (default 20, "clamped 1–1440"), `web.cache_exempt_hosts`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Cache files under `~/.hermes/cache/web/`.
- **Config / env:** As above; `security.website_blocklist`, `security.allow_private_urls`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Only successful responses are cached. Failures always retry the backend, responses served by the one-shot keyless rescue are never cached… and URLs matched by your `security.website_blocklist` are never served from cache. Cached extracts re-run the normal truncation pipeline, so a different `char_limit` on the second call works off the same stored scrape." (`web-search.md:77`) "**Local development URLs are never cached.** Anything on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `*.local`, single-label LAN hostnames, or private/link-local IP ranges (`192.168.*`, `10.*`, `172.16-31.*`) bypasses the extract cache entirely — dev servers, hot-reload builds, and chat-GUI artifact previews change on every save, and a cached copy would show you a stale build." (`web-search.md:79`) "**Testing over the public internet?** Staging deploys and tunnel URLs are public DNS, so the local-dev rule can't catch them — list them in `web.cache_exempt_hosts`… Entries match exactly, as a `*.` wildcard, or as a domain suffix (`mysite.dev` also covers `preview.mysite.dev`)" (`web-search.md:81`) with the example `web: {cache_exempt_hosts: [mysite.vercel.app, "*.ngrok-free.app"]}`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Bucketed limits + request coalescing + a never-cache list for anything that changes on save. The local-dev exemption is the kind of detail that only shows up after real use.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### SearXNG backend (self-hosted setup)  `id: docs-features.web-searxng`
- **Surface:** Config + Env
- **Where:** `web-search.md` → **"SearXNG (free, self-hosted)"**.
- **What it does:** "SearXNG is a privacy-respecting, open-source metasearch engine that aggregates results from 70+ search engines. **No API key required** — just point Hermes at a running SearXNG instance." (`web-search.md:136`)
- **How it works:** **Option A — Self-host with Docker (recommended)**, all documented steps: "1. Create a working directory" (`mkdir -p ~/searxng/searxng`, `cd ~/searxng`); "2. Write a `docker-compose.yml`" — verbatim service block with `image: searxng/searxng:latest`, `container_name: searxng`, `ports: ["8888:8080"]`, `volumes: ["./searxng:/etc/searxng:rw"]`, `environment: [SEARXNG_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8888/]`, `restart: unless-stopped`; "3. Start the container"; steps 4–5 enable the JSON format and copy the generated `settings.yml` out of the container (`docker cp ~/searxng/searxng/settings.yml searxng:/etc/searxng/settings.yml`, `docker restart searxng`); "6. Verify it works" — `curl -s "http://localhost:8888/search?q=test&format=json" | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'{len(d[\"results\"])} results')"` ("You should see something like `10 results`. If you get a `403 Forbidden`, JSON format is still disabled — recheck step 4."); "7. Configure Hermes" — `SEARXNG_URL=http://localhost:8888` in `.env` plus `web: {search_backend: "searxng"}`, "Or set via `hermes tools` → Web Search & Extract → SearXNG". **Option B — Use a public instance**: "Public SearXNG instances are listed at searx.space. Filter by instances that have **JSON format enabled** (shown in the table)." with `SEARXNG_URL=https://searx.example.com`.
- **Inputs / options:** `SEARXNG_URL`; `web.search_backend: "searxng"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** As above.
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::caution Public instances Public instances have rate limits, variable uptime, and may disable JSON format at any time. For production use, self-hosting is strongly recommended." Pairing (`web-search.md:264-268`): "SearXNG handles search; you need a separate provider for `web_extract`" → `web: {search_backend: "searxng", extract_backend: "firecrawl"}` ("or keenable, exa, parallel").
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.
