"Later sources override earlier ones on name collision." (`:122`) Sub-category table (`:128-135`), all 6 rows verbatim: `plugins/` (root) — "General plugins — tools, hooks, slash commands, CLI commands, bundled skills" — "`PluginManager` (kind: `standalone` or `backend`)"; `plugins/platforms/<name>/` — "Gateway channel adapters (`ctx.register_platform()`)" — "`PluginManager` (kind: `platform`, one level deeper)"; `plugins/image_gen/<name>/` — "Image-generation backends" — "`PluginManager` (kind: `backend`, one level deeper)"; `plugins/memory/<name>/` — "Memory providers (subclass `MemoryProvider`)" — "**Own loader** in `plugins/memory/__init__.py` (kind: `exclusive` — one active at a time)"; `plugins/context_engine/<name>/` — "Context-compression engines" — "**Own loader** in `plugins/context_engine/__init__.py` (one active at a time)"; `plugins/model-providers/<name>/` — "LLM provider profiles (`register_provider(ProviderProfile(...))`)" — "**Own loader** in `providers/__init__.py` (lazily scanned on first `get_provider_profile()` call)".
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `HERMES_ENABLE_PROJECT_PLUGINS`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "User plugins at `~/.hermes/plugins/model-providers/<name>/` and `~/.hermes/plugins/memory/<name>/` override bundled plugins of the same name — last-writer-wins in `register_provider()` / `register_memory_provider()`. Drop a directory in, and it replaces the built-in without any repo edits." (`:137`)
- **Rebuild notes:** n/a
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Plugins are opt-in (allow-list + deny-list)  `id: docs-features.plugins-optin`
- **Surface:** Config + CLI
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Plugins are opt-in (with a few exceptions)"**.
- **What it does:** "**General plugins and user-installed backends are disabled by default** — discovery finds them (so they show up in `hermes plugins` and `/plugins`), but nothing with hooks or tools loads until you add the plugin's name to `plugins.enabled`… This stops third-party code from running without your explicit consent." (`:141`)
- **How it works:** Config block verbatim (`:144-159`): `plugins: {enabled: [my-tool-plugin, disk-cleanup], disabled: [noisy-plugin], hook_callback_timeout: 30}` with the deny-list comment "optional deny-list — always wins if a name appears in both" and the timeout comment "wall-clock cap (seconds) for timeout-bounded in-process Python plugin hook callbacks (hot-path observers + pre_tool_call). Default 30; set 0 to disable; values above 600 are clamped. Timed-out pre_tool_call callbacks fail closed (block the tool). Caller-thread hooks such as subagent_stop are never moved onto a timeout worker. Shell hooks keep their own per-entry timeout under the top-level hooks: key."
- **Inputs / options:** Three state-flip commands verbatim (`:163-166`): `hermes plugins` ("interactive toggle (space to check/uncheck)"); `hermes plugins enable <name>` ("add to allow-list"); `hermes plugins disable <name>` ("remove from allow-list + add to disabled"). Install prompt: "After `hermes plugins install owner/repo`, you're asked `Enable 'name' now? [y/N]` — defaults to no. Skip the prompt for scripted installs with `--enable` or `--no-enable`." (`:168`) Pinning (`:170-183`): `hermes plugins install owner/repo --ref 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567` — "pin a full immutable commit (tags, branches, and abbreviated SHAs are not accepted)". "Hermes checks out the commit detached, verifies that `HEAD` exactly matches the requested SHA, and records the canonical source, installed revision, and pin status in the current profile. `hermes plugins update` refuses to move a pinned plugin; choose a new exact commit explicitly with `hermes plugins install <source> --force --ref <new-commit>`. The profile-local install metadata contains no config values, environment values, secrets, or capability grants."
- **Outputs / side effects:** Config writes; install metadata.
- **Config / env:** `plugins.enabled`, `plugins.disabled`, `plugins.hook_callback_timeout`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Bypass table (`:189-197`), all 7 rows verbatim: "**Bundled platform plugins** (IRC, Teams, etc. under `plugins/platforms/`)" — "Auto-loaded so every shipped gateway channel is available. The actual channel turns on via `gateway.platforms.<name>.enabled`"; "**Bundled backends** (image-gen providers under `plugins/image_gen/`, etc.)" — "Auto-loaded so the default backend \"just works\". Selection happens via `<category>.provider`"; "**Memory providers**" — "All discovered; exactly one is active, chosen by `memory.provider`"; "**Context engines**" — "All discovered; one is active, chosen by `context.engine`"; "**Model providers**" — "All bundled providers under `plugins/model-providers/` discover and register at the first `get_provider_profile()` call"; "**Pip-installed `backend` plugins**" — "Opt-in via `plugins.enabled` (same as general plugins)"; "**User-installed platforms** (under `~/.hermes/plugins/platforms/`)" — "Opt-in via `plugins.enabled` — third-party gateway adapters need explicit consent". "In short: **bundled \"always-works\" infrastructure loads automatically; third-party general plugins are opt-in.**" (`:199`) Migration (`:267`): "When you upgrade to a version of Hermes that has opt-in plugins (config schema v21+), any user plugins already installed under `~/.hermes/plugins/` that weren't already in `plugins.disabled` are **automatically grandfathered** into `plugins.enabled`… Bundled standalone plugins are NOT grandfathered."
- **Rebuild notes:** Deny-list always wins; grandfather existing user installs but never bundled ones.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Approval transports (`ctx.register_approval_transport`)  `id: docs-features.plugins-approval-transports`
- **Surface:** Plugin + Config
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Approval transports"**.
- **What it does:** "An approval transport changes **where a human sees and answers** an existing Hermes tool-approval request. It does not decide whether a command needs approval and it is not an authorization-policy API." (`:212`)
- **How it works:** Example verbatim (`:216-224`): a `present(request)` function that delivers `request.command` / `request.description` to a UI, waits for the authenticated human response, and returns `request.respond(choice)` where choice ∈ `once/session/always/deny`; registered with `ctx.register_approval_transport("my-ui", present)`. "`present` may be synchronous or async. Hermes runs it on a bounded worker and enforces the canonical `approvals.timeout` even if the plugin does not. The request is immutable and contains redacted display text, its host presentation class (`cli` or `gateway`), the host timeout, allowed choices, and an opaque request ID/digest." (`:226`)
- **Inputs / options:** Config verbatim (`:236-242`): `plugins: {enabled: [my-approval-plugin]}` plus `security: {approval: {transport: my-ui, transport_fallback: deny}}` — "default".
- **Outputs / side effects:** Approval prompts routed elsewhere.
- **Config / env:** `security.approval.transport`, `security.approval.transport_fallback`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Return the result of `request.respond(choice)`; unbound dictionaries and stale or changed request IDs/digests are rejected. A plugin cannot return a scope that the host did not offer (for example, `always` on a once-only request)." (`:230`) "Registration alone does nothing. Enabling the plugin and explicitly selecting its transport are separate consent steps." (`:234`) "Transport exceptions, timeouts, unavailable registrations, invalid choices, and stale responses deny by default. To deliberately show the prompt on the ordinary CLI/TUI/gateway/ACP surface when the selected transport fails, set `transport_fallback: builtin`. Without that exact opt-in, Hermes never materializes the prompt on another surface." (`:244`) "Hermes still owns hardline blocks, sudo-stdin protection, user deny rules, request binding, allowed scopes, persistence, hooks, and final authorization. Hardline commands are blocked before any transport callback. There is intentionally **no plugin approval policy, auto-allow callback, or required `pre_tool_call` policy** in this interface." (`:251`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Let a plugin move *where* a decision is shown, never *whether* one is required. Request binding by opaque id + digest prevents replay.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Plugin types (4) and pluggable-interface map  `id: docs-features.plugins-types`
- **Surface:** Docs

- **How it works:** Types table (`:285-290`), all 4 rows verbatim: **General plugins** — "Add tools, hooks, slash commands, CLI commands" — "Multi-select (enable/disable)" — `~/.hermes/plugins/`; **Memory providers** — "Replace or augment built-in memory" — "Single-select (one active)" — `plugins/memory/`; **Context engines** — "Replace the built-in context compressor" — "Single-select (one active)" — `plugins/context_engine/`; **Model providers** — "Declare an inference backend (OpenRouter, Anthropic, …)" — "Multi-register, picked by `--provider` / `config.yaml`" — `plugins/model-providers/`. Interface map (`:297-317`), all 16 rows verbatim, covering: a tool; a lifecycle hook; a slash command; a `hermes <thing>` subcommand; a bundled skill; an inference backend; a gateway channel; a memory backend; a context-compression strategy; an image-generation backend; a video-generation backend ("Veo, Kling, Pixverse, Grok-Imagine, Runway, …"); a TTS backend ("Config-driven (recommended)… OR Python backend plugin — `ctx.register_tts_provider()`"); an STT backend ("…OR Python backend plugin — `ctx.register_transcription_provider()`"); external tools via MCP; additional skill sources (`hermes skills tap add <repo>`); gateway event hooks (`HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py` in `~/.hermes/hooks/<name>/`); shell hooks (`hooks:` in config.yaml).
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Memory providers and context engines are **provider plugins** — only one of each type can be active at a time. Model providers are also plugins, but many load simultaneously." (`:291`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Publish a "where do I add X" routing table — it is the single most useful page in an extensible system.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### One-click install links (`hermes://`)  `id: docs-features.plugins-deeplinks`
- **Surface:** Desktop app
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"One-click install links (Desktop)"**; also **Settings → Plugins → Install from Git**.
- **What it does:** "Hermes Desktop registers the `hermes://` URL scheme, so a website, README, or chat message can link straight to a plugin install." (`:356`)
- **How it works:** All three link forms verbatim (`:360-362`): `hermes://plugin/install?repo=owner/repo` ("main install link"); `hermes://plugin/install?repo=owner/repo&enable=1` ("enable the agent plugin after install"); `hermes://plugin/install?repo=owner/repo&force=1` ("replace an existing install"). "Clicking one opens Hermes and shows a **confirmation dialog** — the repo id, a \"Before you install\" note, and GitHub browse + clone links — then shallow-clones the repo to detect what it ships (an **agent plugin** — backend Python, a **desktop plugin** — app UI, or both). You pick the components with checkboxes and confirm." (`:365`)
- **Inputs / options:** Query params `repo`, `enable`, `force`. HTML anchor example: `<a href="hermes://plugin/install?repo=owner/repo&enable=1">Install in Hermes</a>`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A guarded install.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** "Nothing is installed until you do; deep links never auto-install, and agent-plugin installs go through the same install-time security scanning as `hermes plugins install`." (`:365`) "Hybrid repos (agent + desktop halves in one repo) use one link and one dialog… Legacy `hermes://plugin-agent/…` and `hermes://plugin-desktop/…` URLs route into the same dialog. In dev builds (`npm run dev`) the scheme is `hermes-dev://`." (`:374`) "MCP servers have the equivalent link form."
- **Rebuild notes:** Deep links must open a dialog, never act. A separate dev scheme avoids clobbering the release registration.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented (see the `desktop-*` shards for the dialog).

### Plugin capabilities and consent  `id: docs-features.plugins-capabilities`
- **Surface:** Config + CLI
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Plugin capabilities and consent"**.
- **What it does:** "Plugins can declare the privileged host surfaces they want in their `plugin.yaml`." (`:392`)
- **How it works:** Declaration verbatim (`:394-399`): `capabilities: [tools.override, llm.model_override]` with comments "replace built-in tools" / "pick the model for host-owned LLM calls". "When a plugin declares capabilities, `hermes plugins install` (and `hermes plugins enable`) shows the list with one-line risk descriptions and asks once. Consenting records the grant under `plugins.entries.<id>.granted_capabilities` together with a consent hash and timestamp. Declining leaves the plugin enabled with those capabilities off — a well-behaved plugin probes with `ctx.has_capability()` and degrades gracefully." (`:402`)
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes plugins capabilities` / `hermes plugins capabilities my-plugin`. Complete capability→legacy-key table (`:428-437`), all 7 rows verbatim: `tools.override` → `allow_tool_override`; `llm.provider_override` → `llm.allow_provider_override`; `llm.model_override` → `llm.allow_model_override`; `llm.agent_id_override` → `llm.allow_agent_id_override`; `llm.profile_override` → `llm.allow_profile_override`; `llm.task_override` → `llm.allow_task_override`; `gateway.platform_actions` → `allow_platform_actions`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `plugins.entries.<id>.granted_capabilities` + consent hash + timestamp.
- **Config / env:** As above.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "**Update re-consent:** if a plugin update declares capabilities you haven't granted, `hermes plugins update` surfaces the additions and asks again. New capabilities stay off until you consent — a plugin update can never silently widen its access." (`:412`) "**Non-interactive sessions fail closed:** installing or updating without a TTY completes the install, but declared capabilities are *not* granted." (`:418`) "A gate is open when *either* the capability is granted *or* the legacy key is set — existing configs keep working unchanged." (`:439`) ":::warning Not a sandbox Capabilities are a **consent and audit layer**, not isolation. Plugins run as regular in-process Python: a malicious plugin can ignore every gate here. Granting a capability is a statement of trust in the plugin author — it is not a code audit, and Hermes has not reviewed the plugin's code. Only install plugins from sources you trust." (`:441-448`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Consent hashes + update re-consent, plus an explicit statement that this is not a sandbox. The honesty is the feature.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Platform actions (`ctx.platform_actions`)  `id: docs-features.plugins-platform-actions`
- **Surface:** Plugin
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Platform actions"**.
- **What it does:** "`ctx.platform_actions` gives a plugin a minimal, capability-gated verb set for acting on connected chat platforms through the live gateway adapter registry — the sanctioned alternative to monkeypatching an adapter." (`:452`)
- **How it works:** "**It is off by default**: every call re-checks the `gateway.platform_actions` capability (legacy key `plugins.entries.<id>.allow_platform_actions`), and an ungranted call returns a structured error instead of acting." Documented v1 verbs (`:459-465`): `await ctx.platform_actions.add_reaction(platform="telegram", chat_id="-100123", message_id="456", emoji="👍")` and `await ctx.platform_actions.set_thread_title(...)` — "both `async`, both return a plain dict, and neither ever raises into hook dispatch".
- **Inputs / options:** `platform`, `chat_id`, `message_id`, `emoji` (and the thread-title arguments).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Reactions / thread titles on the live platform.
- **Config / env:** `gateway.platform_actions` capability; legacy `plugins.entries.<id>.allow_platform_actions`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Never raises into hook dispatch; ungranted calls return a structured error.
- **Rebuild notes:** Re-check the capability on every call, not once at registration.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Community plugin index (`hermes plugins search`)  `id: docs-features.plugins-index`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Discovering community plugins"**.
- **What it does:** "`hermes plugins search <term>` searches the **community plugin index** — a static, machine-readable JSON catalog of community plugins. Matching is fuzzy across name, description, and tags." (`:499`)
- **How it works:** All five documented invocations verbatim (`:504-508`): `hermes plugins search telegram` ("fuzzy search"); `hermes plugins search` ("browse the whole index"); `hermes plugins search --capability platform` ("filter by declared capability"); `hermes plugins search media --json` ("machine-readable output"); `hermes plugins search --refresh` ("bypass the 24h local cache"). Install by bare name: `hermes plugins install hermes-media-studio`. "**How the index is fetched.** The index lives at a canonical URL (`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-plugin-index/main/index.json`, overridable via `hermes config set plugins.index_url <url>`). Fetches are cached under `~/.hermes/cache/plugin_index.json` for 24 hours; when the remote is unreachable the stale cache is used, and when there is no cache at all a bundled seed copy ships with Hermes — so search works fully offline." (`:522`)
- **Inputs / options:** Complete entry format verbatim (`:528-541`): `{"name", "description", "author", "tags", "repo", "ref" (40-char commit SHA), "subdir", "homepage", "capabilities", "api_version", "added_at"}`. "`repo` is the `owner/name` GitHub identifier, `ref` pins an immutable commit SHA, and optional `subdir` supports monorepos. The bundled seed file (`hermes_cli/data/plugin_index.json` in the repo) is the format reference."
- **Outputs / side effects:** A 24h cache file.
- **Config / env:** `plugins.index_url`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "If a name matches more than one entry, the candidates are listed and nothing is installed. Explicit `owner/repo` or Git-URL identifiers never touch the index… An explicit `--ref <sha>` always overrides the index pin." (`:518`) ":::warning Indexed ≠ audited Inclusion in the community index means the entry's metadata was reviewed — **it is not a code audit**." (`:554-560`) "**Submitting a plugin.** The index is maintained as a plain JSON file — submit a pull request to the hermes-plugin-index repository… Review covers the entry's *metadata* only." (`:547`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Static JSON index + local cache + a bundled seed = offline-capable discovery with no server to run.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### Plugin packs (`hermes-pack.yaml`)  `id: docs-features.plugins-packs`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Plugin packs"**.
- **What it does:** "A **plugin pack** is a declarative, shareable YAML file (`hermes-pack.yaml`) that pins a set of plugins — like sharing a modpack. Installing a pack fans out to ordinary pinned installs; nothing new exists at runtime." (`:566`)
- **How it works:** Complete pack schema verbatim (`:572-590`): `name`, `description`, `author`, `version`, `plugins:` (entries with `name` "bare community-index name…" + `ref`, or `repo` "…or explicit owner/repo (or git URL)" + `ref` + optional `subdir` "optional monorepo path"), `config:` ("optional, non-secret seeds only"), `skills: []` ("declared list only (not auto-installed yet)").
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes plugins pack show ./hermes-pack.yaml` ("dry-run review"); `hermes plugins pack install ./hermes-pack.yaml` ("review → confirm → install"); `hermes plugins pack export`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Installs recorded "with the same provenance in `plugins/.install-metadata.json`, so two installs of the same pack resolve identically".
- **Config / env:** `plugins.entries.<id>` seeds.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "**Consent is never bulk-granted.** `pack install` shows a mandatory review screen (every plugin, source, pinned ref, and the capabilities it declares), then asks **one** confirmation for the pack contents. After that, each plugin's declared capabilities go through the standard per-plugin capability-consent prompt… There is no `--yes`, and non-interactive sessions cannot install packs." (`:606`) "**Secrets never travel in packs.** `config:` seeds are limited to non-secret `plugins.entries.<id>` keys — secret-shaped key names (`*token*`, `*key*`, `*password*`, …), capability grants, and the deprecated `allow_*` trust gates are rejected on install and stripped on export… Existing user values in `plugins.entries.<id>` always win over pack seeds." (`:613`) "**Partial failure.** Each plugin installs independently; failures are reported per plugin, the rest continue, and the command exits non-zero if any plugin failed." (`:621`) "**Export caveats.** `pack export` only includes plugins with known Git provenance… Local-only plugins are listed as warning comments… The `skills:` list is parsed and displayed at install time but not yet auto-installed." (`:625`)
- **Rebuild notes:** No `--yes` for a bulk-trust operation; strip secret-shaped keys on export.
- **Verification:** **partial (documented gap)** — packs implemented; the `skills:` list is parsed but "not yet auto-installed".

### Install-time security scanning  `id: docs-features.plugins-security-scan`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Install-time security scanning"**.
- **What it does:** "Every `hermes plugins install` and `hermes plugins update` runs a static security scan over the plugin tree before it is activated (inspired by Claude Cowork's skill & plugin security scanning)." (`:635`)
- **How it works:** "The scanner reuses the same threat-pattern engine as the Skills Hub guard — exfiltration of credential stores, reverse shells, destructive commands, persistence mechanisms, obfuscated execution, and prompt injection in documentation files — with plugin-aware exemptions: a provider plugin reading its **own** API key from the environment (the documented `requires_env` pattern) is not flagged." Verdict table (`:645-649`), all 3 rows verbatim: **safe** — "Installs normally, no extra output"; **caution** — "Findings are shown; you confirm `Install anyway? [y/N]` (or pass `--force`)"; **dangerous** — "Blocked. `--force` does **not** override".
- **Inputs / options:** `--force` (caution only); `plugins.scan_on_install: false`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Findings printed; install blocked or gated.
- **Config / env:** `plugins.scan_on_install`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "On `hermes plugins update`, a dangerous verdict on the updated tree disables the plugin until you review the findings and re-enable it." (`:651`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Three verdicts with `--force` honoured only at the middle tier.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `hermes plugins` interactive UI  `id: docs-features.plugins-interactive-ui`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes plugins` with no arguments.
- **What it does:** "opens a composite interactive screen".
- **How it works:** Screen verbatim (`:665-676`): `Plugins` / `  ↑↓ navigate  SPACE toggle  ENTER configure/confirm  ESC done` / `  General Plugins` / ` → [✓] my-tool-plugin — Custom search tool` / `   [ ] webhook-notifier — Event hooks` / `   [ ] disk-cleanup — Auto-cleanup of ephemeral files [bundled]` / `  Provider Plugins` / `     Memory Provider          ▸ honcho` / `     Context Engine           ▸ compressor`. Behaviors verbatim (`:678-680`): "**General Plugins section** — checkboxes, toggle with SPACE. Checked = in `plugins.enabled`, unchecked = in `plugins.disabled` (explicit off)."; "**Provider Plugins section** — shows current selection. Press ENTER to drill into a radio picker where you choose one active provider."; "Bundled plugins appear in the same list with a `[bundled]` tag."
- **Inputs / options:** Keys: ↑↓ navigate, SPACE toggle, ENTER configure/confirm, ESC done.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Config writes (`:684-688`): `memory: {provider: "honcho"}` ("empty string = built-in only"); `context: {engine: "compressor"}` ("default built-in compressor").
- **Config / env:** `memory.provider`, `context.engine`, `plugins.enabled`, `plugins.disabled`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** State table (`:695-699`), all 3 rows verbatim: `enabled` — "Loaded on next session" — in enabled Yes — in disabled No; `disabled` — "Explicitly off — won't load even if also in `enabled`" — "(irrelevant)" — Yes; `not enabled` — "Discovered but never opted in" — No — No. "The default for a newly-installed or bundled plugin is `not enabled`." "In a running session, `/plugins` shows which plugins are currently loaded." (`:703`)
- **Rebuild notes:** Distinguish "explicitly off" from "never opted in" — the two states have different upgrade semantics.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `ctx.inject_message()`  `id: docs-features.plugins-inject-message`
- **Surface:** Plugin
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Injecting Messages"**.
- **What it does:** "Plugins can inject messages into a CLI conversation or a known gateway session." (`:709`)
- **How it works:** **Signature:** `ctx.inject_message(content: str, role: str = "user", *, session_key: str | None = None) -> bool`. CLI behaviour, all four rules verbatim (`:727-730`): "If the agent is **idle** (waiting for user input), the message is queued as the next input and starts a new turn."; "If the agent is **mid-turn** (actively running), the message interrupts the current operation — the same as a user typing a new message and pressing Enter."; "For non-`\"user\"` roles, the content is prefixed with `[role]` (e.g. `[system] ...`)."; "Returns `True` if the message was queued successfully." Gateway behaviour, all nine rules verbatim (`:733-741`): "`session_key` is required and must identify an existing gateway session. It is the stable routing key, not the CLI session ID."; "Hermes reuses that session's stored platform, chat, thread, profile, and conversation history. Plugins cannot supply a new chat route through this API."; "Hermes rechecks the stored route against the gateway's current authorisation rules before dispatch."; "Routes that relied only on an adapter-time or upstream authorisation decision are rejected unless Hermes can revalidate them from current core allowlists, pairing, or explicit allow-all configuration."; "Injected text is always conversational input. It cannot invoke slash commands, approve tools, or resolve pending confirmation and clarification prompts."; "The route and conversation are pinned while dispatch is pending. Hermes drops the request if topic recovery changes the route or the session rotates before handling starts."; "The request enters the platform adapter's normal message path. Active sessions use the existing busy-session queue rather than starting a competing turn."; "Returns `True` when the live gateway accepts the request for asynchronous dispatch. This does not confirm that the agent turn or platform delivery has completed."; "Returns `False` when `session_key` is omitted, the permission is not granted, or no live gateway can accept the request."
- **Inputs / options:** `content`, `role`, `session_key`. Example session key: `"agent:main:telegram:dm:123456789"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A queued turn.
- **Config / env:** `plugins.entries.<plugin>.allow_gateway_injection: true` — "It is disabled by default for every plugin."
- **Edge cases / guards:** ":::warning Only grant gateway injection to plugins you trust. Hermes checks this host API permission and restricts it to existing session routes, but Python plugins run in-process and this setting is not a sandbox." ":::note This plugin API does not expose a public HTTP endpoint or CLI command for external processes. The plugin must already know the target gateway `session_key`."
- **Rebuild notes:** Re-validate a stored route against current authorization before dispatch — a stored route is not a standing grant.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

### `ctx.call_mcp()` from plugins  `id: docs-features.plugins-call-mcp`
- **Surface:** Plugin
- **Where:** `plugins.md` → **"Calling MCP servers from plugins"**.
- **What it does:** "`ctx.call_mcp()` lets a plugin call a tool on one of the user's configured MCP servers — synchronously, from any hook or tool handler — routing through Hermes' existing native MCP client (same connections, trust-tier gates, circuit breaker, and reconnect logic as model-invoked MCP tools; never a parallel client)." (`:767`)
- **How it works:** **Signature:** `ctx.call_mcp(server: str, tool: str, arguments: dict | None = None, timeout: float = 30) -> dict`. Example verbatim: `ctx.call_mcp("knowledge_rag", "query_knowledge", {"query": "deploy runbook"}, timeout=30)` with the comments "server name from mcp.servers", "tool on that server", "seconds; clamped to 1–600". "Returns a stable envelope: `{\"ok\": True, \"result\": ...}` (plus `structuredContent` when the server provides it) or `{\"ok\": False, \"error\": \"...\"}`. Results over ~64 KB are truncated and flagged with `\"truncated\": True`." (`:784`)
- **Inputs / options:** `server`, `tool`, `arguments`, `timeout`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** An MCP tool call.
- **Config / env:** `plugins.entries.<plugin>.mcp_allowlist: ["knowledge_rag", "github"]`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** "A plugin has **no MCP access by default**. The operator must grant each server explicitly." (`:788`) All four rules verbatim (`:796-799`): "Calling a server not in the list raises `PermissionError` naming the exact config key to set."; "The grant is per-server and per-plugin — never ambient authority over every configured server, and `\"*\"` wildcards are not honored."; "Every call has an enforced timeout (default 30 s) so a hung MCP server cannot stall the hook or tool pipeline that invoked it."; "MCP servers return untrusted content. Treat `result` as data, not instructions — don't feed it into privileged decisions (approvals, command execution) without validation." ":::warning Granting `mcp_allowlist` gives the plugin the same access to that MCP server as the model has — including any write-capable tools the server exposes."
- **Rebuild notes:** Per-server, per-plugin allowlist with no wildcard, and an error that names the exact config key to set.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented.

## Page: `browser.md` — Browser Automation

### Browser Automation toolset (overview)  `id: docs-features.browser-overview`
- **Surface:** Toolset
- **Where:** toolset `browser`; docs sidebar "Browser" (`sidebar_position: 5`); enabled via config `toolsets` list or `hermes config set toolsets '["hermes-cli", "browser"]'`
- **What it does:** Gives the agent a full browser-automation toolset with seven backend options (Browser Use cloud, Browserbase cloud, Browser Use CLI driver, Firecrawl cloud, Camofox local, Lightpanda local engine, local Chromium-family via CDP, plain local browser mode) so it can navigate sites, click elements, fill forms and extract information.
- **How it works:** Pages are represented as **accessibility trees** — text-based snapshots — instead of pixels. Interactive elements get ref IDs like `@e1`, `@e2` that the agent passes to `browser_click` / `browser_type`. Implementation lives in `tools/browser_tool.py` (built-in tools), `tools/browser_use_cli.py` (Browser Use driver / `browser_exec`), `tools/browser_camofox.py` + `tools/browser_camofox_state.py`, `tools/browser_lightpanda.py`, `tools/browser_cdp_tool.py`, `tools/browser_dialog_tool.py`, `tools/browser_supervisor.py`, `tools/browser_extension_router.py`, `hermes_cli/browser_connect.py`. Defaults live in `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:573-680` under the `browser` block.
- **Inputs / options:** Documented key capabilities list: multi-provider cloud execution (Browser Use, Browserbase, Firecrawl); local Chromium-family integration via CDP (Chrome, Brave, Chromium, Edge); cloud anti-bot support (stealth, residential proxies, CAPTCHA solving on Browser Use Cloud); persistent cloud profiles (cookies, localStorage, saved passwords); session isolation (one browser session per task); automatic cleanup (inactive sessions closed after timeout); vision analysis (screenshot + AI analysis).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Browser sessions (local processes or cloud sessions), screenshots under `~/.hermes/cache/screenshots/`, truncated snapshots under `~/.hermes/cache/web/`, optional recordings under `~/.hermes/browser_recordings/`.
- **Config / env:** `toolsets` must include `browser`; whole `browser.*` config tree; provider credential env vars (`BROWSER_USE_API_KEY`, `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY`, `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID`, `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`, `CAMOFOX_URL`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** Docs say to prefer `web_search` / `web_extract` for simple retrieval — browser tools are for *interaction*. Documented limitations: text-based interaction only (no pixel coordinates), snapshot truncation, cloud session timeouts tied to the provider plan, cost (cloud credits), and **no file downloads**.
- **Rebuild notes:** Model the toolset as a driver abstraction (`backend`) × browser-source abstraction (`cloud_provider` / `engine` / `cdp_url`), with a stable ref-ID accessibility-tree snapshot as the sole page representation. A better version would make ref IDs stable across snapshots (hash of the DOM path) so a plan built on snapshot N still works at snapshot N+1, and add a first-class download channel.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — 13 browser tools present in `tools_full.json` (`browser_back`, `browser_cdp`, `browser_click`, `browser_console`, `browser_dialog`, `browser_exec`, `browser_get_images`, `browser_navigate`, `browser_press`, `browser_scroll`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_type`, `browser_vision`), tool schemas registered at `tools/browser_tool.py:2781-2908` and `:6372-6491`.

### Nous Subscription browser (Tool Gateway path)  `id: docs-features.browser-nous-subscription`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** `hermes setup --portal`; or `hermes model` / `hermes tools` → **Browser Automation** → **Nous Subscription**
- **What it does:** Lets paid Nous Portal subscribers run browser automation through the Tool Gateway with no separate browser API keys.
- **How it works:** Writes the browser selection to `browser.cloud_provider: nous`; browser calls are proxied by the Tool Gateway rather than a direct vendor SDK. New installs run `hermes setup --portal` to log in and enable every gateway tool at once.
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes setup --portal` (new installs); `hermes model` or `hermes tools` picker row **Nous Subscription** (existing installs).
- **Outputs / side effects:** `browser.cloud_provider: nous` in `config.yaml`; browser traffic billed against the Nous subscription.
- **Config / env:** `browser.cloud_provider: nous`; Nous Portal credentials from `hermes setup --portal`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Requires a paid Nous Portal subscription. `browser.engine` (Lightpanda) is ignored while the Nous subscription browser is active (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:598-601`).
- **Rebuild notes:** Treat the subscription as just another `cloud_provider` value so the rest of the stack is provider-agnostic. A better version would show remaining subscription browser-minutes in `/browser status`.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `browser.cloud_provider` is the single selection key; precedence comment naming the Nous subscription browser at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:598-601`.

### Browser Use cloud mode  `id: docs-features.browser-browseruse-cloud`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/.env` → `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY`; selected via `hermes tools` → Browser Automation → Browser Use
- **What it does:** Runs managed Chromium in the Browser Use cloud, with stealth, residential proxies, CAPTCHA solving, and reusable browser profiles.
- **How it works:** Credentials come from `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY` (API key from browser-use.com); the active provider comes from `browser.cloud_provider: browser-use`. Browser Use Cloud enables stealth and residential proxies by default and supports persistent profiles for cookies, localStorage and saved passwords.
- **Inputs / options:** `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=***` in `~/.hermes/.env`; alternatively `browser-use auth login` for the Browser Use CLI's own cloud browsers.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Cloud browser sessions billed to the Browser Use account; persistent cloud profiles retain cookies/localStorage/passwords across sessions.
- **Config / env:** `browser.cloud_provider: browser-use`; env `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The `.env` key supplies **credentials only** — it does not select the provider once a selection exists. A selected provider with a missing key errors with guidance to run `hermes tools`, instead of silently rerouting. Never-configured setups still autodetect from available credentials.
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep credential presence and provider selection strictly separate, and fail loudly on "selected but unkeyed". A better version would validate the key at selection time and print the remaining cloud quota.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `browser.cloud_provider` is the selection key; explicit-selection-wins semantics documented in the `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py` browser block.

### Browserbase cloud mode  `id: docs-features.browser-browserbase`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/.env` → `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` + `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID`; selected via `hermes tools` → Browser Automation → Browserbase
- **What it does:** Uses Browserbase-managed cloud browsers as an alternative cloud provider, with anti-bot tooling.
- **How it works:** Two credentials are required (`BROWSERBASE_API_KEY`, `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID`, from browserbase.com); selection is `browser.cloud_provider: browserbase`. Sessions are released via the Browserbase API using the `REQUEST_RELEASE` status.
- **Inputs / options:** `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY=***`; `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID=your-project-id-here`. Optional env: `BROWSERBASE_PROXIES` (default `"true"`), `BROWSERBASE_ADVANCED_STEALTH` (default `"false"`, requires Scale Plan), `BROWSERBASE_KEEP_ALIVE` (default `"true"`, requires paid plan), `BROWSERBASE_SESSION_TIMEOUT` (seconds, max `21600` = 6 hours; examples 600 / 1800 / 21600; default = project default).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Cloud sessions consuming Browserbase credits; sessions explicitly released on cleanup.
- **Config / env:** `browser.cloud_provider: browserbase`; env `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY`, `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID`, `BROWSERBASE_PROXIES`, `BROWSERBASE_ADVANCED_STEALTH`, `BROWSERBASE_KEEP_ALIVE`, `BROWSERBASE_SESSION_TIMEOUT`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** If paid features aren't on the plan, Hermes falls back automatically — **first disabling `keepAlive`, then proxies** — so browsing still works on free plans. Same explicit-selection-wins rule as other providers.
- **Rebuild notes:** Implement the graded fallback as an ordered list of optional session features, dropping one at a time on 4xx "plan required" responses. A better version would probe plan entitlements once and cache them instead of failing then retrying.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — provider selection key present; degradation order is documented in the page's stealth note.

### Browser Use mode / `browser_exec` driver (default)  `id: docs-features.browser-use-mode`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** default when `browser.backend` is unset and the `browser-use` CLI is runnable; forced with `browser.backend: "browser-use"`; disabled with `/browser use off` or `browser.backend: "off"`
- **What it does:** Replaces the eleven built-in browser tools with a single `browser_exec` tool: the agent writes and executes Python inside the browser to click, type, drag, scrape and interact with pages, via Browser Use CLI 3.0.
- **How it works:** `tools/browser_use_cli.py:727` defines `browser_exec(code, session="", timeout_s=_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_S, task_id=None, local=False)`. The mode is a **driver** that composes with the configured browser source — local Chrome, Nous-subscription cloud browser, Browserbase, Firecrawl or Browser Use cloud browsers. If the CLI can't run, Hermes falls back to the built-in browser tools automatically. `_blocked_url_in_code()` scans submitted code for blocked URLs before execution (`tools/browser_use_cli.py:739-741`).
- **Inputs / options:** `code` (required Python using pre-imported helpers such as `new_tab("https://example.com")`, `page_info()`, `goto_url()`, `capture_screenshot()`); `session=<name>` — isolates browser work per name on every backend (own harness daemon: own IPC socket, log and state; on cloud backends its own browser); `timeout_s`; `task_id`; `local` (forces a real-profile local session even under a cloud backend — only exposed when `browser.use_real_profile` is on). `/browser use` switches to the mode, `/browser use off` reverts.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Program output from the executed Python; one harness daemon process per session name; browser state persisted per daemon.
- **Config / env:** `browser.backend` (`""` default / `"browser-use"` / `"off"`); Browser Use's own cloud browsers need `browser-use auth login` or `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Because the mode executes model-written Python on the machine, `browser_exec` is **only offered to sessions that also have terminal access** — platforms configured without the terminal toolset keep the default browser tools. **Camofox is the one exception** to the composition rule: it has no CDP endpoint for the harness to attach to, so Camofox setups automatically keep the built-in browser tools. Omitting `session` uses the shared default daemon (fine for one-at-a-time browsing); parallel subagents should each pass a distinct name.
- **Rebuild notes:** Gate code-execution browser drivers on the same trust level as terminal access, and key daemons by session name so concurrency is opt-in but cheap. A better version would sandbox the generated Python (seccomp/namespace) so `browser_exec` no longer needs the terminal-toolset gate.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — signature and `local` argument at `tools/browser_use_cli.py:727-732`; `BACKEND_DISABLED` referenced by the `/browser use off` handler at `hermes_cli/cli_commands_mixin.py:2648`; backend semantics documented in `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:573-584`.

### Firecrawl cloud mode  `id: docs-features.browser-firecrawl`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/.env` → `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`; then `hermes setup tools` → Browser Automation → Firecrawl
- **What it does:** Uses Firecrawl cloud browsers, which come with built-in scraping, as the browser provider.
- **How it works:** API key from firecrawl.dev in the form `fc-***`; selection written by the `hermes setup tools` picker.
- **Inputs / options:** `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=fc-***`; optional `FIRECRAWL_API_URL` (self-hosted instance, default `https://api.firecrawl.dev`, example `http://localhost:3002`); optional `FIRECRAWL_BROWSER_TTL` (session TTL in seconds, default `300`, example `600`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Cloud browser sessions on Firecrawl; scrape results returned inline.
- **Config / env:** `browser.cloud_provider` set to Firecrawl by the picker; env `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`, `FIRECRAWL_API_URL`, `FIRECRAWL_BROWSER_TTL`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Same explicit-selection-wins rule; self-hosted instances require `FIRECRAWL_API_URL` to be reachable from the Hermes host.
- **Rebuild notes:** Expose the TTL as a config key as well as an env var so it can be profile-scoped. A better version would reuse the same Firecrawl credential for `web_extract`'s Firecrawl tier automatically.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — Firecrawl is a `web.provider_tier` ring vendor (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:547-553`) and a selectable browser provider.

### Hybrid routing: cloud for public URLs, local for LAN/localhost  `id: docs-features.browser-hybrid-routing`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** automatic when a cloud provider is configured; `browser.auto_local_for_private_urls`
- **What it does:** When a cloud provider is configured, Hermes auto-spawns a **local Chromium sidecar** for URLs that resolve to a private/loopback/LAN address, while public URLs keep using the cloud provider in the same conversation.
- **How it works:** URL classification in `tools/browser_tool.py:1913-1970` (`_url_is_private`, including the manual 172.16.0.0/12 handling at `:1939`) and routing decision at `:2005`. Private ranges recognised: `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `192.168.x.x`, `10.x.x.x`, `172.16-31.x.x`, `*.local`, `*.lan`, `*.internal`, IPv6 loopback `::1`, link-local `169.254.x.x`. The sidecar uses the same `agent-browser` CLI as pure local mode. Sidecar sessions carry a `::local` task-id suffix, and `cleanup_browser()` reaps both the cloud session and the sidecar for a bare task id (`tools/browser_tool.py:5790-5805`).
- **Inputs / options:** `browser.auto_local_for_private_urls: true|false` (default `true`); `browser.allow_private_urls: true|false` (default `false`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** A second local Chromium process per task when a private URL is visited; the cloud provider never sees the private URL.
- **Config / env:** `browser.auto_local_for_private_urls` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:603`), `browser.allow_private_urls` (`:590`), `browser.cloud_provider`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** With auto-routing disabled, private URLs are rejected with the exact message `"Blocked: URL targets a private or internal address"` (`tools/browser_tool.py:4167`, `:4255`) unless `browser.allow_private_urls: true`. **Post-navigation redirects from a public URL onto a private address are still blocked** — no redirect-to-internal trick. A separate guard rejects cloud metadata endpoints with `"Blocked: URL targets a cloud metadata endpoint"` (`tools/browser_tool.py:4165`, `:4244`). Requires `agent-browser` installed (auto-installed by `hermes setup tools` → Browser Automation).
- **Rebuild notes:** Classify by resolved IP, not hostname string, and re-check after every redirect hop. A better version would let the user allowlist specific internal hosts for cloud access rather than an all-or-nothing `allow_private_urls`.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `_url_is_private` at `tools/browser_tool.py:1913`; metadata-endpoint guard at `:4165` is an additional protection the page does not name (minor doc gap).

### Real profile browsing (use your own logins)  `id: docs-features.browser-real-profile`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `browser.use_real_profile` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`; Desktop **Capabilities → Tools → Browser → Use My Real Browser Profile** (the switch sits above the backend options), or **Settings → Config** under the `browser` section
- **What it does:** Lets the agent browse **as you**, with your existing logins and cookies, instead of the default clean throwaway profile.
- **How it works:** Hermes copies the default browser's **active** profile (`Local State → profile.last_used`) — cookies, saved logins, preferences — into a managed snapshot under `~/.hermes/browser-profile/<browser>/`, then launches your **real browser binary** on that snapshot and attaches its browsing engine. Launching the real binary (rather than a bundled Chromium with mock-keychain switches) is what keeps OS-encrypted cookies decryptable — on macOS Chrome cookies are Keychain-encrypted and a mock-keychain launch would silently drop all of them. The live profile is never opened directly: the snapshot is a separate directory, so it doesn't fight the running browser for the profile lock and sidesteps Chrome 136+'s block on remote-debugging the default profile directory. Auth files are re-synced from the real profile whenever a fresh session launches. Only the active profile is copied.
- **Inputs / options:** `browser.use_real_profile: true|false` (default `false`); `browser.real_profile_pin: "<profile dir>"` e.g. `"Profile 2"` (default `""` = follow last-used); `browser.real_profile_autoclose: true|false` (default `false`); `browser.headed: true` / `AGENT_BROWSER_HEADED=1` to watch it work; `browser_exec`'s `local` argument (only exposed when this toggle is on); CLI `hermes browser close-profile`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Snapshot store at `~/.hermes/browser-profile/`; **deleted on the next browser use when the toggle is turned back off**, so copied credentials don't outlive consent. Sessions run **headless by default** (Chrome's *new* headless mode, which reads the normal cookie store), never stealing focus.
- **Config / env:** `browser.use_real_profile` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:621`), `browser.real_profile_autoclose` (`:631`), `browser.real_profile_pin` (`:639`), `browser.headed` (`:589`), env `AGENT_BROWSER_HEADED`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Supported browsers: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Brave Origin, Chromium (whichever is the OS default) — a non-Chromium default (e.g. Firefox) **fails closed** with a clear message rather than guessing. A pin naming a nonexistent profile directory **fails closed** with a fixable message, never silently falling back to last-used. On a display-less host (servers, CI) it always runs headless regardless of `headed`. **Windows:** a running Chrome/Edge/Brave holds an exclusive deny-all lock on its cookie and login DBs, so Hermes fails fast with a "fully quit the browser and retry" message; real-profile browsing on Windows requires the browser fully quit, including any background/tray instance. macOS and Linux can copy while the browser runs. **Security framing (verbatim intent):** "this is a consent-gated convenience, not an isolation boundary" — a page the agent visits runs with your real logins. Off by default. Works on any backend: automatic on local backends; under a cloud backend the agent opens a real-profile local session on demand via `browser_exec`'s `local` argument, with the cloud backend still serving everything else.
- **Rebuild notes:** Snapshot-then-launch (never touch the live profile dir), re-sync auth files per fresh session, and delete the snapshot on consent withdrawal. A better version would scope the snapshot to a cookie allowlist (only the domains the task needs) so a hostile page can't harvest every login at once.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — full behaviour, fail-closed rules and snapshot-deletion-on-toggle-off are all spelled out in the config comment at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:604-639`.

### `hermes browser close-profile` (real-profile unlock)  `id: docs-features.browser-close-profile`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes browser close-profile`
- **What it does:** Terminates the browser process tree holding your default profile so Hermes can copy it for real-profile browsing.
- **How it works:** `hermes browser` is a helper command group for real-profile browsing; `close-profile` kills the browser process tree bound to that profile, then Hermes retries the snapshot. Armed by `browser.real_profile_autoclose: true`, but **never automatic**: when the profile is locked Hermes always stops and the agent asks the user first; only on approval does it run the command.
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes browser [-h] {close-profile}`; `hermes browser close-profile [-h]`. No other flags.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Destructive — unsaved tabs in that browser are lost. Browser process tree terminated.
- **Config / env:** `browser.real_profile_autoclose` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:631`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** Help text warns it "asks nothing — run only with the user's explicit OK; loses unsaved tabs". If the profile is still locked afterwards (e.g. a background/tray instance relaunched), Hermes stays blocked and tells you to fully quit the browser — **it won't loop or kill again on its own**. No effect on macOS/Linux, where copy-while-running works.
- **Rebuild notes:** Separate "detect lock" from "resolve lock", and make the resolution a user-approved, single-shot action with no retry loop. A better version would offer to copy the profile via a volume-shadow/snapshot API on Windows so the browser never has to close.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `hermes browser --help` shows exactly one subcommand `close-profile` with the destructive warning (evidence: `cli_help/browser.txt`, `cli_help/browser__close-profile.txt`).

### Camofox local mode  `id: docs-features.browser-camofox`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** `CAMOFOX_URL` in `~/.hermes/.env`; selected via `hermes tools` → Browser Automation → Camofox (writes `browser.cloud_provider: camofox`)
- **What it does:** Uses Camofox — a self-hosted Node.js server wrapping Camoufox (a Firefox fork with C++ fingerprint spoofing) — for local anti-detection browsing with no cloud dependency.
- **How it works:** You run the Camofox server yourself (Docker), then point Hermes at it with `CAMOFOX_URL`. Hermes drives it over its HTTP control API (`GET /tabs`, `DELETE /sessions/<user_id>`, tab creation) from `tools/browser_camofox.py` with state in `tools/browser_camofox_state.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** Server-side `make` targets documented on the page: `make up` (build and start with default container settings; auto-detects `aarch64` on M1/M2, `x86_64` on Intel), `make down` (stop and remove the default container), `make reset` (force clean rebuild after upgrading VERSION/RELEASE), `make fetch` (just download binaries without building), `make build` (build the image without starting the default container), `make up ARCH=x86_64`, `make up VERSION=135.0.1 RELEASE=beta.24`. Custom `docker run` documented with `--name camofox-browser`, `--restart unless-stopped`, `-p 9377:9377`, `-p 6080:6080`, `-p 5901:5900`, `-e CAMOFOX_PORT=9377`, `-e ENABLE_VNC=1`, `-e VNC_BIND=0.0.0.0`, `-e VNC_RESOLUTION=1920x1080`, `-e MAX_OLD_SPACE_SIZE=2048`, `-v ~/.camofox-docker:/root/.camofox`. Hermes-side: `CAMOFOX_URL=http://localhost:9377`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Browser sessions on the Camofox server; with VNC enabled the browser runs headed and can be watched at `http://localhost:6080` (noVNC) or via a native VNC client at `localhost:5901`.
- **Config / env:** `browser.cloud_provider: camofox`; env `CAMOFOX_URL`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `CAMOFOX_URL` is **only the server address** — setting it no longer selects the backend once a browser selection exists (never-configured setups still autodetect it). Camofox has no CDP endpoint, so Camofox setups always keep the built-in browser tools (Browser Use mode is unavailable) and `browser_cdp` / `browser_dialog` do not work. If you already ran `make up`, stop and remove that default container (`make down`) before starting a custom one.
- **Rebuild notes:** Model the anti-detection browser as a remote HTTP control API rather than CDP; expect no dialog/frame instrumentation. A better version would expose a CDP-compatible shim so the supervisor and Browser Use driver work uniformly.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `browser.camofox` config subtree at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:649-666`; implementation in `tools/browser_camofox.py`.

### Camofox Docker loopback rewriting  `id: docs-features.browser-camofox-loopback`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `browser.camofox.rewrite_loopback_urls` / `browser.camofox.loopback_host_alias` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`; env `CAMOFOX_REWRITE_LOOPBACK_URLS`, `CAMOFOX_LOOPBACK_HOST_ALIAS`
- **What it does:** When Camofox runs in Docker, rewrites page URLs with loopback hosts so the containerized browser can open web apps served from the host machine.
- **How it works:** Page navigation URLs whose host is `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1` are rewritten to the configured alias (default `host.docker.internal`) before being sent to Camofox. `CAMOFOX_URL` itself is **not** changed.
- **Inputs / options:** `browser.camofox.rewrite_loopback_urls: true|false` (default `false`); `browser.camofox.loopback_host_alias: host.docker.internal` (default; a LAN IP can be used instead). Env equivalents `CAMOFOX_REWRITE_LOOPBACK_URLS=true`, `CAMOFOX_LOOPBACK_HOST_ALIAS=host.docker.internal`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Navigation targets differ from the URL the agent asked for; e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:3000` opens as `http://host.docker.internal:3000` inside the container.
- **Config / env:** `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:661-665`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Only applies to **page navigation URLs** with loopback hosts — not to `CAMOFOX_URL`. Leave it disabled for non-Docker Camofox installs, where the browser already runs on the host and loopback URLs are already correct.
- **Rebuild notes:** Rewrite at the navigation boundary only, and log the original + rewritten URL so debugging isn't confusing. A better version would auto-detect containerization and offer the rewrite instead of requiring a flag.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — both keys with the documented defaults at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:661-665`.

### Camofox persistent browser sessions  `id: docs-features.browser-camofox-persistence`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `browser.camofox.managed_persistence` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`
- **What it does:** Makes cookies and logins survive across agent restarts instead of each Camofox session getting a random identity.
- **How it works:** Hermes sends a deterministic profile-scoped `userId` to Camofox so the server can reuse the same Firefox profile across sessions; skips server-side context destruction on cleanup so cookies and logins survive between agent tasks; and scopes the `userId` to the active Hermes profile so different Hermes profiles get different browser profiles (profile isolation). The stable `userId` is derived from the profile-scoped directory `~/.hermes/browser_auth/camofox/` (or the equivalent under `$HERMES_HOME` for non-default profiles). The actual browser profile data lives on the Camofox server, keyed by that `userId`.
- **Inputs / options:** `browser.camofox.managed_persistence: true` (default `false`). Requires a full Hermes restart to pick up the config.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Persistent Firefox profile on the Camofox server; Hermes-side state directory `~/.hermes/browser_auth/camofox/`.
- **Config / env:** `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:652-655`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Nested path matters** — Hermes reads `browser.camofox.managed_persistence`, *not* a top-level `managed_persistence`; a top-level key is silently ignored and Hermes falls back to a random ephemeral `userId`, losing login state every session. Hermes does **not** force persistence on the server: it only sends a stable `userId`; if the server build always calls `browser.newContext()` without loading a stored profile, sessions cannot persist. Documented verification procedure: (1) start Hermes and Camofox, (2) open a login site in a browser task and sign in manually, (3) end the browser task normally, (4) start a new browser task, (5) open the same site — you should still be signed in; if step 5 logs you out, check the config path, confirm a full restart, and verify the server version supports per-user persistent profiles. To fully reset, clear the profile on the Camofox server **and** remove the Hermes profile's state directory.
- **Rebuild notes:** Derive the persistence key from the profile directory so profile isolation is automatic; validate the config path and warn on the common top-level mistake. A better version would reject unknown top-level config keys outright instead of silently ignoring them.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `managed_persistence` default `False` with the ephemeral-userId fallback documented at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:651-655`.

### Externally managed Camofox sessions (tab adoption)  `id: docs-features.browser-camofox-external`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `browser.camofox.user_id` / `.session_key` / `.adopt_existing_tab`; env `CAMOFOX_USER_ID`, `CAMOFOX_SESSION_KEY`, `CAMOFOX_ADOPT_EXISTING_TAB`
- **What it does:** Lets Hermes operate inside a Camofox identity that another app already drives (a desktop assistant, a custom integration, another agent) instead of spawning its own isolated profile.
- **How it works:** Setting `user_id` opts the session into "externally managed" mode. `session_key` (a.k.a. `listItemId`) is sent on tab creation and used to match an existing tab during adoption; it defaults to a per-task value (`task_<id>`) if unset. With `adopt_existing_tab: true`, on the first browser tool call after a process start Hermes issues `GET /tabs?userId=<user_id>` with a **5-second timeout**; if any tab has `listItemId == session_key` it adopts the most recently created one in that group; otherwise it adopts the most recently created tab for the user (any `listItemId`); if no tabs exist or the request fails it falls back to creating a new tab on the next operation.
- **Inputs / options:** `browser.camofox.user_id: shared-camofox` (default `""`); `browser.camofox.session_key: visible-tab` (default `""`); `browser.camofox.adopt_existing_tab: true|false` (default `false`). Env forms `CAMOFOX_USER_ID`, `CAMOFOX_SESSION_KEY`, `CAMOFOX_ADOPT_EXISTING_TAB` — **env vars take precedence over `config.yaml`**.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Hermes skips destructive cleanup at task end (same as `managed_persistence: true`), so the other app's tab/cookies/profile survive. Hermes does **not** call `DELETE /sessions/<user_id>` — that endpoint wipes all user data and would nuke the external app's session.
- **Config / env:** `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:656-660`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Adoption only fires until `tab_id` is populated for the session. If the external app closes the adopted tab mid-run, the next browser tool call surfaces a Camofox error — **Hermes does not re-poll for a fresh tab on every call**. If `session_key` is left unset and only `user_id` is set, Hermes shares cookies and the profile with the external app but opens its own tab alongside instead of reusing one. **Concurrency:** the external app and Hermes can drive the same `userId` simultaneously, but Camofox does not coordinate per-tab focus between clients — coordinate ownership at the application layer (e.g. the external app pauses while Hermes runs).
- **Rebuild notes:** Model adoption as a one-shot rehydration keyed on (`userId`, `sessionKey`) with a short timeout and a create-new fallback. A better version would subscribe to tab lifecycle events so a closed tab triggers re-adoption instead of an error.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `user_id`, `session_key`, `adopt_existing_tab` present with documented defaults at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:656-660` ("Rehydrate tab_id from Camofox before creating a new tab").

### Camofox VNC live view  `id: docs-features.browser-camofox-vnc`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** automatic in navigation responses when Camofox runs headed
- **What it does:** Surfaces a VNC URL so the user can watch the Camofox browser live.
- **How it works:** When Camofox runs in headed mode (visible browser window), it exposes a VNC port in its health check response. Hermes automatically discovers this and includes the VNC URL in navigation responses, so the agent can share a link.
- **Inputs / options:** Server-side `ENABLE_VNC=1`, `VNC_BIND`, `VNC_RESOLUTION`, published ports `6080` (noVNC) and `5901`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A VNC/noVNC URL embedded in the `browser_navigate` response text.
- **Config / env:** n/a on the Hermes side — discovered from Camofox's health check.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Only present when Camofox runs headed with VNC enabled; headless Camofox exposes no port and no URL appears.
- **Rebuild notes:** Discover observability endpoints from the backend's health check rather than configuring them twice. A better version would render the live view inline in the web dashboard instead of handing out a raw URL.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — Camofox health-check handling in `tools/browser_camofox.py`.

### Lightpanda local engine  `id: docs-features.browser-lightpanda`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** `hermes tools` → Browser Automation → **Lightpanda**; or `browser.cloud_provider: local` + `browser.engine: lightpanda`; or env `AGENT_BROWSER_ENGINE=lightpanda`
- **What it does:** Uses Lightpanda — an open-source headless browser written from scratch in Zig — as the local browser engine: instant startup, 16x lower memory and 9x faster than Chrome, which matters for agents living on small VMs for long stretches.
- **How it works:** Lightpanda is a **local engine** (a browser source, like "Local Browser"), not a cloud provider. Install the binary on `PATH`, then select it. Two driver paths: **(a) Browser Use mode (the default)** — Hermes launches `lightpanda serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port <free>` itself, one process per `browser_exec` session name (or per task), and points the Browser Use CLI at it; no Chromium, Playwright or Node.js needed. The process is reaped after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, on exit, and by the orphan sweep if Hermes crashes. **(b) Built-in browser tools (`/browser use off`)** — Hermes drives Lightpanda through `agent-browser --engine lightpanda` over CDP, the same way it drives local Chrome. Implementation in `tools/browser_lightpanda.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** `browser.engine`: `auto` (Chrome, default) | `lightpanda` | `chrome` (force Chrome explicitly). Env `AGENT_BROWSER_ENGINE=auto|lightpanda|chrome`. `browser.cloud_provider: local`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** One `lightpanda serve` process per session/task, reaped on timeout/exit/crash-sweep.
- **Config / env:** `browser.engine` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:588-602`), `browser.cloud_provider`, env `AGENT_BROWSER_ENGINE`; passed to agent-browser v0.25.3+ as `--engine <value>`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **No graphical renderer** — `capture_screenshot()` is unavailable in Browser Use mode and the tool description tells the model to work text-first. It also **holds one page per session**, so the model is told to call `new_tab()` once and `goto_url()` afterwards (upstream issue lightpanda-io/browser#1962). With the built-in tools there is **automatic Chrome fallback**: Lightpanda handles navigate, snapshot, click, type, scroll, back, press, eval, and Hermes transparently retries on Chrome for anything else; screenshots and `browser_vision` are routed straight to Chrome (`tools/browser_tool.py:5477-5537`, fallback reason string "Lightpanda has no graphical renderer for screenshots; used Chrome for vision capture."). **`browser.engine` is the lowest-precedence browser setting** — a cloud provider (including the Nous subscription browser, and on never-configured setups any `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` / `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env`), Camofox, a `browser.cdp_url` / `/browser connect` override, or `browser.use_real_profile` all take precedence. Picking Lightpanda in `hermes tools` writes `cloud_provider: local` for you; `/browser status` and `hermes doctor` report when the engine is configured but shadowed, and by what.
- **Rebuild notes:** Treat the engine as the lowest-precedence knob and always report *why* it is inactive rather than silently ignoring it. A better version would let per-request capability negotiation pick Lightpanda for text-only steps and Chrome only for screenshot steps automatically, per action rather than per session.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — precedence comment at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:598-601`; shadow-reporting helper printing "⚠ browser.engine is 'lightpanda' but it is NOT in use: {reason}" at `hermes_cli/cli_commands_mixin.py:59` using `lightpanda_engine_status` / `_using_lightpanda_engine` from `tools/browser_tool.py`.

### `/browser connect` — local Chromium-family browser via CDP  `id: docs-features.browser-connect`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** interactive CLI slash command `/browser connect` (also `/browser connect ws://host:port`)
- **What it does:** Attaches the Hermes browser tools to your own running Chrome, Brave, Chromium or Edge instance over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so you can watch the agent work in real time, use your own cookies/sessions, and avoid cloud browser costs.
- **How it works:** `/browser connect` with no argument auto-launches/connects at `http://127.0.0.1:9222`; with an argument it connects to a specific CDP endpoint. If no browser is running with remote debugging, Hermes attempts to auto-launch a supported Chromium-family browser with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`. Detection includes Brave, Brave Origin/Nightly, Google Chrome, Chromium and Microsoft Edge, with Linux install paths and binary names `brave-origin`, `brave-origin-nightly`, `/opt/brave.com/brave-origin/brave-origin`, `/opt/brave.com/brave-origin-nightly/brave-origin`, `/opt/brave-bin/brave`, `/snap/bin/brave`. Dispatch at `hermes_cli/cli_commands_mixin.py:2613` ("Handle /browser connect|disconnect|status — manage live Chromium-family CDP connection"), CDP-URL parsing at `:2662`, session flush at `:2696`, success message "🌐 Browser connected to live Chromium-family browser via CDP" at `:2778`; implementation helpers in `hermes_cli/browser_connect.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** `/browser connect` — auto-launch/connect at `http://127.0.0.1:9222`; `/browser connect ws://host:port` — connect to a specific CDP endpoint; `/browser status` — check current connection; `/browser disconnect` — detach and return to cloud/local mode; `/browser use` — switch to Browser Use mode; `/browser use off` — revert to the built-in browser tools. Usage banner: `Usage: /browser connect|disconnect|status|use` (`:2888`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Sets the CDP endpoint for the session and clears existing browser sessions so the next tool call uses the new backend. Injects a system note telling the agent the user connected their browser tools to a live browser and that it is user-visible (`:2786-2792`); on disconnect injects the corresponding note (`:2813`) and prints "🌐 Browser disconnected from live Chromium-family browser" (`:2807`). If not connected, `/browser disconnect` prints "Browser is not connected to a live Chromium-family browser (already using default mode)" (`:2818`).
- **Config / env:** `browser.cdp_url` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:604`) is the persistent equivalent; `browser.backend` for the `use`/`use off` sub-branch (`:2639`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** **`/browser connect` is an interactive-CLI slash command — it is not dispatched by the gateway.** Running it inside a WebUI, Telegram, Discord or other gateway chat sends the message to the agent as plain text and the command does not execute; start Hermes from the terminal (`hermes` or `hermes chat`). Failure message: "Browser not connected — start a Chromium-family browser with remote debugging and retry /browser connect" (`:2765`) / "and retry /browser connect." (`hermes_cli/browser_connect.py:1376`). **Chrome 136+ silently refuses to open the remote debugging port when `--remote-debugging-port` is combined with the default user-data-dir** — the browser launches but nothing listens on 9222 and there is no error message; the fix is always passing `--user-data-dir` pointing somewhere other than the default profile (e.g. `$HOME/.hermes/chrome-debug`). Applies to Chrome, Chromium, Edge and Brave builds that picked up the change. Without `--user-data-dir`, launching while a regular instance is already running typically opens a new window on the existing process, which was not started with the debug flag.
- **Rebuild notes:** Ship the exact launch command lines per OS/browser and detect the Chrome-136 silent failure by probing `/json/version` after launch. A better version would auto-create the dedicated debug profile and offer a one-click "launch debuggable browser" from the CLI.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — subcommand dispatch, messages and usage text at `hermes_cli/cli_commands_mixin.py:2613-2892`.

### Documented manual CDP launch commands  `id: docs-features.browser-cdp-launch-recipes`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** browser.md → "Local Chromium-family browser via CDP" → tip block
- **What it does:** Gives copy-paste commands to start a Chromium-family browser with CDP enabled on a dedicated profile, so `/browser connect` works.
- **How it works:** Each recipe passes `--remote-debugging-port=9222`, `--user-data-dir=$HOME/.hermes/chrome-debug` (quoted on macOS), `--no-first-run` and `--no-default-browser-check`, backgrounded with `&`.
- **Inputs / options:** Four documented recipes: Linux — Brave (`brave-browser`); Linux — Google Chrome (`google-chrome`); macOS — Brave (`"/Applications/Brave Browser.app/Contents/MacOS/Brave Browser"`); macOS — Google Chrome (`"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome"`). Verification command: `curl http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A fresh browser process listening on port 9222 with a separate profile directory at `$HOME/.hermes/chrome-debug`.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** `--no-first-run --no-default-browser-check` skips the first-launch wizard for the fresh profile. No Windows recipe is documented (doc gap).
- **Rebuild notes:** Store these as data (a per-platform launch table) rather than prose so the CLI can run them. A better version would offer `hermes browser launch-debug` to run the right one automatically.
- **Verification:** doc drift — documentation-only content; only Linux and macOS recipes are given although `/browser connect` supports Windows browsers (see real-profile Windows notes).

### WSL2 + Windows Chrome guidance (prefer MCP)  `id: docs-features.browser-wsl2-guidance`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** browser.md → "WSL2 + Windows Chrome: prefer MCP over `/browser connect`"
- **What it does:** Tells users running Hermes inside WSL2 who want to control a Chrome window on the Windows host to use a Windows-side browser MCP server rather than `/browser connect`.
- **How it works:** Reasons given: `/browser connect` expects Hermes itself to reach a usable CDP endpoint; modern Chrome live-debugging sessions often expose a host-local endpoint not directly reachable from WSL the way a classic `9222` port is; the cleanest integration is a Windows-side browser MCP server attaching to Chrome with Hermes talking to that MCP server.
- **Inputs / options:** Recommended tool: `chrome-devtools-mcp` through Hermes MCP support. Cross-reference: `../../guides/use-mcp-with-hermes.md#wsl2-bridge-hermes-in-wsl-to-windows-chrome`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a (guidance only)
- **Config / env:** MCP server configuration (see the MCP feature page).
- **Edge cases / guards:** n/a
- **Rebuild notes:** Document the cross-boundary case explicitly; agents in a VM/container should reach host browsers via a host-side agent, not raw ports. A better version would ship a first-class WSL bridge that detects the host Chrome automatically.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — guidance only; MCP support exists (see the `mcp.md` page entries).

### Local browser mode (`agent-browser`)  `id: docs-features.browser-local-mode`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** implicit default when no cloud credentials are set and `/browser connect` is not used
- **What it does:** Runs the browser tools against a local Chromium install driven by the `agent-browser` CLI.
- **How it works:** Hermes shells out to `agent-browser`, which resolves automatically via `npx agent-browser` on first browser-tool use. The same CLI backs the hybrid-routing local sidecar.
- **Inputs / options:** Optional pre-install `npm install -g agent-browser` to avoid the one-time npx fetch. `hermes setup tools → Browser Automation` auto-installs it.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A local Chromium process per task; a one-time npx download on first use if not pre-installed.
- **Config / env:** `browser.command_timeout` (default `30` seconds, for screenshot/navigate/etc. — **undocumented on this page**), `browser.inactivity_timeout`, `AGENT_BROWSER_ARGS`, `AGENT_BROWSER_ENGINE`, `AGENT_BROWSER_HEADED`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Requires Node/npx available on the host. The `browser` toolset must be in the config's `toolsets` list.
- **Rebuild notes:** Resolve the driver lazily through the platform package manager and cache the resolution. A better version would vendor a static driver binary so first use has no network dependency.
- **Verification:** partial — implemented as documented, but `browser.command_timeout` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:586`) governs local browser command timeouts and is **not** mentioned anywhere on browser.md (doc gap).

### `AGENT_BROWSER_ARGS` — extra Chromium launch flags  `id: docs-features.browser-agent-browser-args`
- **Surface:** Env
- **Where:** environment variable `AGENT_BROWSER_ARGS`
- **What it does:** Passes extra Chromium launch flags to the local browser, comma- or newline-separated.
- **How it works:** Hermes **auto-injects** `--no-sandbox,--disable-dev-shm-usage` when it detects root or AppArmor-restricted unprivileged user namespaces (Ubuntu 23.10+, DGX Spark, many container images), so most users don't need to set this.
- **Inputs / options:** `AGENT_BROWSER_ARGS=--no-sandbox` (example); comma- or newline-separated list of flags.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Flags appended to the Chromium launch command line.
- **Config / env:** env only.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Setting it disables the auto-injection** — so a manual value must include `--no-sandbox` / `--disable-dev-shm-usage` if the host needs them.
- **Rebuild notes:** Auto-detect sandbox-hostile hosts and inject the minimum flags; make the manual override additive-with-warning rather than replacing. A better version would merge user flags with auto-detected ones and only warn on conflicts.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — auto-injection behaviour is documented in the browser env section; behaviour matches the local `agent-browser` launch path in `tools/browser_tool.py`.

### `browser_navigate`  `id: docs-features.browser-tool-navigate`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** tool `browser_navigate`
- **What it does:** Navigates to a URL. Must be called before any other browser tool; initializes the session.
- **How it works:** `tools/browser_tool.py:4175` — `browser_navigate(url: str, task_id: Optional[str] = None) -> str`. Runs the SSRF guards (`:4165`, `:4167`) and hybrid-routing decision (`:2005`) before dispatching to the active backend. Registered at `tools/browser_tool.py:2781` / `:6372`. Returns an automatic snapshot subject to `browser.snapshot_threshold`.
- **Inputs / options:** `url` (required); `task_id` (optional, session isolation). Example prompt from the docs: `Navigate to https://github.com/NousResearch`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Creates/initializes the browser session; returns page state including an automatic snapshot; on Camofox with VNC also returns a VNC URL; starts session recording if `browser.record_sessions` is on.
- **Config / env:** `browser.snapshot_threshold`, `browser.allow_private_urls`, `browser.auto_local_for_private_urls`, `browser.record_sessions`, `browser.command_timeout`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Blocked URLs return `{"success": false, "error": "Blocked: URL targets a private or internal address"}` or `"Blocked: URL targets a cloud metadata endpoint"`.
