## Page: `mcp.md` — MCP (Model Context Protocol)

### MCP client support (overview)  `id: docs-features.mcp-overview`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/config.yaml` → `mcp_servers:`; `hermes chat`
- **What it does:** Lets Hermes connect to external MCP tool servers so the agent can use tools that live outside Hermes — GitHub, databases, file systems, browser stacks, internal APIs.
- **How it works:** Ships with the standard install — no extra step. Add a server under `mcp_servers` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`, start `hermes chat`, and ask for the MCP-backed capability; Hermes discovers the server's tools and uses them like any other tool. Implementation: `tools/mcp_tool.py` (client, sampling, elicitation, filtering), `hermes_cli/mcp_config.py`, `hermes_cli/mcp_startup.py`, `hermes_cli/mcp_security.py`, `hermes_cli/mcp_catalog.py`, `hermes_cli/mcp_picker.py`, `tools/mcp_oauth.py`, `tools/mcp_oauth_manager.py`, `tools/mcp_dashboard_oauth.py`, `tools/mcp_schema_cache.py`, `tools/mcp_stdio_watchdog.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** Documented capability list: access to external tool ecosystems without writing a native Hermes tool first; local stdio servers and remote HTTP MCP servers in the same config; automatic tool discovery and registration at startup; utility wrappers for MCP resources and prompts when supported by the server; per-server filtering so you expose only the MCP tools you want Hermes to see. Quick-start example: `filesystem` with `command: "npx"` and `args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/home/user/projects"]`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** MCP tools registered into the normal tool registry under a prefixed name; one runtime toolset per contributing server.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.*` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Coming from Claude Code, the `mcpServers` block in `~/.claude.json` maps to `mcp_servers` in Hermes' `config.yaml`, and `hermes import-agent claude-code` migrates it (along with skills and instructions) automatically.
- **Rebuild notes:** Treat MCP as a first-class tool source registered into the same registry as native tools, with per-server namespacing and filtering. A better version would let the user browse and pin exact tool schema versions so a server update can't silently change a tool's contract.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — client implementation in `tools/mcp_tool.py` (config schema documented in its module docstring at `:14-80`).

### `hermes mcp` command group  `id: docs-features.mcp-cli`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp [subcommand]`
- **What it does:** Manages MCP server connections and runs Hermes as an MCP server.
- **How it works:** `hermes mcp` with no subcommand opens the interactive catalog picker (the documented default).
- **Inputs / options:** Thirteen subcommands (11 unique + 2 aliases): `serve` (run Hermes as an MCP server, exposing conversations to other agents); `add` (add an MCP server — discovery-first install); `remove` / `rm` (remove an MCP server); `list` / `ls` (list configured MCP servers); `test` (test MCP server connection); `configure` / `config` (toggle tool selection); `login` (force re-authentication for an OAuth-based MCP server); `reauth` (re-authenticate one OAuth MCP server, or all with `--all`); `picker` (interactive catalog picker, also the default for `hermes mcp`); `catalog` (list Nous-approved MCPs available for one-click install); `install` (install a catalog MCP by name). Group-level flags: `-h/--help`; `--accept-hooks` (auto-approve unseen shell hooks without a TTY prompt, equivalent to `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1` / `hooks_auto_accept: true`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Writes to `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (`mcp_servers`) and `~/.hermes/.env`; OAuth tokens to `~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/`.
- **Config / env:** `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS`, `hooks_auto_accept`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `reauth` requires either a `name` or `--all` (the positional is optional; omit it with `--all`).
- **Rebuild notes:** Make the bare command the interactive picker so discovery is the default path, with scriptable subcommands underneath. A better version would add `hermes mcp doctor` to test every configured server at once.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — full subcommand list from `hermes mcp --help` (evidence: `cli_help/mcp.txt`).

### `hermes mcp add` (discovery-first install)  `id: docs-features.mcp-add`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp add <name> [options]`
- **What it does:** Adds an MCP server to config, discovering its transport details and tools first.
- **How it works:** Takes a positional server `name` used as the config key under `mcp_servers`.
- **Inputs / options:** `name` (positional, required — server name used as config key); `-h/--help`; `--url URL` (HTTP/SSE endpoint URL); `--command MCP_COMMAND` (stdio command, e.g. `npx`); `--args ...` (arguments for the stdio command — **must be the last option**); `--auth {oauth,header}` (auth method); `--preset PRESET` (known MCP preset name); `--connect-timeout CONNECT_TIMEOUT` (timeout in seconds for initial connection and tool discovery); `--env [ENV ...]` (environment variables for stdio servers, `KEY=VALUE`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** A new `mcp_servers.<name>` block in `config.yaml`.
- **Config / env:** writes `mcp_servers.<name>.command|args|env|url|auth|connect_timeout`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `--args` consumes the rest of the command line, so it must come last. A `--preset` only supplies defaults — anything else passed on the same command line still wins.
- **Rebuild notes:** Accept transport flags and a preset in one command, with the preset as the lowest-precedence layer. A better version would probe the server before writing config and refuse to persist an unreachable entry unless forced.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — all eight options from `hermes mcp add --help` (evidence: `cli_help/mcp__add.txt`).

### MCP catalog — one-click install for Nous-approved MCPs  `id: docs-features.mcp-catalog`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp` (picker), `hermes mcp catalog`, `hermes mcp install <name>`
- **What it does:** Ships a curated catalog of MCP servers Nous staff has reviewed and merged, disabled by default, installable in one command.
- **How it works:** Catalog entries are stored under `optional-mcps/` in the hermes-agent repo — **presence in that directory means Nous approval. There is no community submission tier; entries are added by merging a PR.** Manifests live at `optional-mcps/<name>/manifest.yaml` (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/tree/main/optional-mcps). Implementation: `hermes_cli/mcp_catalog.py`, `hermes_cli/mcp_picker.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes mcp` — interactive picker (default); `hermes mcp catalog` — plain-text list, scriptable; `hermes mcp install <name>` — install a catalog entry by name (`hermes mcp install [-h] identifier`, where identifier is a catalog entry name **or `official/<name>`**). The picker shows each entry with its status — documented example rows: `n8n available Manage and inspect n8n workflows from Hermes`, `linear enabled Linear issue/project management (remote OAuth)`, `github installed (disabled) GitHub repo + PR tools`. Hit `Enter` on a row to install (and walk through any required credentials), enable, disable, or uninstall.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Cloned repos, bootstrap commands run, credentials written to `~/.hermes/.env`, and `mcp_servers.<name>` written to `config.yaml`.
- **Config / env:** `~/.hermes/.env` for API keys and non-secret values (base URLs); `mcp_servers.<name>.auth: oauth` for remote OAuth entries.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Catalog entries can require an **API key** (Hermes prompts at install time and writes the value to `~/.hermes/.env`; non-secret values like base URLs go to the same file), **OAuth (remote MCP)** (written as `auth: oauth` in config; the MCP client opens a browser on first connection), or **OAuth (third-party provider like Google/GitHub)** (Hermes points you at `hermes auth <provider>` if you haven't authenticated already). **MCPs are never auto-updated** — re-run `hermes mcp install <name>` to refresh after a Hermes update if a manifest version changed. **GitHub is deliberately not in the catalog**: its hosted MCP requires each client to bring its own OAuth app (generic dynamic client registration is rejected), and Hermes's bundled `github/*` skills driving the `gh` CLI are a more capable integration; on Desktop, GitHub mentions instead offer the `github-auth` skill when `gh` isn't signed in yet.
- **Rebuild notes:** Gate a curated catalog behind PR review with the manifest directory itself as the approval record, and never auto-update installed entries. A better version would sign manifests and verify the signature at install time.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — **65** catalog directories exist under `optional-mcps/` (airtable, algolia, alltrails, amplitude, asana, atlassian, attio, aws-knowledge, betterstack, buildkite, calendly, canva, circleci, clickup, close, cloudflare, cloudinary, comfy-cloud, context7, craft, datadog, deepwiki, dropbox, figma, fireflies, gamma, gitlab, globalping, grafana, hugging_face, indeed, intercom, kiwi, klaviyo, linear, microsoft-learn, miro, mixpanel, monday, motherduck, n8n, neon, netlify, notion, paypal, plaid, postman, prisma-postgres, railway, robinhood, semgrep, sentry, square, strava, stripe, supabase, todoist, trivago, twelve-data, twilio-docs, unreal-engine, vercel, webflow, wolfram, wordpress-com) — and `github` is indeed absent, matching the doc's claim.

### MCP catalog trust model  `id: docs-features.mcp-catalog-trust`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** mcp.md → "Trust model"; web dashboard MCP page
- **What it does:** States exactly what installing a catalog entry executes, and what the user should read before installing.
- **How it works:** Installing a catalog entry runs whatever the manifest specifies — `git clone`, the entry's `bootstrap` commands (`pip install`, `npm install`, etc.), and ultimately the MCP server's own code. Manifests are gated by PR review into the hermes-agent repo, so Nous has reviewed each entry before it shipped — **but you should still read the manifest before installing**, especially the `source:` field's repository, the `install.bootstrap:` commands, and any `transport.command:` invocation.
- **Inputs / options:** Inspect `optional-mcps/<name>/manifest.yaml` on GitHub; the picker prints the manifest's `source:` URL at install time.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Arbitrary code execution scoped to whatever the manifest declares.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** The **web dashboard's MCP page** surfaces the same detail per catalog entry — transport, auth type, the endpoint URL (HTTP) or command + args (stdio), the git install source/ref and bootstrap commands, and setup notes — with the `source:` rendered as a **clickable link**, so you can inspect exactly what an entry connects to or runs before clicking Install.
- **Rebuild notes:** Surface every executable field of a manifest in the install UI before the user commits, and state plainly that review ≠ sandboxing. A better version would run bootstrap commands in a container by default.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — catalog manifests present under `optional-mcps/<name>/`; picker in `hermes_cli/mcp_picker.py`.

### MCP tool selection at install time  `id: docs-features.mcp-tool-selection`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp install <name>` → checklist "Select tools for '<name>' (SPACE toggle, ENTER confirm)"
- **What it does:** After credentials are configured, probes the MCP server to list every tool it exposes and lets you check exactly which ones Hermes registers.
- **How it works:** Pre-checked rows come from, in order: (1) **your prior selection** if you've installed this entry before — reinstalls preserve what you had and the manifest's defaults don't override it; (2) **the manifest's `tools.default_enabled`** if the entry declares one (some catalog entries pre-prune mutating or rarely-useful tools); (3) **everything** if neither applies. Submitting with ENTER writes only the checked tools into `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include`. **If you select everything, no filter is written** (cleanest config shape, identical behavior).
- **Inputs / options:** SPACE toggles a row, ENTER confirms. Documented example rows: `[x] find_issues Find issues matching a query`, `[x] get_issue Get a single issue`, `[x] create_issue Create a new issue`, `[ ] delete_workspace Delete a Linear workspace`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include` (or `tools.exclude` for `default_excluded` entries), or no filter at all.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include` / `.exclude`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Entries with very large auto-generated surfaces (e.g. `cloudflare`, ~3,300 OpenAPI endpoint tools) instead declare `tools.default_excluded` — a curated block-list of names and glob patterns; installing one of these **skips the checklist entirely** and writes `tools.exclude`, so everything not matched stays enabled **including tools the server adds later**; edit `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.exclude` to re-enable a family. **If the probe fails** (server unreachable, OAuth not yet completed, backing service not running) the install still succeeds: the manifest's `tools.default_enabled` is applied directly if declared, or no filter is written if not — re-run `hermes mcp configure <name>` once reachable.
- **Rebuild notes:** Preserve a prior selection over a manifest default on reinstall, and treat "all selected" as "no filter" so config stays minimal. A better version would diff the server's tool list on each connect and prompt about newly-added tools instead of silently including them under an exclude-list.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — install/probe flow in `hermes_cli/mcp_catalog.py` and `hermes_cli/mcp_picker.py`; `cloudflare` catalog entry present under `optional-mcps/cloudflare/`.

### `hermes mcp configure` (update tool selection later)  `id: docs-features.mcp-configure`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp configure <name>` (alias `hermes mcp config`)
- **What it does:** Reopens the install-time tool checklist with your current selection pre-checked.
- **How it works:** Documented use: when you want more tools enabled, or when the server has added new tools you want to opt into.
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes mcp configure [-h] name` — `name` (positional, required, server name to configure); `-h/--help`. No other flags.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Rewrites `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include`.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Also the documented recovery path when the install-time probe failed.
- **Rebuild notes:** Make the post-install editor the same widget as the install-time one so there's one code path. A better version would show which tools are new since the last configure.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `hermes mcp configure --help` shows exactly one positional (evidence: `cli_help/mcp__configure.txt`).

### MCP manifest version compatibility  `id: docs-features.mcp-manifest-version`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp` picker
- **What it does:** Keeps the catalog forward-compatible when a newer manifest schema ships than the installed Hermes understands.
- **How it works:** Manifests pin a `manifest_version`. If a PR adds an entry with a newer `manifest_version` than the installed Hermes understands, the picker **surfaces a warning (`⚠ '<name>' requires a newer Hermes`) for that entry instead of silently hiding it**.
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes update` to install the latest Hermes when the warning appears.
- **Outputs / side effects:** The entry is shown but not installable on the current version.
- **Config / env:** manifest `manifest_version` field.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Silently hiding would leave the user thinking the entry doesn't exist — the warning is deliberate.
- **Rebuild notes:** Version the manifest schema and surface incompatibility as a visible, actionable row rather than filtering it out. A better version would state which Hermes version is required.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — manifest handling in `hermes_cli/mcp_catalog.py`.

### Runtime `${ENV_VAR}` and context-variable substitution  `id: docs-features.mcp-env-substitution`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.command`, `.args`, `.url`, `.headers`; catalog manifests' `transport.*`
- **What it does:** Resolves `${VAR}` placeholders inside a server's transport fields at server-connect time from environment variables, which include everything in `~/.hermes/.env`.
- **How it works:** Substitution applies to `transport.command`, `transport.args`, `transport.url` and `headers`. Useful when a catalog entry references a value configured elsewhere — e.g. `${HOME}/foo` or `${MY_PROVIDER_TOKEN}`.
- **Inputs / options:** Environment placeholders `${VAR}`. **Cursor-style context variables** are also substituted (**case-sensitive**): `${userHome}` (home directory), `${workspaceFolder}` (session workspace root), `${workspaceFolderBasename}`, and `${pathSeparator}` / `${/}` (the OS path separator).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Resolved command lines / URLs / headers at connect time.
- **Config / env:** everything in `~/.hermes/.env` plus the process environment.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Distinct from `${INSTALL_DIR}` in catalog manifests**, which is substituted at *install time* with the path the catalog cloned the entry's repo into. Full details in `/docs/reference/mcp-config-reference`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Resolve at connect time (not load time) so a `.env` edit takes effect on reconnect; keep install-time and runtime placeholder namespaces distinct. A better version would fail loudly on an unresolved placeholder rather than passing the literal `${VAR}` through.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — substitution handling in `tools/mcp_tool.py` / `hermes_cli/mcp_config.py`; full reference cross-linked to `/docs/reference/mcp-config-reference`.

### Catalog `suggest:` metadata (Desktop composer pills)  `id: docs-features.mcp-suggest`
- **Surface:** Desktop app
- **Where:** Desktop app composer → one-click "Add &lt;server&gt;" pill
- **What it does:** Lets a catalog manifest advertise keywords and hostnames so a UI can offer a one-click install when your draft mentions them.
- **How it works:** A manifest may declare an optional `suggest:` block with `keywords:` and/or `hosts:` lists. UI surfaces (currently the Desktop app's composer) offer the pill when your draft mentions one of the keywords **as a completed word**, or contains a pasted link whose **hostname ends with one of the host suffixes**.
- **Inputs / options:** manifest `suggest.keywords`, `suggest.hosts`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** An "Add &lt;server&gt;" pill in the composer.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Purely advisory** — installs still flow through the same validated catalog/config paths. Most hosted remote entries (Atlassian, Sentry, Notion, Stripe, Vercel, Supabase, and friends) declare it. On Desktop, GitHub mentions instead offer the `github-auth` skill when `gh` isn't signed in yet.
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep suggestion metadata advisory and route the actual install through the validated path, so a manifest can't shortcut consent. A better version would let the user mute suggestions per server.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — catalog entries for atlassian, sentry, notion, stripe, vercel, supabase all present under `optional-mcps/`.

### Stdio MCP servers  `id: docs-features.mcp-stdio`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>` with `command` / `args` / `env`
- **What it does:** Runs an MCP server as a local subprocess talking over stdin/stdout.
- **How it works:** Documented example: `github` with `command: "npx"`, `args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]`, `env: {GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN: "***"}`.
- **Inputs / options:** `command` (string — executable), `args` (list), `env` (mapping of environment variables passed to the stdio server).
- **Outputs / side effects:** A child process per server.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.command|args|env`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Documented "use stdio when": the server is installed locally; you want low-latency access to local resources; you are following MCP server docs that show `command`, `args`, and `env`. **Stdio env filtering** applies (see `mcp-stdio-env-filtering`). `identity_header` is ignored on stdio with a warning (stdio transports have no headers).
- **Rebuild notes:** Spawn per-server subprocesses with an explicit env allowlist, never the inherited shell env. A better version would sandbox each stdio server (namespace/seccomp) rather than relying on env hygiene alone.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — stdio transport handling in `tools/mcp_tool.py` (module docstring example at `:14-32`).

### HTTP MCP servers  `id: docs-features.mcp-http`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>` with `url` / `headers`
- **What it does:** Connects Hermes directly to a remote HTTP MCP endpoint.
- **How it works:** Documented example: `remote_api` with `url: "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"` and `headers: {Authorization: "Bearer ***"}`.
- **Inputs / options:** `url` (string — HTTP MCP endpoint), `headers` (mapping of HTTP headers).
- **Outputs / side effects:** HTTP/SSE connection; no local subprocess.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.url|headers`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Documented "use HTTP when": the MCP server is hosted elsewhere; your organization exposes internal MCP endpoints; you do not want Hermes spawning a local subprocess for that integration.
- **Rebuild notes:** Support both transports in the same config namespace so switching is a two-key edit. A better version would auto-detect SSE vs streamable-HTTP rather than requiring the URL shape to imply it.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — HTTP transport handling in `tools/mcp_tool.py`.

### OAuth-authenticated HTTP MCP servers (`auth: oauth`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-oauth`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.auth: oauth`; `hermes mcp login <server>`, `hermes mcp reauth`
- **What it does:** Handles OAuth 2.1 for hosted MCP servers (Cloudflare, Linear, Sentry, Atlassian, Asana, Figma, Stripe, …) that require it instead of a static bearer token.
- **How it works:** Hermes handles **discovery, client identification, PKCE, token exchange, refresh, and step-up auth** via the MCP Python SDK. It identifies itself with a **Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD)** on servers that support one, and falls back to **Dynamic Client Registration (DCR)** on those that don't — both automatic, nothing to configure. On first connect Hermes prints an authorize URL, opens the browser when possible, and waits for the OAuth callback on a local loopback port. Implementation: `tools/mcp_oauth.py`, `tools/mcp_oauth_manager.py`, `tools/mcp_dashboard_oauth.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** `auth: oauth`; optional `oauth:` sub-block with `client_id`, `client_secret`, `redirect_port`, `redirect_uri`, `redirect_host`, `client_name`. CLI: `hermes mcp login <name>` (force re-authentication for one server), `hermes mcp reauth [name] [--all]` (re-authenticate one OAuth server, or every OAuth server in config one at a time).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Tokens cached at `~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/<server>.json` with **0o600 perms**; subsequent runs reuse them silently until refresh fails.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.auth`, `.oauth.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Figma** — its hosted endpoint (`https://mcp.figma.com/mcp`) allowlists DCR by **exact `client_name`**: bare `"Hermes Agent"` 403s, while `"Claude Code"` and `"Codex"` succeed, so Hermes auto-sets `oauth.client_name: "Claude Code"` for `mcp.figma.com`. **Config auto-reload race** — editing `~/.hermes/config.yaml` from inside a running session auto-reloads MCP connections with a **30s timeout**, which is not enough for an interactive OAuth flow; add the entry, then run `hermes mcp login <server>` from a fresh terminal, which waits the full **5 minutes**.
- **Rebuild notes:** Automate CIMD-then-DCR fallback and cache tokens at 0o600 per server. A better version would surface token expiry in `hermes mcp list` so a silent refresh failure is visible before a tool call fails.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — OAuth modules present (`tools/mcp_oauth.py`, `tools/mcp_oauth_manager.py`, `tools/mcp_dashboard_oauth.py`); `login` and `reauth --all` confirmed in `cli_help/mcp__login.txt` and `cli_help/mcp__reauth.txt`; `figma` catalog entry present under `optional-mcps/figma/`.

### MCP OAuth on remote / headless hosts  `id: docs-features.mcp-oauth-remote`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.oauth.redirect_port` / `.redirect_uri` / `.redirect_host`; Desktop MCP setup UI; interactive paste-back prompt
- **What it does:** Provides four documented ways to complete an MCP OAuth flow when Hermes runs on a different machine than your browser, so the loopback callback can still be delivered.
- **How it works:** **(1) Hermes Desktop (automatic)** — running the OAuth sign-in from the Desktop app's MCP setup UI against a remote backend makes Desktop host the callback listener on *your* machine and relay the authorization back to the gateway automatically, with no tunnel, paste or proxy; requires both the Desktop app and the backend to be up to date. **(2) Paste-back (no setup)** — on an interactive terminal Hermes prints "Or paste the redirect URL here…" alongside the authorize URL; open the URL, approve, copy the full URL the browser ends up on (**the redirect will show a connection error — that's expected**), paste it at the prompt; bare `?code=…&state=…` query strings work too. **(3) SSH port forward** — `ssh -N -L <port>:127.0.0.1:<port> user@host` in a separate terminal, then let the redirect flow normally. **(4) Proxied callback (`redirect_uri`)** — when a public HTTPS endpoint forwards to the host (e.g. a Tailscale Funnel or reverse proxy pointed at the callback port), set `oauth.redirect_uri` and the browser redirect reaches Hermes on its own.
- **Inputs / options:** `oauth.redirect_port: 8765` (fixed port for the proxy to target); `oauth.redirect_uri: "https://oauth.example.ts.net/callback"`; `oauth.redirect_host: localhost`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Token written to `~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/<server>.json`.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.oauth.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **WAF rejects `127.0.0.1` redirect URIs** — a few providers front their authorization server with a WAF that 403s any authorize request whose query string contains a literal `127.0.0.1` (Reclaim.ai's AWS API Gateway is a known example — every attempt returns `{"message":"Forbidden"}` before reaching the OAuth app); set `oauth.redirect_host: localhost` to use `http://localhost:<port>/callback` instead — **the callback listener still binds `127.0.0.1` either way**. For fully headless gateways (messaging bot, no interactive terminal at all), the optional `mcp-oauth-remote-gateway` skill walks the agent through completing the flow manually and writing tokens where Hermes expects them. Full walkthrough (DCR-less servers e.g. Slack, pre-registered `client_id`/`client_secret`, scope customization, re-auth) in `/guides/oauth-over-ssh.md#mcp-servers`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Offer paste-back on any interactive terminal as the zero-setup fallback and let a proxy own the redirect for headless hosts. A better version would let the CLI print a QR/short code so a phone browser can complete the flow.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — remote OAuth relay in `tools/mcp_dashboard_oauth.py`; redirect knobs handled in `tools/mcp_oauth.py`.

### MCP OAuth pitfall — providers without automatic registration  `id: docs-features.mcp-oauth-no-dcr`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.oauth.client_id` / `.client_secret`
- **What it does:** Documents servers that reject Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) and how to supply your own OAuth client.
- **How it works:** Some servers reject the DCR step that bare `auth: oauth` relies on — Google's official Drive server (`https://drivemcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1`) returns a `400 Bad Request`, so no OAuth client is created and no token is acquired. Fix: create an OAuth client in the provider's console and add `oauth.client_id` + `oauth.client_secret` to config, then run `hermes mcp login <name>` — with a pre-registered client, Hermes skips registration and runs the normal browser authorization flow.
- **Inputs / options:** `oauth.client_id: "<your-oauth-client-id>"`, `oauth.client_secret: "<your-oauth-client-secret>"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Token acquired via the standard authorization-code flow.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.oauth.client_id|client_secret`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **The symptom is subtle** — these servers also serve `tools/list` *without* auth, so `hermes mcp login` can list the tools and look like it worked, but every real tool call later times out. `hermes mcp login` **now detects this** (it checks that a token actually landed on disk) and tells you to supply your own OAuth client. Atlassian is named as a second affected provider.
- **Rebuild notes:** Verify success by checking that a token file exists, not by whether the connection returned a tool list. A better version would attempt an authenticated no-op call as the login success test.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — token-on-disk check in the login path (`tools/mcp_oauth_manager.py`); `atlassian` catalog entry present under `optional-mcps/atlassian/`.

### mTLS / client certificates for MCP  `id: docs-features.mcp-mtls`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.client_cert` / `.client_key`
- **What it does:** Supports remote HTTP MCP servers requiring mutual TLS (client-certificate authentication).
- **How it works:** `_resolve_client_cert(server_name, config)` at `tools/mcp_tool.py:1511` resolves the config and passes the certificate to the underlying HTTP client for the TLS handshake. It returns `None` if neither `client_cert` nor `client_key` is set (`:1517`), a single absolute path string for a combined PEM (`:1518`), or a `(cert, key)` / `(cert, key, password)` tuple for the list forms (`:1521-1522`).
- **Inputs / options:** Three documented shapes for `client_cert` — **a single combined PEM path** (`client_cert: "~/.certs/mcp-client.pem"`); **a `[cert, key]` 2-tuple** (`client_cert: ["~/.certs/mcp-client.crt", "~/.certs/mcp-client.key"]`, equivalent to `client_cert` + `client_key`); **a `[cert, key, password]` 3-tuple** where the third element is the key passphrase for an encrypted private key (`client_cert: ["…crt", "…key", "${MCP_KEY_PASSWORD}"]`). You can also keep cert and key fully separate via `client_cert` (combined PEM) plus an explicit `client_key`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Client certificate presented during the TLS handshake.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.client_cert`, `.client_key`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Paths support `~` expansion. A **missing file raises a clear, server-scoped error rather than an opaque TLS handshake failure**. Specifying both the list form and a separate `client_key` errors: "MCP server '<name>': specify either client_cert as a list [cert, key] OR client_cert + client_key, not both" (`tools/mcp_tool.py:1553-1554`); the 3-tuple's password element is validated at `:1566`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Accept all three PEM shapes and reject ambiguous combinations with a named error mentioning the server. A better version would support OS keystore references instead of on-disk PEM paths.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `_resolve_client_cert` at `tools/mcp_tool.py:1511-1570`, including the mutual-exclusion error at `:1553`.

### Per-user identity header (`identity_header`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-identity-header`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.identity_header`
- **What it does:** Sends a caller-identity header on every request to remote HTTP/SSE MCP servers that key behaviour on it — per-user rate limits, audit trails, multi-tenant routing.
- **How it works:** Config block `{name, value_from, value}`. `value_from: static` sends the literal `value` from `config.yaml`. `value_from: profile` sends the **active Hermes profile name, resolved once at connect time** — useful when multiple profiles on one machine talk to the same server and it needs to tell them apart. Documented at `tools/mcp_tool.py:40` ("optional per-user identity header attached").
- **Inputs / options:** `identity_header.name` (e.g. `"X-User-Id"`); `identity_header.value_from` — `"static"` (default) or `"profile"`; `identity_header.value` (**required for static**).
- **Outputs / side effects:** One extra HTTP header per request.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.identity_header.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **An explicit entry in the server's `headers` mapping with the same name (any casing) always wins** — the identity header never overrides your own header config. **Invalid `identity_header` blocks are warned about and ignored** — they never block the server from connecting. **On stdio servers the key is ignored with a warning** (stdio transports have no headers).
- **Rebuild notes:** Let explicit headers win over derived ones and degrade a malformed block to a warning rather than a connection failure. A better version would support a signed identity assertion (JWT) instead of a plaintext header value.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `identity_header` documented in the config schema at `tools/mcp_tool.py:40`.

### MCP config reference — common keys  `id: docs-features.mcp-config-keys`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/config.yaml` → `mcp_servers.<name>.*`
- **What it does:** The full documented per-server key table.
- **How it works:** Hermes reads MCP config from `~/.hermes/config.yaml` under `mcp_servers`; the schema is mirrored in `tools/mcp_tool.py`'s module docstring (`:14-80`).
- **Inputs / options:** Fifteen documented keys. `command` (string — executable for a stdio MCP server); `args` (list — arguments for the stdio server); `env` (mapping — environment variables passed to the stdio server); `url` (string — HTTP MCP endpoint); `headers` (mapping — HTTP headers for remote servers); `client_cert` (string | list — combined PEM path, or `[cert, key]` / `[cert, key, password]`); `client_key` (string — client private-key PEM path when separate from `client_cert`); `identity_header` (mapping — `{name, value_from: static|profile, value}`); `timeout` (number — tool call timeout); `connect_timeout` (number — initial connection timeout, **also bounds the MCP `initialize` handshake**); `idle_timeout_seconds` (number — recycle a stdio server after this many seconds without a tool call, `0` = never, default; the server restarts transparently on the next tool call); `max_lifetime_seconds` (number — recycle a stdio server after this total age, `0` = never, default; restarts transparently on next use); `enabled` (bool — if `false`, Hermes skips the server entirely); `supports_parallel_tool_calls` (bool — if `true`, tools from this server may run concurrently); `tools` (mapping — per-server tool filtering and utility policy). Also documented elsewhere on the page: `auth`, `oauth`, `sampling`, `elicitation`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Governs connection, discovery, filtering and lifetime for one server.
- **Config / env:** all under `mcp_servers.<name>`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Minimal stdio example: `filesystem` with `command: "npx"`, `args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/tmp"]`. Minimal HTTP example: `company_api` with `url` + `headers.Authorization`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep one flat per-server key namespace covering both transports so users don't learn two schemas. A better version would ship a JSON Schema for `mcp_servers` and validate on load.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — key set present in the config schema docstring at `tools/mcp_tool.py:14-80`, including `idle_timeout_seconds` (`:26`), `max_lifetime_seconds` (`:27`), `supports_parallel_tool_calls` (`:35`) and `identity_header` (`:40`).

### Recycling memory-heavy stdio MCP servers  `id: docs-features.mcp-recycling`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.idle_timeout_seconds` / `.max_lifetime_seconds`
- **What it does:** Tears down and transparently restarts a memory-heavy stdio MCP server after an idle period or total age, so a resident Chromium doesn't leak hundreds of MB.
- **How it works:** Browser-based MCP servers (e.g. `@playwright/mcp`) keep a full Chromium resident after their first tool call — memory that never gets released. With recycling enabled the server is torn down after the idle/lifetime limit, then **restarted transparently the next time one of its tools is called; its tools stay registered the whole time**. Watchdog implementation: `tools/mcp_stdio_watchdog.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** `idle_timeout_seconds: 900` (recycle after 15 min without a tool call; `0` = never, default); `max_lifetime_seconds: 86400` (and at least once a day regardless; `0` = never, default). Documented example uses `playwright` with `command: "npx"`, `args: ["-y", "@playwright/mcp@latest", "--headless"]`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Subprocess killed and respawned; tool registry unchanged.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.idle_timeout_seconds`, `.max_lifetime_seconds`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Both default to `0` (never recycle) — it's strictly opt-in. Only applies to stdio servers.
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep the tool registry stable across a recycle so the model never sees tools disappear; restart lazily on the next call. A better version would recycle on an RSS threshold rather than a clock.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — watchdog module `tools/mcp_stdio_watchdog.py`; both keys documented at `tools/mcp_tool.py:26-27`.

### MCP presets (`--preset`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-presets`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp add <name> --preset <preset>`
- **What it does:** Fills in the transport details for well-known MCP servers so you don't have to look up the command and args.
- **How it works:** The preset only supplies defaults — anything else (env vars, headers, filtering) passed on the same command line still wins. Documented example `hermes mcp add codex --preset codex` writes the equivalent of `mcp_servers: codex: {command: "codex", args: ["mcp-server"]}`.
- **Inputs / options:** One documented preset: **`codex`** — the Codex CLI's MCP server (`codex mcp-server` over stdio); requires the `codex` CLI on PATH.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `mcp_servers.<name>.command|args` written to `config.yaml`.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** You can pick any local name — `hermes mcp add my-codex --preset codex` is fine; the preset only provides the `command`/`args` defaults.
- **Rebuild notes:** Make presets pure defaults so explicit flags always win, and decouple the preset name from the config key. A better version would resolve presets from the catalog rather than a separate hard-coded table.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `--preset PRESET` flag confirmed by `hermes mcp add --help` (evidence: `cli_help/mcp__add.txt`).

### MCP tool name prefixing  `id: docs-features.mcp-tool-prefix`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** registered tool names of the form `mcp_<server_name>_<tool_name>`
- **What it does:** Prefixes MCP tools so they don't collide with built-in tool names.
- **How it works:** Registered name = `mcp_<server_name>_<tool_name>`, with dots and hyphens normalised to underscores. Documented examples: server `filesystem` + MCP tool `read_file` → `mcp_filesystem_read_file`; server `github` + `create-issue` → `mcp_github_create_issue`; server `my-api` + `query.data` → `mcp_my_api_query_data`.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (automatic)
- **Outputs / side effects:** Prefixed names in the tool registry and in tool-call traces.
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** In practice you usually do not need to call the prefixed name manually — Hermes sees the tool and chooses it during normal reasoning.
- **Rebuild notes:** Namespace by server and normalise separator characters so any upstream naming convention survives. A better version would keep a display name distinct from the wire name so the model reads readable tool names.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — MCP registration in `tools/mcp_tool.py`; the prefix pattern is also visible in the toolset naming (`mcp-<server>`).

### MCP tool-result sanitization (Unicode TAG stripping)  `id: docs-features.mcp-tag-stripping`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** applied to every MCP tool result, resource content, and tool description
- **What it does:** Strips invisible Unicode TAG characters (U+E0000–U+E007F) that render as nothing in terminals and chat UIs but are fully visible to the model — a classic prompt-injection smuggling channel for a malicious or compromised server.
- **How it works:** `tools/ansi_strip.py` defines the plane-14 tag range — comment "Unicode TAG characters (U+E0000–U+E007F). Deprecated as language tags" at `:45`, pattern `[\U000E0000-\U000E007F]` at `:58`, detector `_HAS_UNICODE_TAG` at `:62`, and the stripping helper at `:102-110` with a fast path that returns the input unchanged when no plane-14 tag characters are present.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (always on)
- **Outputs / side effects:** Sanitised text reaching the model.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Legitimate emoji tag sequences (regional flags like 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿) are preserved.** Related agent-side guidance about zero-width characters, bidi embeddings/overrides/isolates and tag characters lives at `agent/learn_prompt.py:159`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Strip the smuggling range at the tool-result boundary, not in the UI, and keep a fast path so the common case costs nothing. A better version would log a warning naming the server whenever tag characters were stripped, so a compromised server is detectable.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — range, regex and helper at `tools/ansi_strip.py:45-110`.

### MCP `_meta` passthrough with reserved-key filtering  `id: docs-features.mcp-meta`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** every MCP tool result
- **What it does:** Surfaces a server's vendor `_meta` mapping to the model alongside the result content, while dropping protocol-reserved keys.
- **How it works:** `_is_reserved_mcp_meta_key(key)` at `tools/mcp_tool.py:1102` returns True when a `modelcontextprotocol` or `mcp` label is followed by at least one more label (`modelcontextprotocol.io/...`, `tools.mcp.com/...`) — the check is `label in ("modelcontextprotocol", "mcp") and i < len(labels) - 1` (`:1117`). `_strip_reserved_meta_keys(meta)` at `:1122` drops those keys (`:1131`). Applied to tool results at `:6348` via `_strip_reserved_meta_keys(mcp_field(result, "meta", "meta"))`; server-level `_meta` is also surfaced (`:6324-6331`).
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (automatic)
- **Outputs / side effects:** A filtered `_meta` object next to the result content, or **no `_meta` field at all if nothing model-facing remains**.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Vendor namespaces like `com.example/handoff` pass through; protocol-reserved prefixes are dropped, matching the MCP spec's key-name rules.
- **Rebuild notes:** Pass vendor metadata to the model but filter the protocol's own reserved namespace, and omit an empty `_meta` entirely. A better version would let the user allowlist which vendor namespaces reach the model.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `_is_reserved_mcp_meta_key` at `tools/mcp_tool.py:1102-1120`, `_strip_reserved_meta_keys` at `:1122-1131`, application at `:6348`.

### MCP utility tools (resources & prompts wrappers)  `id: docs-features.mcp-utility-tools`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `mcp_<server>_list_resources`, `mcp_<server>_read_resource`, `mcp_<server>_list_prompts`, `mcp_<server>_get_prompt`
- **What it does:** Registers four utility tools per server wrapping MCP resources and prompts, when the server supports them.
- **How it works:** Registered per server with the same prefix pattern — documented examples `mcp_github_list_resources`, `mcp_github_get_prompt`. The wrappers are **capability-aware**: Hermes only registers resource utilities if the MCP session actually supports resource operations, and only registers prompt utilities if the session actually supports prompt operations.
- **Inputs / options:** Four tools: `list_resources`, `read_resource`, `list_prompts`, `get_prompt`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Four extra tools per capable server.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.resources: false` disables `list_resources` + `read_resource`; `tools.prompts: false` disables `list_prompts` + `get_prompt`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** A server that exposes callable tools but no resources/prompts **will not get those extra wrappers**. The docs state this twice — the troubleshooting section notes wrappers appear only when (1) your config allows them and (2) the server session actually supports the capability, which "keeps the tool list honest".
- **Rebuild notes:** Probe capabilities before registering wrappers so the tool list never advertises something the server can't do. A better version would surface which capabilities each server negotiated in `hermes mcp list`.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — capability-gated registration in `tools/mcp_tool.py`.

### MCP per-server tool filtering (`tools.include` / `tools.exclude`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-tool-filtering`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include` / `.exclude` / `.prompts` / `.resources`; `mcp_servers.<name>.enabled`
- **What it does:** Controls which tools each MCP server contributes to Hermes, for fine-grained management of the tool namespace and as a security control.
- **How it works:** **Disable a server entirely** — `enabled: false` makes Hermes skip the server completely and **not even attempt a connection**. **Whitelist** — `tools.include: [create_issue, list_issues]` registers only those tools. **Blacklist** — `tools.exclude: [delete_customer]` registers all server tools except the excluded ones. **Precedence:** if both are present, **`include` wins** (documented example: `include: [create_issue]` + `exclude: [create_issue, delete_issue]` → `include` wins). **Utility filtering** — `tools.prompts: false` disables `list_prompts` + `get_prompt`; `tools.resources: false` disables `list_resources` + `read_resource`.
- **Inputs / options:** `enabled` (bool); `tools.include` (list of names/globs); `tools.exclude` (list of names/globs); `tools.prompts` (bool); `tools.resources` (bool).
- **Outputs / side effects:** A reduced tool surface for that server.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.*`, `.enabled`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **If your config filters out all callable tools and disables or omits all supported utilities, Hermes does not create an empty runtime MCP toolset for that server** — keeping the tool list clean. Documented as a security control: disable dangerous tools you don't want the model to see; expose only a minimal whitelist for a sensitive server; disable resource/prompt wrappers when you don't want that surface exposed.
- **Rebuild notes:** Make `include` unambiguously win over `exclude` and suppress empty toolsets so the registry stays honest. A better version would let filters be expressed per-tool-annotation (read-only vs mutating) rather than per-name.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — filtering logic in `tools/mcp_tool.py`; catalog installs write `tools.include` / `tools.exclude` via `hermes_cli/mcp_catalog.py`.

### MCP filter glob patterns  `id: docs-features.mcp-globs`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include` / `.exclude` entries
- **What it does:** Lets filter entries be fnmatch-style globs alongside exact names, so huge auto-generated tool surfaces can be filtered by product family.
- **How it works:** Supported metacharacters `*`, `?`, `[...]`, matched **case-sensitively**. `include: ["*_dns_*"]` registers every tool whose name contains `_dns_`. Documented as essential for surfaces like Cloudflare's API MCP (`?codemode=false`, ~3,300 tools) where excluding endpoints one at a time is impractical.
- **Inputs / options:** Documented example: `cloudflare` with `url: "https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp?codemode=false"`, `auth: oauth`, `tools.exclude: ["*_radar_*", "*_accounts_dlp_*", "*_zones_web3_*"]`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Whole families of tools registered/excluded at once.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.tools.include|exclude`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Entries without glob metacharacters (`*`, `?`, `[`) match exactly** — `docs` excludes only the tool named `docs`, never `docs_search`. Matching is case-sensitive.
- **Rebuild notes:** Auto-detect metacharacters so a plain name is never accidentally a prefix match. A better version would offer a dry-run showing exactly which tool names a filter matches before saving.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — glob handling in `tools/mcp_tool.py`; `cloudflare` catalog entry present under `optional-mcps/cloudflare/`.

### MCP runtime behaviour — discovery, dynamic tool discovery, reload, toolsets  `id: docs-features.mcp-runtime`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** startup; slash command `/reload-mcp`; toolset `mcp-<server>`
- **What it does:** Discovers MCP servers at startup, reacts to server-pushed tool-list changes at runtime, allows a manual reload, and exposes one runtime toolset per contributing server.
- **How it works:** **Discovery time** — Hermes discovers MCP servers at startup and registers their tools into the normal tool registry (`hermes_cli/mcp_startup.py`). **Dynamic Tool Discovery** — servers can send a `notifications/tools/list_changed` notification; on receipt Hermes automatically re-fetches the server's tool list and updates the registry, **no manual `/reload-mcp` required**; useful for servers whose capabilities change dynamically (a server that adds tools when a new database schema is loaded, or removes tools when a service goes offline). **Reloading** — `/reload-mcp` reloads MCP servers from config and refreshes the available tool list. **Toolsets** — each configured MCP server also creates a runtime toolset named `mcp-<server>` when it contributes at least one registered tool, making MCP servers easier to reason about at the toolset level.
- **Inputs / options:** Slash command `/reload-mcp`; toolset name `mcp-<server>`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Tool registry updated; toolsets created/removed.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **The refresh is lock-protected** so rapid-fire notifications from the same server don't cause overlapping refreshes. **Prompt and resource change notifications (`prompts/list_changed`, `resources/list_changed`) are received but not yet acted on** — a documented gap.
- **Rebuild notes:** Lock the refresh path and drive it from server notifications so a manual reload is only a fallback. A better version would also act on prompt/resource change notifications, closing the documented gap.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — startup discovery in `hermes_cli/mcp_startup.py`; notification handling and list-cache invalidation in `tools/mcp_tool.py` (`_list_cache_meta` at `:2497`, reset at `:3897`).

### MCP stdio environment filtering  `id: docs-features.mcp-stdio-env-filtering`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** stdio MCP server spawn
- **What it does:** Prevents accidental secret leakage by not passing the full shell environment to stdio MCP servers.
- **How it works:** For stdio servers, Hermes does **not** blindly pass your full shell environment — only the explicitly configured `env` plus a safe baseline are passed through.
- **Inputs / options:** `mcp_servers.<name>.env` mapping.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A restricted child-process environment.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.env`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** A server that expects an inherited variable must have it listed explicitly in `env`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Default-deny the environment and require explicit passthrough. A better version would list, at connect time, which requested variables were dropped so misconfiguration is visible.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — env handling in `tools/mcp_tool.py`; security helpers in `hermes_cli/mcp_security.py`.

### MCP parallel tool calls (`supports_parallel_tool_calls`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-parallel`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.supports_parallel_tool_calls`
- **What it does:** Opts a server's tools into concurrent execution within a single tool-call batch.
- **How it works:** By default MCP tools run **sequentially — one at a time**. When `supports_parallel_tool_calls: true`, Hermes may execute multiple tools from that server at the same time within a single tool-call batch, just like it does for built-in read-only tools (`web_search`, `read_file`, etc.).
- **Inputs / options:** `supports_parallel_tool_calls: true|false` (default false). Documented example: `docs` with `command: "docs-server"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Concurrent MCP tool execution.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.supports_parallel_tool_calls` (`tools/mcp_tool.py:35`, `:77`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** Documented caution: only enable for servers whose tools are safe to run at the same time; **if tools read and write shared state, files, databases, or external resources, review the read/write race conditions before enabling this setting**.
- **Rebuild notes:** Default to sequential and make concurrency an explicit per-server assertion by the operator. A better version would read MCP tool annotations (`readOnlyHint`) and parallelise per tool rather than per server.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — key at `tools/mcp_tool.py:35` with the "Parallel tool call opt-in: per-server `supports_parallel_tool_calls`" note at `:77`.

### MCP sampling support (`sampling/createMessage`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-sampling`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.sampling`
- **What it does:** Lets an MCP server request LLM inference from Hermes via the `sampling/createMessage` protocol — useful for servers that need LLM capabilities but don't have their own model access.
- **How it works:** **Enabled by default** for all MCP servers (when the MCP SDK supports it). The sampling handler includes a sliding-window rate limiter (`self._rate_timestamps` checked against `max_rpm` at `tools/mcp_tool.py:1821`), per-request timeouts, and tool-loop depth limits (`:1954-1965`) to prevent runaway usage. Metrics (request count, errors, tokens used) are tracked per server instance.
- **Inputs / options:** Eight documented `sampling` keys: `enabled` (bool, default `true`); `model` (string, override model for sampling requests, optional — e.g. `"openai/gpt-4o"`); `max_tokens_cap` (int, max tokens per sampling response, **default 4096** — `_safe_numeric(config.get("max_tokens_cap", 4096), 4096, int)` at `tools/mcp_tool.py:1797`); `timeout` (int, seconds per request, default 30); `max_rpm` (int, max requests per minute, **default 10** — `:1795`); `max_tool_rounds` (int, max tool-use rounds in sampling loops, **default 5**, minimum 0 — `:1798-1799`); `allowed_models` (list, allowlist of model names the server may request, **empty = any** — `:1802`); `log_level` (string audit log level — `debug`, `info`, or `warning`, default `info`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** LLM calls billed to the user's provider on the server's behalf; per-server metrics.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.sampling.*`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `max_tool_rounds: 0` **disables tool loops entirely** — "Tool loops disabled for server '<name>' (max_tool_rounds=0)" (`tools/mcp_tool.py:1954-1957`); exceeding the limit errors with "(max {max_tool_rounds} rounds)" (`:1961-1965`). Rate-limit breach reports "({max_rpm} requests/minute)" (`:2049-2054`). A model not in `allowed_models` is refused: "MCP server '%s' requested model '%s' not in allowed_models" (`:2068-2070`). Disable per server with `sampling: {enabled: false}` — the docs' example names the server `untrusted_server`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Rate-limit, cap tokens, bound tool rounds and allowlist models per server, because sampling spends the user's inference budget on the server's behalf. A better version would require explicit user consent the first time a server samples, and show spend per server.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — every default matches code: `max_rpm=10` (`tools/mcp_tool.py:1795`), `max_tokens_cap=4096` (`:1797`), `max_tool_rounds=5` minimum 0 (`:1798-1799`), `allowed_models=[]` (`:1802`); config schema comments at `:60-64`.

### MCP elicitation support (`elicitation/create`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-elicitation`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `mcp_servers.<name>.elicitation`
- **What it does:** Lets an MCP server ask the user for structured input mid-tool-call, routed through Hermes's existing approval surface.
- **How it works:** Requires mcp Python SDK ≥ 1.11.0 (`tools/mcp_tool.py:403` — "Added in mcp Python SDK 1.11.0 (Jul 2025); servers use elicitation to…"; when the types aren't importable it logs "MCP elicitation types not available -- elicitation disabled" at `:411`). Hermes routes **form-mode** elicitations through its approval surface — an interactive prompt in the CLI/TUI, or approval buttons on gateway platforms like Telegram and Slack — so the request reaches you wherever the session lives. Per-server metrics (requests, accepted, declined, errors) are tracked on the handler.
- **Inputs / options:** Two documented `elicitation` keys: `enabled` (bool, **default `true`**); `timeout` (int, seconds to wait for your answer, **default 300**).
- **Outputs / side effects:** An approval prompt on the active surface; the user's structured answer returned to the server.
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.elicitation.enabled`, `.timeout`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **URL-mode elicitations (where a server points you at an external URL) are declined as unsupported.** The 5-minute default timeout mirrors the gateway approval default so users on async surfaces have time to respond before the server gives up.
- **Rebuild notes:** Reuse the existing approval channel so elicitation works on every surface, and decline URL-mode outright rather than opening arbitrary links. A better version would render the elicitation JSON Schema as a real form on rich surfaces instead of a text prompt.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — SDK-version gate and graceful disable at `tools/mcp_tool.py:403-411`.

### Running Hermes as an MCP server (`hermes mcp serve`)  `id: docs-features.mcp-serve`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes mcp serve`
- **What it does:** Makes Hermes itself an MCP server so other MCP-capable agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, any MCP client) can use Hermes's messaging capabilities — list conversations, read message history, and send messages across all connected platforms.
- **How it works:** Starts a **stdio** MCP server; **the MCP client (not you) manages the process lifecycle**. Implementation: `mcp_serve.py`. It reads conversation data directly from Hermes's session store — `~/.hermes/state.db` is the primary source, with `sessions.json` kept only as a legacy fallback. A background thread polls the database for new messages and maintains an in-memory event queue. For sending, it uses the same internal send engine (`tools/send_message_tool.py`) that powers cron delivery and the `hermes send` CLI.
- **Inputs / options:** `hermes mcp serve` (normal mode); `hermes mcp serve --verbose` / `-v` (debug logging on stderr); `--accept-hooks` (auto-approve unseen shell hooks without a TTY prompt, equivalent to `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1` / `hooks_auto_accept: true`); `-h/--help`. Client config example for Claude Code's `~/.claude/claude_desktop_config.json`: `{"mcpServers": {"hermes": {"command": "hermes", "args": ["mcp", "serve"]}}}`, or with an explicit path `"/home/user/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/hermes"`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A stdio MCP server process; reads from `state.db`; sends messages through the running gateway.
- **Config / env:** `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS`, `hooks_auto_accept`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **The gateway does NOT need to be running for read operations** (listing conversations, reading history, polling events). It **DOES** need to be running for send operations, since the platform adapters need active connections. Documented "when to use this": you want Claude Code, Cursor or another coding agent to send and read Telegram/Discord/Slack messages through Hermes; you want a single MCP server bridging to all of Hermes's connected messaging platforms at once; you already have a running Hermes gateway with connected platforms.
- **Rebuild notes:** Read from the durable session DB so the read surface works without the live gateway, and reuse the existing send engine for writes. A better version would expose an HTTP transport so remote clients don't need to spawn the process.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `mcp_serve.py` module docstring lists the tool surface at `:9-13`; flags confirmed by `hermes mcp serve --help` (evidence: `cli_help/mcp__serve.txt`).

### `hermes mcp serve` tool surface (10 tools)  `id: docs-features.mcp-serve-tools`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** tools exposed by `hermes mcp serve` to the connecting MCP client
- **What it does:** Exposes ten tools matching OpenClaw's channel bridge surface plus a Hermes-specific channel browser.
- **How it works:** Defined in `mcp_serve.py`: `conversations_list` (`:645`), `conversation_get` (`:702`), `messages_read` (`:735`), `attachments_fetch` (`:787`), `events_poll` (`:834`), `events_wait` (`:863`), `messages_send` (`:897`), `channels_list` (`:930`), plus `permissions_list_open` and `permissions_respond` (module docstring `:9-13`).
- **Inputs / options:** `conversations_list` — list active messaging conversations, filter by platform or search by name (returns session keys needed for `messages_read`; `limit` coerced to default 50, min 1, **max 200** at `mcp_serve.py:660`). `conversation_get` — detailed info about one conversation by `session_key` (`:702-706`). `messages_read` — recent message history for a conversation, by `session_key` (`limit` default 50, min 1, max 200 at `:748`). `attachments_fetch` — extract non-text attachments (images, media) from a specific message, by `session_key` + `message_id` from `messages_read` (`:787-798`). `events_poll` — poll for new conversation events since a cursor position, e.g. `events_poll(after_cursor=0)` (non-blocking; `limit` default 20, min 1, max 200 at `:852`). `events_wait` — long-poll / block until the next event arrives, e.g. `events_wait(after_cursor=42, timeout_ms=30000)`. `messages_send` — send a message through a platform (e.g. `telegram:123456`, `discord:#general`); accepts channel IDs from `channels_list` and human-friendly channel names (`:897-904`). `channels_list` — list available messaging targets across all platforms (Hermes-specific extra). `permissions_list_open` — list pending approval requests observed during this bridge session. `permissions_respond` — allow or deny a pending approval request.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Reads from `state.db`; `messages_send` delivers through the live gateway; `permissions_respond` resolves an approval.
- **Config / env:** none beyond the Hermes home.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Event types are `message`, `approval_requested`, `approval_resolved`. **The event queue is in-memory and starts when the bridge connects** — older messages are available through `messages_read`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Pair a non-blocking poll with a long-poll wait over one cursor so clients choose their latency/cost trade-off. A better version would push events over a notification channel instead of polling.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — all ten names present in `mcp_serve.py` (docstring `:9-13`; handlers at `:645`, `:702`, `:735`, `:787`, `:834`, `:863`, `:897`, `:930`).

### `hermes mcp serve` event system  `id: docs-features.mcp-serve-events`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `events_poll` / `events_wait` on the `hermes mcp serve` bridge
- **What it does:** Gives MCP clients near-real-time awareness of incoming conversations via a live event bridge that polls Hermes's session database.
- **How it works:** A background thread polls the DB and maintains an in-memory queue; `POLL_INTERVAL = 0.2  # seconds between DB polls (200ms)` at `mcp_serve.py:308`, used by the wait path (`self._new_event.wait(timeout=min(remaining, POLL_INTERVAL))` at `:429`) and the poll loop (`time.sleep(POLL_INTERVAL)` at `:530`). Polling is **mtime-optimized** — it skips work when files are unchanged.
- **Inputs / options:** `events_poll(after_cursor=<int>)` (non-blocking); `events_wait(after_cursor=<int>, timeout_ms=<int>)` (blocks up to the timeout).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Event objects of types `message`, `approval_requested`, `approval_resolved`.
- **Config / env:** reads `~/.hermes/state.db`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The queue is in-memory and starts when the bridge connects — history before that is only reachable through `messages_read`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Poll at a fixed short interval with an mtime fast path, and expose a cursor so clients can resume. A better version would use SQLite's update hook or a filesystem watcher instead of a 200ms poll.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `POLL_INTERVAL = 0.2` with the "(200ms)" comment at `mcp_serve.py:308`.

### `hermes mcp serve` current limits  `id: docs-features.mcp-serve-limits`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** mcp.md → "Current limits"
- **What it does:** States four known limitations of the embedded MCP server.
- **How it works:** (1) The embedded `hermes mcp serve` exposes a **stdio-only** MCP server today — for HTTP, run a separate adapter, or (much more commonly) use the MCP **client** side of Hermes, which already speaks both stdio and HTTP (`url` + `headers` in `mcp_servers.yaml` / `config.yaml`). (2) Event polling at **~200ms intervals** via mtime-optimized DB polling (skips work when files are unchanged). (3) **No `claude/channel` push notification protocol yet.** (4) **Text-only sends** — no media/attachment sending through `messages_send`.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** These are documented gaps, not bugs.
- **Rebuild notes:** State transport and payload limits explicitly so integrators don't discover them at runtime. A better version would add an HTTP transport and media sends, closing two of the four.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the 200ms interval is confirmed at `mcp_serve.py:308`; stdio-only serve confirmed by `hermes mcp serve --help` exposing no transport flags (evidence: `cli_help/mcp__serve.txt`).

### MCP troubleshooting guide  `id: docs-features.mcp-troubleshooting`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** mcp.md → "Troubleshooting"
- **What it does:** Gives three named failure modes with checks.
- **How it works:** **(1) MCP server not connecting** — verify MCP deps are installed (already in the standard install) with `cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent && uv pip install -e ".[mcp]"`, check `node --version` and `npx --version`, then verify your config and restart Hermes. **(2) Tools not appearing** — possible causes: the server failed to connect; discovery failed; your filter config excluded the tools; the utility capability does not exist on that server; the server is disabled with `enabled: false`. If you are intentionally filtering, this is expected. **(3) Why didn't resource or prompt utilities appear?** — because Hermes only registers those wrappers when both (a) your config allows them and (b) the server session actually supports the capability; this is intentional and keeps the tool list honest.
- **Inputs / options:** Diagnostic commands `uv pip install -e ".[mcp]"`, `node --version`, `npx --version`; also `hermes mcp test <name>` (`hermes mcp test [-h] name`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.<name>.enabled`, `.tools`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The troubleshooting list does not mention `hermes mcp test`, which is the most direct connection check.
- **Rebuild notes:** Pair each symptom with the config key that causes it so users can self-diagnose without reading the whole page. A better version would point at `hermes mcp test <name>` as step one.
- **Verification:** partial — content matches behaviour, but `hermes mcp test` (evidence: `cli_help/mcp__test.txt`) exists and is **not** mentioned in the troubleshooting section (doc gap).

### MCP example use cases  `id: docs-features.mcp-examples`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** mcp.md → "Example use cases"
- **What it does:** Three end-to-end config + prompt pairs showing the filtering model in practice.
- **How it works:** **GitHub with a minimal issue-management surface** — stdio `npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github` with `env.GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN`, `tools.include: [list_issues, create_issue, update_issue]`, `tools.prompts: false`, `tools.resources: false`; prompt "Show me open issues labeled bug, then draft a new issue for the flaky MCP reconnection behavior." **Stripe with dangerous actions removed** — HTTP `https://mcp.stripe.com` with `headers.Authorization`, `tools.exclude: [delete_customer, refund_payment]`; prompt "Look up the last 10 failed payments and summarize common failure reasons." **Filesystem server for a single project root** — stdio `npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /home/user/my-project`; prompt "Inspect the project root and explain the directory layout." A fourth combined "Full example" shows `github` (include + `prompts: false`), `stripe` (exclude + `resources: false`) and `legacy` (`enabled: false`) in one config.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (illustrative)
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `mcp_servers.*`
- **Edge cases / guards:** The filesystem example scopes the server to a single root by passing the path as an argument — the sandbox boundary is the server's, not Hermes's.
- **Rebuild notes:** Pair each config example with the natural-language prompt it enables, so the value is legible without running it. A better version would ship these as installable catalog presets.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — config shapes match the documented key table (`tools/mcp_tool.py:14-80`).
