## Page: `web-dashboard.md` — Hermes Web Dashboard

### `hermes dashboard` (web dashboard)  `id: docs-features.dash-launch`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes dashboard`; `http://127.0.0.1:9119`
- **What it does:** Starts a local web server and opens a browser-based UI for managing configuration, API keys, MCP servers, messaging pairing, webhooks, the gateway, memory, credentials, sessions, logs, analytics, cron jobs, and skills — instead of editing YAML or running CLI commands.
- **How it works:** **The dashboard runs entirely on your machine — no data leaves localhost** (by default). Implemented in `hermes_cli/web_server.py` (FastAPI) with a React SPA in `web/`, built to `hermes_cli/web_dist/` and served as a static SPA.
- **Inputs / options:** Documented flags: `--port` (default `9119`); `--host` (default `127.0.0.1`); `--no-open` (don't auto-open the browser); `--insecure` (**deprecated / no-op**); `--isolated` (when launched from a named profile, run a dedicated per-profile server instead of routing to the machine dashboard). Documented examples: `hermes dashboard --port 8080`; `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0`; `hermes dashboard --no-open`. Subcommand `register`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A local HTTP server; browser opened unless `--no-open`.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.*` in `config.yaml`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Hosted-mode auth uses Nous Portal OAuth; `hermes setup --portal` also wires up the model and tool gateway.
- **Rebuild notes:** Ship one FastAPI process serving both the SPA and its API, bound to loopback by default. A better version would offer a read-only mode for exposure without write risk.
- **Verification:** **doc drift** — the Options table omits three real flags: **`--skip-build`** ("Skip the web UI build step and serve the existing dist directly. Useful for non-interactive contexts (Windows Scheduled Tasks, CI) where npm may not be available"), **`--stop`** ("Stop all running Hermes web server processes and exit"), and **`--status`** ("List running Hermes web server processes and exit"); it also omits that `--port 0` means "auto-assign by OS" (evidence: `cli_help/dashboard.txt`).

### Dashboard multi-profile management  `id: docs-features.dash-profiles`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** profile switcher in the sidebar; URL `?profile=<name>`; `--isolated`
- **What it does:** Makes one dashboard server a **machine-level** management surface for every profile on the machine.
- **How it works:** A profile switcher in the sidebar (**visible whenever more than one profile exists**) decides which profile the management pages read and write — **Config, API Keys, Skills, MCP, Models, and the Chat tab all follow it**. **While a profile other than the dashboard's own is selected, an amber banner names the managed profile so the write target is never ambiguous.** **The selection lives in the URL (`?profile=<name>`)**, so deep links like `http://127.0.0.1:9119/skills?profile=worker` land with the switcher preselected and survive refresh. **Launching the dashboard from a profile alias routes to the machine dashboard instead of starting a second server:** `worker dashboard` opens the browser at `?profile=worker` if one is already running, or starts the machine dashboard with "worker" preselected if not.
- **Inputs / options:** Sidebar switcher; `?profile=<name>` URL param; `--isolated` to opt out and run a dedicated server scoped to that profile (**the pre-unification behavior — useful if you deliberately expose different profiles' dashboards with different auth**).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Reads/writes scoped to the selected profile's `HERMES_HOME`.
- **Config / env:** per-profile `HERMES_HOME`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **The Chat tab follows the switcher too** — a scoped chat spawns its PTY child with the selected profile's `HERMES_HOME`, so the conversation runs with that profile's model, skills, memory, and session history; **switching profiles starts a fresh terminal session**. **What stays per-profile and is *not* absorbed by the switcher:** gateway processes (manage them via `hermes -p <name> gateway …`), each profile's session database, and cron schedulers (the Cron page already aggregates across profiles with its own filter).
- **Rebuild notes:** Put the managed-profile selection in the URL so deep links and refresh both work, and banner loudly whenever writes target a non-default profile. A better version would show a per-page indicator of exactly which file a save will touch.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `--isolated` help text matches ("Default behavior is unified: profile launches attach to (or start) ONE machine-level server and preselect the profile", evidence: `cli_help/dashboard.txt`); profile-scoped plugin/theme resolution at `hermes_cli/web_server.py:18455-18468`.

### Dashboard prerequisites (`web` / `pty` extras)  `id: docs-features.dash-prereqs`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `uv pip install -e ".[web,pty]"` in `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`
- **What it does:** Documents the optional extras the dashboard and its Chat tab need.
- **How it works:** **The default `hermes-agent` install does not ship the HTTP stack or PTY helper.** The **web dashboard** needs FastAPI and Uvicorn (`web` extra); the **Chat** tab also needs `ptyprocess` to spawn the embedded TUI behind a pseudo-terminal (`pty` extra on POSIX).
- **Inputs / options:** `cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent && uv pip install -e ".[web,pty]"`; `".[all]"` includes both extras and is the easiest path if you also want messaging/voice/etc. `pty` pulls in `ptyprocess` (POSIX) or `pywinpty` (native Windows).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Installed dependencies.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **When you run `hermes dashboard` without the dependencies, it will tell you what to install.** **If the frontend hasn't been built yet and `npm` is available, it builds automatically on first launch.** **The Chat tab is part of every `hermes dashboard` launch** — the embedded browser chat pane is always available with no extra flag. Native Windows `pywinpty` still requires WSL for the embedded TUI itself.
- **Rebuild notes:** Make the HTTP stack an optional extra so the base install stays small, and detect-and-instruct rather than crashing. A better version would offer `hermes dashboard --install-deps`.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `--skip-build` exists precisely for "non-interactive contexts (Windows Scheduled Tasks, CI) where npm may not be available. Pre-build with: cd web && npm run build" (evidence: `cli_help/dashboard.txt`).

### Dashboard Status page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-status`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** landing page
- **What it does:** A live overview of the installation.
- **How it works:** **Auto-refreshes every 5 seconds.**
- **Inputs / options:** Four documented blocks: **Agent version** and release date; **Gateway status** — running/stopped, PID, connected platforms and their state; **Active sessions** — count of sessions active in the last 5 minutes; **Recent sessions** — the 20 most recent sessions with model, message count, token usage, and a preview of the conversation.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Read-only.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/status`, `GET /api/sessions`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The React StatusPage also shows `auth_required` / `auth_providers` under "Web server"; a sidebar AuthWidget surfaces the current identity once signed in.
- **Rebuild notes:** Poll one status endpoint on a short interval and derive every landing-page block from it. A better version would use the existing event WebSocket instead of a 5-second poll.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `GET /api/status` and `GET /api/sessions` present in the live-API dump (`api_live/get_all.json`).

### Dashboard resource-pressure banner  `id: docs-features.dash-resource-banner`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** banner at the top of the dashboard, fed by the same status poll
- **What it does:** Warns when the host is low on memory or disk, or restarted under memory pressure.
- **How it works:** Three documented warnings: **"Your agent is almost out of memory and may restart"** — system available memory has dropped to *elevated* (**< 128 MiB or < 15%**) or *critical* (**< 64 MiB or < 5%**) levels, as sampled by the gateway's **30-second heartbeat**; **"Your agent restarted unexpectedly, most likely because it ran out of memory"** — the lifecycle ledger recorded an unclean exit under memory pressure on the previous boot (a suspected OOM kill); **Disk warnings** — the volume holding `~/.hermes` is nearly full (*elevated* below **512 MB** free, *critical* below **256 MB** free).
- **Inputs / options:** No user inputs beyond dismissal.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Banner shown/hidden; **no extra requests** (it rides the status poll).
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/status` → `memory` and `disk` advisory blocks.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Only the most severe active warning shows at a time** — precedence: disk critical > memory critical > OOM restart > disk elevated > memory elevated. **Dismissals are scoped to the current gateway boot:** dismissing a warning surfaces the next active one, a gateway restart or an escalation (elevated → critical) re-opens it, and **a stale heartbeat renders nothing rather than a spurious alert**.
- **Rebuild notes:** Rank warnings and show only the top one, scope dismissals to a boot id, and render nothing on stale data rather than a stale reading. A better version would link each warning to the specific remediation command.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the thresholds match the `/api/status` `memory` and `disk` block documentation on the same page.

### Dashboard Chat tab (embedded TUI over PTY)  `id: docs-features.dash-page-chat`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Chat** tab; `/chat`; `/chat?resume=<id>`
- **What it does:** Embeds the full Hermes TUI (the same interface as `hermes --tui`) directly in the browser, so everything the terminal TUI can do works identically.
- **How it works:** **`/api/pty` opens a WebSocket authenticated with the dashboard's session token**; the server spawns `hermes --tui` behind a POSIX pseudo-terminal; keystrokes travel to the PTY and ANSI output streams back to the browser; **xterm.js's WebGL renderer paints each cell to an integer-pixel grid**, with mouse tracking (SGR 1006), wide characters (Unicode 11), and box-drawing glyphs all rendering natively; **resizing the browser window resizes the TUI via the `@xterm/addon-fit` addon**. Slash commands, model picker, tool-call cards, markdown streaming, clarify/sudo/approval prompts and skin theming all work because **the dashboard is running the real TUI binary**.
- **Inputs / options:** **Resume an existing session:** from the **Sessions** tab click the play icon (▶) next to any session → jumps to `/chat?resume=<id>` and launches the TUI with `--resume`, loading the full history. **Session switcher (right rail):** a ChatGPT-style conversation list beside the terminal — the rail stacks the model picker on top and the session list below it; the list shows the most recent sessions for the active profile with **title (falling back to a message preview), relative last-active time, message count, and the source channel for non-CLI sessions**; click any row to resume in place (the terminal respawns with that conversation's history), the active session is highlighted, **New chat** starts a fresh session, and a refresh control re-pulls the list.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A PTY child process per open chat. **Close the browser tab and the PTY is reaped cleanly on the server; re-opening spawns a fresh session.**
- **Config / env:** `?profile=<name>` scopes the spawned child's `HERMES_HOME`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Prerequisites:** Node.js (same requirement as `hermes --tui`; the TUI bundle is built on first launch); `ptyprocess` (the `pty` extra); **a POSIX kernel (Linux, macOS, or WSL2)** — the `/chat` terminal pane specifically needs a POSIX PTY, so **on a native Windows install the rest of the dashboard works but the `/chat` tab shows a banner telling you to use WSL2**. **The rail is read-only for switching** — delete, rename, export, and bulk cleanup still live on the **Sessions** tab. **On narrow screens it folds into a slide-over panel.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Run the real TUI behind a PTY and stream ANSI rather than reimplementing the UI in the browser — one implementation, zero feature drift. A better version would support reconnecting to a live PTY instead of respawning on tab close.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `/api/pty` WebSocket route present in the FastAPI route dump (`routes_static.txt`).

### Connecting Hermes Desktop to a remote dashboard backend  `id: docs-features.dash-remote-backend`
- **Surface:** Desktop app
- **Where:** Desktop **Settings → Gateways → Remote gateway**; **Remote URL** + **Sign in**
- **What it does:** Lets Hermes Desktop attach to a `hermes dashboard` running on a remote machine (a VM, homelab box, VPS) instead of its own bundled backend.
- **How it works:** **The "remote backend" Desktop connects to *is* a `hermes dashboard` process running on the remote machine** — it has to be up and reachable before anything else matters; **Desktop attaches to it, it doesn't start it for you.** Keep it running under `systemd`/`tmux` so it survives logout and reboots. **The gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/etc.) is a *separate* long-running process** — start it independently; it is **not** the thing the desktop app connects to. **Desktop's "remote backend is ready" probe only hits `GET /api/status`, which is a public endpoint — it answers as soon as *any* dashboard is running on the host.** The live chat connection is a **separate WebSocket to `/api/ws` (and `/api/pty`)** gated by two more checks the status probe never touches.
- **Inputs / options:** Desktop **Remote URL** (e.g. `http://VM_IP:9119`; path prefixes like `/hermes` are supported behind a reverse proxy) and **Sign in**. Env override `HERMES_DESKTOP_REMOTE_URL` — when set it overrides the saved in-app URL (**the Gateway settings panel shows an "env override" badge and disables editing**); you still Sign in with the panel. Documented `systemd` unit: `EnvironmentFile=%h/.hermes/.env`, `ExecStart=/path/to/venv/bin/python -m hermes_cli.main dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9119 --no-open`, with `~/.hermes/.env` carrying `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME`, `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD`, `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_SECRET`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Desktop shell driven by the remote backend; **the session refreshes automatically and survives restarts when `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_SECRET` is set on the backend.**
- **Config / env:** `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_*`; `HERMES_DESKTOP_REMOTE_URL`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Two gating checks:** (1) **You must be authenticated** — a non-loopback bind engages the auth gate; Desktop signs in once and **reuses the resulting session for the WebSocket via a single-use ticket**; **without a configured provider, a non-loopback dashboard fails closed at startup**. (2) **The bind host must allow the client and match the Host header** — a loopback bind only accepts loopback clients, so a remote machine is rejected at the socket layer regardless of credentials; bind non-loopback so the peer-IP guard lets the client through, and **the remote URL must reach the dashboard by the same host it bound to** because the DNS-rebinding guard requires the Host header to match. **Verify with `curl -s http://VM_IP:9119/api/status | jq '.auth_required, .auth_providers'`** — `true` + `"basic"` means Sign in will work; `auth_required: false` means the bind is loopback or the gate didn't engage; `true` with no `"basic"` means the username/password env vars aren't loaded. **If it still fails after signing in, grab a fresh `desktop.log` (Settings → Gateways → Open logs) plus the dashboard's logs from the same retry window and look for the `/api/ws` close code — 4403 = chat WS rejected by the request guard (Host/peer mismatch); 4401 = the WS ticket didn't authenticate.** Documented troubleshooting: "Remote gateway incomplete" (no remote URL entered); 401 / "Invalid credentials" (**the backend returns the same generic error for unknown user and wrong password, so check both**); no "Sign in" button, asks for a session token instead (the basic provider isn't active); signed out on every restart (set a stable `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_SECRET`); connection refused / times out (backend bound to `127.0.0.1`, or a firewall/VPN is blocking the port).
- **Rebuild notes:** Make the readiness probe check the same gates the live connection needs, or document loudly that it doesn't — a green light that means nothing is worse than none. A better version would have Desktop probe `/api/ws` reachability directly and report the close code inline.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the `basic` auth plugin exists at `plugins/dashboard_auth/basic`; `dashboard.basic_auth` config block at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1764`.

### Dashboard Config page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-config`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Config** tab
- **What it does:** A form-based editor for `config.yaml` with **all 150+ configuration fields auto-discovered from `DEFAULT_CONFIG`** and organized into tabbed categories.
- **How it works:** **Fields with known valid values (terminal backend, skin, approval mode, etc.) render as dropdowns; booleans render as toggles; everything else is a text input.** The frontend renders widgets from `GET /api/config/schema`.
- **Inputs / options:** Documented categories: **model** (default model, provider, base URL, reasoning settings); **terminal** (backend local/docker/ssh/modal, timeout, shell preferences); **display** (skin, tool progress, resume display, spinner settings); **agent** (max iterations, gateway timeout, service tier); **delegation** (subagent limits, reasoning effort); **memory** (provider selection, context injection settings); **approvals** (dangerous command approval mode — smart/manual/off); "and more — every section of config.yaml has corresponding form fields". Four actions: **Save** (writes changes to `config.yaml` immediately); **Reset to defaults** (reverts all fields to defaults — **doesn't save until you click Save**); **Export** (downloads the current config as JSON); **Import** (uploads a JSON config file to replace the current values).
- **Outputs / side effects:** `config.yaml` writes.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/config`, `GET /api/config/defaults`, `GET /api/config/schema`, `PUT /api/config`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Config changes take effect on the next agent session or gateway restart.** The dashboard edits the same `config.yaml` that `hermes config set` and the gateway read from.
- **Rebuild notes:** Derive the whole form from a schema generated from the defaults table so a new config key needs no UI work. A better version would show which running processes must restart for each changed key.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `GET /api/config/schema` present in the live dump (`api_live/config_schema.json`), and `config_defaults.json` records **785 leaf keys** — far more than the page's "150+" claim, so the number is a conservative understatement rather than an error.

### Dashboard API Keys page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-apikeys`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **API Keys** tab
- **What it does:** Manages the `.env` file where API keys and credentials are stored.
- **How it works:** Keys are grouped by category. Each key shows **whether it's currently set (with a redacted preview of the value), a description of what it's for, a link to the provider's signup/key page, an input field to set or update the value, and a delete button to remove it.**
- **Inputs / options:** Four documented categories: **LLM Providers** (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, etc.); **Tool API Keys** (Browserbase, Firecrawl, Keenable, ElevenLabs, etc.); **Messaging Platforms** (Telegram, Discord, Slack bot tokens, etc.); **Agent Settings** (non-secret env vars like `API_SERVER_ENABLED`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** `~/.hermes/.env` writes.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/env`, `PUT /api/env` (`{"key": "VAR_NAME", "value": "secret"}`), `DELETE /api/env` (`{"key": "VAR_NAME"}`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Advanced/rarely-used keys are hidden by default behind a toggle.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Show set/unset plus a redacted preview and a link to the issuing provider, so a user can audit and fix in one place. A better version would validate a key's shape (or test it) before saving.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the env-var catalogue backing this page has **671 documented** and **1056 code-referenced** variables (evidence: `env_vars_doc.txt`, `env_vars_code.txt`).

### Dashboard Sessions page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-sessions`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Sessions** tab
- **What it does:** Browse and inspect all agent sessions.
- **How it works:** Each row shows the session title, source platform icon (CLI, Telegram, Discord, Slack, cron), model name, message count, tool call count, and how long ago it was active. **Live sessions are marked with a pulsing badge.**
- **Inputs / options:** Eight documented controls: **Filter** — **Chats / Automation / All** tabs (*Chats*, the default, shows human conversations and hides automation noise — cron, tool, API, ACP sessions; *Automation* shows only those; *All* shows everything), plus an **exact-source dropdown** narrowing to a single channel; **search respects the active filter**. **Search** — full-text search across all message content **using FTS5**, with highlighted snippets and auto-scroll to the first matching message when expanded. **Stats** — a summary bar with total sessions, how many are active in the store, archived count, total messages, and a per-source breakdown. **Expand** — click a session to load its full message history; messages are color-coded by role (user, assistant, system, tool) and rendered as Markdown with syntax highlighting. **Tool calls** — assistant messages with tool calls show collapsible blocks with the function name and JSON arguments. **Rename** — set or clear a session's title inline (pencil icon). **Export** — download a session (metadata + full message history) as JSON (download icon). **Prune** — the header "Prune old sessions" button deletes ended sessions older than N days. **Delete** — remove a session and its message history with the trash icon.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Session-store writes (rename, archive, delete, prune); JSON downloads.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/sessions`, `/api/sessions/{id}`, `/api/sessions/{id}/messages`, `/api/sessions/search`, `/api/sessions/stats`, `PATCH /api/sessions/{id}`, `GET /api/sessions/{id}/export`, `POST /api/sessions/prune`, `DELETE /api/sessions/{id}`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `GET /api/sessions/{id}/messages` **returns the latest 500 messages in chronological order by default**; use `limit` (**maximum 500**), `offset`, and `order=oldest|latest` for explicit pagination.
- **Rebuild notes:** Split human conversations from automation noise by default, and back search with FTS5 so it stays fast at scale. A better version would let a filter combine source and date range in the URL.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — all nine session endpoints present in the FastAPI route dump (`routes_static.txt`, `api_live/get_all.json`).

### Dashboard Logs page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-logs`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Logs** tab
- **What it does:** Views agent, gateway, and error log files with filtering and live tailing.
- **How it works:** Log lines are fetched from `GET /api/logs`.
- **Inputs / options:** Six documented controls: **File** — switch between `agent`, `errors`, and `gateway`; **Level** — `ALL`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`; **Component** — `all`, `gateway`, `agent`, `tools`, `cli`, `cron`; **Lines** — 50, 100, 200, or 500; **Auto-refresh** — toggle live tailing that polls for new log lines **every 5 seconds**; **Color-coded** — log lines colored by severity (red for errors, yellow for warnings, dim for debug).
- **Outputs / side effects:** Read-only.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/logs` with query parameters `file` (agent/errors/gateway), `lines` (count), `level`, `component`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Poll-based tailing, not a stream.
- **Rebuild notes:** Expose file/level/component/lines as query parameters so the UI is a thin filter over one endpoint. A better version would stream over WebSocket instead of a 5-second poll.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `GET /api/logs` present in the live GET dump.

### Dashboard Analytics page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-analytics`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Analytics** tab
- **What it does:** Usage and cost analytics computed from session history.
- **How it works:** Select a time period (7, 30, or 90 days).
- **Inputs / options:** Four documented views: **Summary cards** — total tokens (input/output), cache hit percentage, total estimated or actual cost, total session count with daily average; **Daily token chart** — stacked bar chart of input and output token usage per day, with hover tooltips showing breakdowns and cost; **Daily breakdown table** — date, session count, input tokens, output tokens, cache hit rate, and cost per day; **Per-model breakdown** — each model used, its session count, token usage, and estimated cost.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Read-only.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/analytics/usage` with query parameter `days` (default 30).
- **Edge cases / guards:** The numbers are a **local debug estimate** — per the config comment at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py`'s `dashboard` block, they count only successful main-agent responses with a usable `response.usage` and **silently exclude every auxiliary call** (context compression, title generation, vision, session search, web extract, smart approval, MCP routing, plugin LLM access) plus provider-side retries, fallback attempts, and any call whose usage block didn't come back; **cache writes are also missing from the API response**. Hence the token/cost surfaces are **hidden by default**.
- **Rebuild notes:** State the estimate's exclusions in the config comment and hide the surface by default, rather than presenting an incomplete number as a bill. A better version would reconcile against the provider's own usage API.
- **Verification:** partial — `GET /api/analytics/usage` exists, but the page never mentions that these surfaces are **hidden by default** or that the numbers exclude every auxiliary call, which the config default's own comment states explicitly (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1682-1690`) — doc gap.

### Dashboard Cron page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-cron`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Cron** tab
- **What it does:** Creates and manages scheduled cron jobs from the browser.
- **How it works:** Backed by the same `~/.hermes/cron/jobs.json` the CLI uses.
- **Inputs / options:** Six documented controls: **Create** — name (optional), prompt, cron expression (e.g. `0 9 * * *`), and delivery target (local, Telegram, Discord, Slack, or email); **Job list** — each job shows its name, prompt preview, schedule expression, state badge (enabled/paused/error), delivery target, last run time, and next run time; **Pause / Resume**; **Edit** — a pre-filled modal to change prompt, schedule, name, or delivery target; **Trigger now** — immediately execute a job outside its schedule; **Delete**.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `jobs.json` writes; immediate runs.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/cron/jobs`, `POST /api/cron/jobs`, `PUT /api/cron/jobs/{id}`, `POST /api/cron/jobs/{id}/pause|resume|trigger`, `DELETE /api/cron/jobs/{id}`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The Cron page **aggregates across profiles with its own filter** (it is not scoped by the sidebar profile switcher).
- **Rebuild notes:** Expose the same job fields the CLI writes so the two surfaces stay interchangeable. A better version would surface `last_fire_error` and the failure streak inline.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the cron endpoints listed above are present in the route dump; the page's create form covers only a subset of the CLI's flags (no `--goal`, `--workdir`, `--script`, `--continuity`), though the cron page's own docs mention the continuity toggle and model dropdown — a partial doc/UI mismatch.

### Dashboard Profiles page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-profiles`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Profiles** tab; Profile Builder at `/profiles/new`
- **What it does:** Creates and manages profiles — isolated Hermes instances with their own config, skills, and sessions.
- **How it works:** Profile cards each show model/provider, skill count, gateway state, description, and badges (**active, default, alias**).
- **Inputs / options:** Six documented controls: **Profile cards**; **Create** — name + optional clone-from-default / clone-everything / no-bundled-skills, description, and model, with the dedicated **Profile Builder** page (`/profiles/new`) offering the full flow (model, MCPs, skills); **Manage skills & tools** — jumps to the Skills page scoped to that profile (sets the sidebar profile switcher); **Set as active** — flips the sticky default that **future CLI/gateway runs** pick up (same as `hermes profile use`); **Edit model / description / SOUL** — inline editors writing into that profile; **Rename / Delete** — named profiles only.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Profile directories and config writes.
- **Config / env:** per-profile `HERMES_HOME`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **"Set as active" does *not* change what the dashboard manages — that's the profile switcher's job.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep "which profile future runs use" and "which profile this UI manages" as two separate, clearly-labelled controls. A better version would show both states side by side in the sidebar.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — profile descriptions are also consumed by the kanban decomposer (`GET /api/plugins/kanban/profiles`).

### Dashboard Skills page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-skills`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Skills** tab
- **What it does:** Browse, search, and toggle installed skills and toolsets, and install new ones from the hub.
- **How it works:** Skills are loaded from `~/.hermes/skills/` and grouped by category.
- **Inputs / options:** Five documented controls: **Search** — filter installed skills and toolsets by name, description, or category; **Category filter** — click category pills to narrow the list (e.g. MLOps, MCP, Red Teaming, AI); **Toggle** — enable or disable individual skills with a switch (**changes take effect on the next session**); **Toolsets** — a separate view showing built-in toolsets with their active/inactive status, setup requirements, and list of included tools; **Browse hub** — a third view searching the skill hub across all sources (the same as `hermes skills search`), installing any result by identifier **with a live install log**, and offering an **"Update all"** button. Also the **Learn a skill** button (documented on the skills page) opening a panel with a directory field, a URL field, and an open-ended text box.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Skill installs/uninstalls/updates; enable/disable state.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/skills`, `PUT /api/skills/toggle` (`{"name": "skill-name", "enabled": true}`), `GET /api/tools/toolsets`, `GET /api/skills/hub/search`, `POST /api/skills/hub/install|uninstall|update` (backgrounded).
- **Edge cases / guards:** Hub actions are backgrounded with a live log; the Browse-hub scan button also returns the advisory `tier1` field alongside the built-in scanner's verdict.
- **Rebuild notes:** Put install/update behind a backgrounded action with a streamed log, since hub operations are slow and network-bound. A better version would show the security scan verdict inline before install.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — all five endpoint families present in the route dump; `tier1` advisory field documented on `skills.md`.

### Dashboard MCP page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-mcp`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **MCP** tab
- **What it does:** Manages MCP servers without the CLI, editing the same `mcp_servers` block in `config.yaml` that `hermes mcp` reads.
- **How it works:** Two sections — "Your MCP servers" and "Catalog".
- **Inputs / options:** **Your MCP servers:** **Add** — register an HTTP/SSE server (URL) or a stdio server (command + args), with optional `KEY=VALUE` environment variables for stdio servers; **Enable / disable** — toggle a server without deleting it (**a disabled server stays in config so you can re-enable it later; takes effect on the next gateway restart**); **Test** — connect to a server, list its tools, and disconnect, verifying the connection before the agent depends on it; **Remove** — delete a server from the config. **Catalog:** browse the Nous-approved MCP servers (the bundled `optional-mcps/` catalog) and install any of them with one click; **entries that need API keys prompt for them inline; the values go to `.env`**. This is the same catalog `hermes mcp catalog` / `hermes mcp install` use.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `config.yaml` `mcp_servers` writes; `.env` writes for credentials.
- **Config / env:** `GET/POST /api/mcp/servers`, `POST /api/mcp/servers/{name}/test`, `PUT /api/mcp/servers/{name}/enabled`, `DELETE /api/mcp/servers/{name}`, `GET /api/mcp/catalog`, `POST /api/mcp/catalog/install`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Secret-shaped env values are redacted in the list view.** The catalog view also surfaces per-entry transport, auth type, endpoint URL or command + args, git install source/ref and bootstrap commands, and setup notes, with `source:` as a clickable link.
- **Rebuild notes:** Give the GUI the same catalog and the same config file as the CLI, and redact secret-shaped values on read. A better version would run the security-relevant manifest fields through a diff view before install.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — 65 catalog directories under `optional-mcps/`; all seven MCP admin endpoints present in the route dump.

### Dashboard Webhooks page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-webhooks`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Webhooks** tab
- **What it does:** Manages dynamic webhook subscriptions.
- **How it works:** **The webhook platform must be enabled in messaging settings first; the page shows a hint when it isn't.**
- **Inputs / options:** Four documented controls: **Create** — name, description, event filter, delivery target, optional direct-delivery mode, and an agent prompt; **on creation the page surfaces the route URL and the one-time HMAC secret to copy**; **Enable / disable** — toggle a subscription (**disabled routes stay in the subscriptions file but the gateway rejects their incoming events with 403**); **List** — each subscription shows its URL, events, and delivery target; **Delete**.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Subscription file writes; a one-time HMAC secret shown once.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/webhooks`, `POST /api/webhooks` (returns the one-time secret), `PUT /api/webhooks/{name}/enabled`, `DELETE /api/webhooks/{name}`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **The gateway hot-reloads the subscriptions file, so an enable/disable change takes effect on the next event — no restart needed.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Show the HMAC secret exactly once at creation and hot-reload the subscription file so toggles are instant. A better version would let a secret be rotated without recreating the route.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — all four webhook endpoints present in the route dump.

### Dashboard Pairing page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-pairing`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Pairing** tab
- **What it does:** Approves and revokes messaging users without the CLI — how a remote admin onboards Telegram/Discord/etc. users to a paired gateway. **Full parity with `hermes pairing`.**
- **How it works:** Three sections.
- **Inputs / options:** **Pending requests** — each shows platform, code, user, and age, with an **Approve** button; **Approved users** — each shows platform and user, with a **Revoke** button; **Clear pending** — drop all outstanding pairing codes.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Pairing-state writes.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/pairing`, `POST /api/pairing/approve` (`{platform, code}`), `POST /api/pairing/revoke` (`{platform, user_id}`), `POST /api/pairing/clear-pending`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Requires the auth gate when exposed remotely (this page grants messaging access).
- **Rebuild notes:** Mirror the CLI verb-for-verb so a remote admin never needs shell access. A better version would show the requesting user's display name and first message.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — all four pairing endpoints present in the route dump.

### Dashboard Channels page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-channels`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **Channels** tab
- **What it does:** Connects Hermes to any messaging platform from the browser — **full parity with `hermes setup gateway`.**
- **How it works:** The page lists every supported channel with its **live connection status**.
- **Inputs / options:** Documented channel list (17 + 2): **Telegram, Discord, Slack, Matrix, Mattermost, WhatsApp, Signal, BlueBubbles/iMessage, Email, SMS/Twilio, DingTalk, Feishu/Lark, WeCom, WeChat, QQ Bot, Yuanbao**, plus **the API server and webhook endpoints**. Four controls: **Configure** — a per-platform form with exactly the fields that channel needs (bot token, app token, server URL, allowlist, etc.); **Enable / disable** — toggle a channel (**the credential stays on disk; only the active state changes**); **Test** — check whether the channel is configured, enabled, and reporting a live connection from the gateway; **Restart gateway** — trigger a restart right from the page.
- **Outputs / side effects:** **Credentials are written to `~/.hermes/.env` and the enabled flag to `config.yaml`; the gateway connects each enabled channel on its next restart.**
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/messaging/platforms`, `PUT /api/messaging/platforms/{id}` (`{enabled?, env?, clear_env?}`), `POST /api/messaging/platforms/{id}/test`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Secrets render as password inputs and are stored redacted; leaving a field blank keeps the existing value. Required fields are marked and validated.** A **"Setup guide"** link points to the platform's credential docs.
- **Rebuild notes:** Drive the per-platform form from a field descriptor the backend returns, so adding a channel needs no frontend change. A better version would show the last connection error inline per channel.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the three messaging endpoints present in the route dump; blank-keeps-existing semantics implied by the `clear_env` body field.

### Dashboard System page  `id: docs-features.dash-page-system`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** **System** tab
- **What it does:** A consolidated administration panel for installation-wide operations.
- **How it works:** Nine documented sections. **Host** — live system stats: OS / kernel, architecture, hostname, Python and Hermes versions, CPU core count + utilization, memory, disk usage of the Hermes home, uptime, and load average (**CPU/memory/disk come from `psutil` when installed; identity fields are always shown**); the Hermes version shows an **update-status badge** (up to date / N commits behind) and a **Check for updates** button, and when an update is available on a git install an **Update now** button opens a confirmation dialog — **showing how many commits you'll pull** — before running `hermes update` in the background (**on Docker/Nix installs the dashboard can't apply the update in place, so it shows the correct out-of-band command instead**). **Nous Portal** — login status, the active inference provider, and the Tool Gateway routing table (which tools run via the Portal vs. locally), with a link to manage your subscription; a **read-only mirror of `hermes portal`**. **Skill curator** — background skill-maintenance status (active / paused, interval, last run) with pause/resume and a run-now button; mirrors `hermes curator`. **Gateway** — start, stop, and restart the messaging gateway with live status (running/stopped, PID, state). **Memory** — pick the external memory provider (or built-in only), and reset the built-in `MEMORY.md` / `USER.md` stores. **Credential pool** — add and remove the rotating API keys the agent round-robins through (per provider); **keys are redacted in the list; the raw value only ever reaches the agent**. **Operations** — run `doctor`, a security audit, create a backup, restore from a backup archive, update skills, show the system-prompt size breakdown, generate a support dump, or migrate config for retired settings; **each spawns a background action whose live log streams into the page**. **Checkpoints** — see the `/rollback` shadow store size and prune it. **Shell hooks** — list configured hooks with their consent + executable status, **create** a hook (event, command, matcher, timeout, with an opt-in consent grant), and remove one.
- **Inputs / options:** All controls above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Backgrounded actions with streamed logs; gateway lifecycle changes; `.env`/config writes.
- **Config / env:** `GET /api/system/stats`, `GET /api/hermes/update/check` (`?force=1` busts the 6h cache; for git installs that are behind it also returns a `commits` list of `sha`, `summary`, `author`, `at`), `GET /api/portal`, `GET /api/curator` + `PUT .../paused` + `POST .../run`, `POST /api/gateway/start|stop|restart`, `GET /api/memory` + `PUT /api/memory/provider` + `POST /api/memory/reset` (`{target: all|memory|user}`), `GET/POST /api/credentials/pool` + `DELETE /api/credentials/pool/{provider}/{index}` (**1-based index**), `POST /api/ops/doctor|security-audit|backup|import|prompt-size|dump|config-migrate` (backgrounded, tail via `/api/actions/{name}/status`), `GET /api/ops/hooks` + `POST /api/ops/hooks` + `DELETE /api/ops/hooks`, `GET /api/ops/checkpoints` + `POST .../prune`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Hooks run arbitrary commands, so the create form carries a security warning and the hook only fires after consent is granted.** **Security warning on the page:** the dashboard reads and writes your `.env` file, which contains API keys and secrets; it binds to `127.0.0.1` by default — only accessible locally, with no login required — and **binding to any non-loopback address (including `0.0.0.0`) engages the auth gate: the server refuses to start until an auth provider is configured.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Back every long operation with a backgrounded action plus a streamable log endpoint, and gate command-executing features behind an explicit consent grant. A better version would show a dry-run diff for `config-migrate` and `import` before applying.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — all listed admin endpoints appear in the FastAPI route dump (`routes_static.txt` lists 260 routes; `api_live/get_all.json` covers 92 GET routes).

### `/reload` slash command (re-read `.env`)  `id: docs-features.dash-reload`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `/reload` in an interactive CLI session
- **What it does:** Re-reads `~/.hermes/.env` into the running process's environment, so API-key changes made in the dashboard (or by editing `.env`) take effect without restarting.
- **How it works:** Documented output: `You → /reload` → `Reloaded .env (3 var(s) updated)`.
- **Inputs / options:** `/reload` — no arguments.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Process environment updated in place.
- **Config / env:** reads `~/.hermes/.env`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** Useful when you've added a new provider key via the dashboard and want to use it immediately.
- **Rebuild notes:** Reload only the secrets file, not the whole config, so the blast radius of a hot reload is small. A better version would report exactly which variables changed by name (without values).
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `/reload` present in the slash-command catalogue (`slash_commands.json`).

### Dashboard profile-scoped endpoints (`?profile=`)  `id: docs-features.dash-api-profile-scope`
- **Surface:** API
- **Where:** `?profile=<name>` query param (or `"profile"` in the JSON body for writes)
- **What it does:** Scopes a management endpoint's read/write to a specific profile's `HERMES_HOME`.
- **How it works:** **Omitted = the dashboard's own profile. Unknown profile names return `404`.**
- **Inputs / options:** Six documented endpoint families accept it: `/api/config`, `/api/env`, `/api/skills`, `/api/tools/toolsets`, `/api/mcp`, and `/api/model/{info,options,auxiliary,set}`. **The `/api/pty` WebSocket accepts the same parameter to spawn a chat under the selected profile.**
- **Outputs / side effects:** Reads and writes against the named profile's home.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** 404 on unknown names rather than silently falling back.
- **Rebuild notes:** Make profile scoping a uniform query parameter across every management family, and fail loudly on an unknown name. A better version would echo the resolved `HERMES_HOME` in the response so the write target is auditable.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — profile-scoped resolution helpers (`get_process_hermes_home`, `get_default_hermes_root`) used throughout `hermes_cli/web_server.py`.

### `GET /api/status` resource blocks  `id: docs-features.dash-api-status`
- **Surface:** API
- **Where:** `GET /api/status`
- **What it does:** Returns agent version, gateway status, platform states, and active session count, plus two advisory resource blocks.
- **How it works:** **The two resource blocks never affect the `components`/`overall` health verdict.** **`memory`** is distilled from the gateway's 30-second heartbeat and the lifecycle ledger, with fields `pressure` (`ok` / `elevated` / `critical` / `unknown`), `gateway_rss_mb`, `system_total_mb`, `system_available_mb`, `swap_used_mb`, `sampled_at`, `boot_id`, `last_boot_unclean`, `last_boot_suspected_oom`; **pressure is `elevated` below 128 MiB (or 15%) of available system memory and `critical` below 64 MiB (or 5%)** — the same levels at which a subsequent unclean exit would be flagged as a suspected OOM kill. **`disk`** is a live `shutil.disk_usage()` sample of the volume holding `~/.hermes`, with fields `pressure`, `free_mb`, `total_mb`, `used_percent`, `sampled_at`; **pressure is `elevated` below 512 MB free (or ≥85% used with under 4 GB headroom) and `critical` below 256 MB free (or ≥95% used with under 1 GB headroom)**.
- **Inputs / options:** No parameters.
- **Outputs / side effects:** JSON including `auth_required` and `auth_providers`.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Heartbeats older than 150 seconds (or future-dated) keep their numbers but degrade `pressure` to `unknown`, so a dead gateway's last sample can't masquerade as a live reading.** **Both collectors are fail-safe: any sampling error degrades the block to `{"pressure": "unknown"}` instead of failing the status endpoint.** **The numbers are coarse (whole MB, whole-percent) since `/api/status` is public.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep advisory telemetry out of the health verdict, degrade stale samples to `unknown` rather than showing them, and coarsen numbers on a public endpoint. A better version would expose the precise values on an authenticated endpoint alongside the coarse public one.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `/api/status` is a public endpoint (Desktop's readiness probe relies on that), confirmed by the page's own remote-backend section.

### Dashboard auth gate (gated mode)  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-gate`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** engaged automatically on a non-loopback bind
- **What it does:** Requires a verified session for every request when the dashboard is bound to a public or non-loopback address.
- **How it works:** **The gate is on if and only if the bind host is not `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, or `localhost`.** Binding to `0.0.0.0` (or any RFC1918 / LAN address) engages it. Every request must carry a verified session cookie or it's bounced to the login page. **Operator-owned dashboards bound to loopback are unaffected — no auth, no login page.**
- **Inputs / options:** Three bundled providers: **Username/password** (`basic`) — the simplest way to put auth on a self-hosted / on-prem / homelab dashboard, no external IDP, **"Use it only on a trusted network or behind a VPN — not for public-internet exposure"**; **OAuth (Nous Portal)** (`nous`) — for hosted deployments and any dashboard reachable over the public internet, and the recommended path for a remote Hermes Desktop connection; **Self-hosted OIDC** (`self-hosted`) — bring your own identity provider via standard OpenID Connect (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, Google, GitHub via an OIDC bridge), **suitable for public-internet exposure when fronted by a conformant OIDC server**.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Login redirect; session cookies.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.oauth.*`, `dashboard.basic_auth.*`, `dashboard.public_url`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **`--insecure` is a no-op** — since the June 2026 hardening it no longer bypasses dashboard authentication: a non-loopback bind always requires an auth provider; **it's accepted for backward compatibility but ignored, with a warning.** "If you want an auth-free dashboard, bind to `127.0.0.1` and reach it over an SSH tunnel or Tailscale."
- **Rebuild notes:** Derive the gate purely from the bind address so it cannot be forgotten, and turn the old bypass flag into a warned no-op rather than removing it. A better version would also gate plugin routes, which are currently skipped by the middleware.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `--insecure` help text reads "DEPRECATED / NO-OP… As of the June 2026 hardening it no longer disables authentication — a public bind always requires an auth provider (password or OAuth). Bind 127.0.0.1 + tunnel to keep it local." (evidence: `cli_help/dashboard.txt`).

### Dashboard fail-closed auth semantics  `id: docs-features.dash-fail-closed`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0` with no provider configured
- **What it does:** Refuses to bind when the gate would engage but no `DashboardAuthProvider` is registered — **there is no "default-deny but accept everything" fallback; a misconfigured gated dashboard never starts.**
- **How it works:** **Interactively** (a real terminal) with no provider configured, Hermes offers to set one up on the spot: pick **username & password** (writes `dashboard.basic_auth` to `config.yaml` and you're running in seconds) or **OAuth** (points you at `hermes dashboard register`). **Non-interactive callers — Docker/s6, CI, piped runs — skip the prompt and hit the fail-closed error**, so an unattended deploy still never starts without auth.
- **Inputs / options:** The interactive setup prompt's two choices.
- **Outputs / side effects:** The documented error message names the failing provider reasons and the two fixes: `Password: set dashboard.basic_auth.username + password_hash in config.yaml`; `OAuth: run \`hermes dashboard register\` (Nous Portal) or install a DashboardAuthProvider plugin`; and states "There is no unauthenticated public-bind option — to keep it local, bind 127.0.0.1 and tunnel in (SSH / Tailscale)."
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.basic_auth`, `dashboard.oauth`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Declaring a non-loopback `public_url` always engages the gate, even when the backend binds to loopback** — "This prevents the local SPA session token from becoming a remote authentication mechanism through the proxy."
- **Rebuild notes:** Fail closed on missing auth, and offer interactive remediation only when a human is actually there. A better version would print the exact config snippet to paste, pre-filled with a generated hash.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `dashboard.basic_auth` at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1764`, `dashboard.oauth` at `:1739`, `dashboard.public_url` at `:1810`.

### Nous Portal dashboard auth provider  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-nous`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** bundled plugin `plugins/dashboard_auth/nous`
- **What it does:** Authenticates the dashboard against Nous Portal via OAuth — **the provider suitable for exposing a dashboard to the public internet**, because every login is verified against your Nous account.
- **How it works:** **Always installed and auto-loaded**; it **auto-registers a `DashboardAuthProvider` named `nous` when a client ID is configured**. Client ID shape is `agent:{id}`.
- **Inputs / options:** **Two ways to get a client ID.** **CLI — `hermes dashboard register`:** run it on the host where the dashboard lives; it resolves your existing Nous login (`hermes setup` first if needed), registers a self-hosted OAuth client with the Portal, and writes `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` into `~/.hermes/.env`; flags `--name NAME` (human-readable label, default auto-generated), `--redirect-uri REDIRECT_URI` (public HTTPS callback for an internet-facing host, e.g. `https://hermes.example.com/auth/callback`; omit for localhost-only), and `--portal-url PORTAL_URL` (override the Portal base URL, also settable via `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PORTAL_URL`, "mainly for testing against a staging/preview portal"). **GUI — the Local Dashboards page** at `https://portal.nousresearch.com/local-dashboards` to register, name, manage, and revoke self-hosted dashboards; copy the `agent:{id}` into `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` or `dashboard.oauth.client_id`; **this is also where you revoke a dashboard registered via the CLI.**
- **Outputs / side effects:** `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` written to `.env`; a registered OAuth client at the Portal.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.oauth.client_id` (canonical, `config.yaml`); env `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` (operator override, wins when set non-empty); `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PORTAL_URL`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Per the Hermes convention (`~/.hermes/.env` is for API keys / secrets only), `config.yaml` is the recommended place to set these values** for local dev, on-prem, and any deployment you control directly; **the environment-variable path exists so a hosting platform's secret injection can push per-deploy `client_id`s without editing `config.yaml` inside the image — that's its primary purpose.** **Empty environment values are treated as unset**, so a provisioned-but-not-populated platform secret can't accidentally shadow a valid `config.yaml` entry. Worked example: `hermes setup` → `hermes dashboard register` → `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9119 --no-open` → sign in at `/login` with **Sign in with Nous Research**; verify with `curl -s http://<host>:9119/api/status | jq '.auth_required, .auth_providers'` returning `true` and `["nous"]`; `GET /api/auth/me` returns `provider: nous`. For an internet-facing host, register with `--redirect-uri` and set `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Ship the OAuth provider as an always-installed plugin that registers itself only once configured, so it's a no-op for loopback users. A better version would let `register` also write `dashboard.oauth.client_id` into `config.yaml` (its own recommended surface) rather than `.env`.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — plugin directory `plugins/dashboard_auth/nous` exists; `hermes dashboard register --help` confirms all three flags and the `.env` write (evidence: `cli_help/dashboard__register.txt`).

### Username/password dashboard auth provider (`basic`)  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-basic`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** bundled plugin `plugins/dashboard_auth/basic`
- **What it does:** Authenticates with a **username and password** instead of an OAuth redirect — for a self-hosted "just put a password on my dashboard" deployment with no OAuth IDP.
- **How it works:** It plugs into the same gate as the OAuth provider: **the login page renders a credential form for this provider (instead of a "Log in with X" button), and everything downstream of login — session cookies, transparent refresh, WS tickets, logout, the audit log — is identical to the OAuth path.** **Sessions are stateless HMAC-signed tokens the provider mints itself, so there's no database and no external IDP.** **Password hashing uses stdlib `scrypt` (no third-party dependency).** It **activates only when `username` plus either `password_hash` (preferred) or `password` are configured** — otherwise it's a no-op, so OAuth users and loopback operators are unaffected.
- **Inputs / options:** **`config.yaml`:** `dashboard.basic_auth.username`; `password_hash` (**preferred — no plaintext at rest**; compute with `python -c "from plugins.dashboard_auth.basic import hash_password; print(hash_password('PW'))"`, format `scrypt$16384$8$1$…$…`); `password` (plaintext, hashed in-memory at load, **less safe at rest**); `secret` (32+ random bytes, base64 or hex — the token-signing key); `session_ttl_seconds` (optional access-token lifetime, **default 12h / 43200**). **Env overrides:** `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME` (required to activate); `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH` (preferred); `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD` (plaintext — **wins over a config `password_hash` so you can rotate via env**); `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_SECRET`; `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_TTL_SECONDS`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A credential form at `/login`; signed session tokens.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.basic_auth.*` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1764`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** **"Use this on trusted networks only — not the public internet"** — it protects a single shared credential with no external identity provider, MFA, or per-user accounts, so it is **not suitable for direct public-internet exposure**; use the Nous or self-hosted-OIDC provider instead. **Set an explicit `secret` for stable sessions:** when `secret` is empty a random per-process signing key is generated — fine for a single process, but **every session is invalidated on restart** and **sessions don't span multiple workers**. **The `/auth/password-login` endpoint is rate-limited per client IP (default 10 attempts/minute → HTTP 429) and returns a single generic `401 Invalid credentials` for both unknown users and wrong passwords, so it can't be used as a username-enumeration oracle.** Worked example: hash the password, append `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME` / `_PASSWORD_HASH` / `_SECRET` (`openssl rand -base64 32`) to `~/.hermes/.env`, `chmod 600 ~/.hermes/.env`, run `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9119 --no-open`, log in, verify `auth_providers` includes `"basic"`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Use stateless HMAC sessions and stdlib scrypt so a password gate needs no database or third-party dependency, and return one generic error for both failure modes. A better version would support per-user accounts so a shared credential isn't the only option.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — plugin directory `plugins/dashboard_auth/basic` exists; config block at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1764`.

### Writing your own password provider  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-custom-password`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** a plugin registering a `DashboardAuthProvider` with `supports_password = True`
- **What it does:** Lets any plugin add a non-redirect auth scheme — LDAP-bind, a credentials database, or anything else.
- **How it works:** **Set `supports_password = True` on your `DashboardAuthProvider` subclass and implement `complete_password_login(*, username, password) -> Session`** — raise `InvalidCredentialsError` on rejection, `ProviderError` if your backing store is down. **The OAuth `start_login` / `complete_login` methods can be left as `NotImplementedError` stubs for a pure-password provider.** **The framework handles the form, the route, the cookies, and refresh for you.**
- **Inputs / options:** `supports_password`, `complete_password_login`, `InvalidCredentialsError`, `ProviderError`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A new credential form on `/login`.
- **Config / env:** plugin system.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `basic` is just one implementation of the extension point.
- **Rebuild notes:** Make password auth a capability flag on the same ABC as OAuth so the framework owns the plumbing either way. A better version would ship a reference LDAP provider.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the `basic` plugin is the shipped example of this extension point.

### Self-hosted OIDC dashboard auth provider  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-oidc`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** bundled plugin `plugins/dashboard_auth/self_hosted`
- **What it does:** Authenticates the dashboard against your own identity provider using **standard OpenID Connect** — no per-IDP code, no Nous Portal involved.
- **How it works:** Configure an **issuer** and a **client_id** (**a public PKCE client — no client secret**). **The plugin fetches the IDP's `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, and `jwks_uri` from `{issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration`, so you never hardcode endpoint URLs.** Like the Nous provider it **auto-loads and only registers itself once configured**, so it's a no-op for loopback dashboards. Verified against and works with **Authentik, Keycloak, Zitadel, Authelia, Auth0, Okta, Google** and any conformant OIDC server.
- **Inputs / options:** **`config.yaml`:** `dashboard.oauth.provider: self-hosted`; `dashboard.oauth.self_hosted.issuer` (required, e.g. `https://auth.example.com/application/o/hermes/`); `.client_id` (required, e.g. `hermes-dashboard`); `.scopes` (optional, default `openid profile email`). **Env overrides** (env wins when set non-empty; an empty value is treated as unset): `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_ISSUER`, `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_CLIENT_ID`, `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_SCOPES`. In your IDP, **register a public application/client with the authorization-code + PKCE (S256) grant** and add `<dashboard public URL>/auth/callback` as an allowed redirect URI.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A "Sign in with Self-Hosted OIDC" button; a verified session.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.oauth.self_hosted.*`; `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **What it verifies:** the OIDC **ID token** (RS256/ES256) against the discovered `jwks_uri`, with **`iss` and `aud` pinned** to your configured `issuer` and `client_id`. **Claim mapping:** `user_id` ← `sub` (**required**); `email` ← `email`; `display_name` ← `name` → `preferred_username` → `nickname` → `email`; `org_id` ← `org_id` / `organization`, else joined `groups`. **The ID token is what establishes identity — the access token is treated as opaque (the OIDC spec does not require it to be a JWT).** **Endpoint URLs are required to be HTTPS (loopback `http://` is allowed for local-dev IDPs), and the discovery document's advertised `issuer` must match your configured one (a trailing-slash difference is tolerated).** Refresh tokens, when issued, are used for silent re-auth via the standard `refresh_token` grant; **logout calls the IDP's RFC 7009 `revocation_endpoint` when advertised**. **Confidential clients (those with a `client_secret`) are not supported yet.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Discover endpoints from the well-known document and pin `iss`/`aud` on the ID token; treat the access token as opaque. A better version would support confidential clients for IDPs that require them.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — plugin directory `plugins/dashboard_auth/self_hosted` exists.

### Worked example: Keycloak OIDC  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-keycloak`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** web-dashboard.md → "Worked example: Keycloak"
- **What it does:** A three-step walkthrough from nothing to a working dashboard login against a local Keycloak.
- **How it works:** **(1) Run Keycloak with a pre-configured realm** — save a realm export as `realm-hermes.json` defining a `hermes` realm, a **public PKCE client** (`hermes-dashboard`), and a test user, imported on boot so nothing needs clicking in the admin UI; start with `docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin -v "$PWD/realm-hermes.json:/opt/keycloak/data/import/realm-hermes.json:ro" quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.0 start-dev --import-realm`. Discovery then lives at `http://localhost:8080/realms/hermes/.well-known/openid-configuration` (issuer `http://localhost:8080/realms/hermes`), admin console at `http://localhost:8080/` (`admin`/`admin`). **(2) Point the dashboard at it** — `export HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_ISSUER="http://localhost:8080/realms/hermes"`, `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_CLIENT_ID="hermes-dashboard"`, `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL="http://localhost:9119"`, then `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9119 --no-open`. **(3) Log in** — open `http://localhost:9119/`, get bounced to `/login`, click **Sign in with Self-Hosted OIDC**, authenticate as `testuser` / `testpassword`, land back authenticated; the sidebar shows `Logged in as Test User via self-hosted` and `GET /api/auth/me` returns `provider: self-hosted`, `email: testuser@example.com`.
- **Inputs / options:** Keycloak 26+ in dev mode (in-memory DB).
- **Outputs / side effects:** A working OIDC login.
- **Config / env:** the three `HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_*` / `PUBLIC_URL` vars.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **The self-hosted plugin permits a loopback `http://` issuer (HTTPS is required for any non-loopback issuer)**, so the local Keycloak works as-is. **`HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL` tells the dashboard its OAuth callback is `http://localhost:9119/auth/callback`.** **Binding to `0.0.0.0` (a non-loopback bind) is what engages the OAuth gate.** If you bind or browse on a different host/port, add that origin's `…/auth/callback` to the client's **Valid redirect URIs** (Clients → hermes-dashboard → Settings); the same pattern works for Authentik, Zitadel, Authelia and others — only the issuer URL and client registration UI differ.
- **Rebuild notes:** Ship a realm export so the example needs zero admin-console clicking. A better version would add the same for Authentik and Zitadel.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — loopback-`http` issuer allowance is stated by the provider's own HTTPS rule on the same page.

### Dashboard public URL override & trusted proxies  `id: docs-features.dash-public-url`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `dashboard.public_url` / `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL`; `dashboard.trusted_proxies`
- **What it does:** Declares the complete public URL the dashboard is reached at, for deploys behind reverse proxies that don't reliably forward `X-Forwarded-*`.
- **How it works:** **By default the dashboard reconstructs the OAuth callback URL from the request — `X-Forwarded-Host` + `X-Forwarded-Proto` + `X-Forwarded-Prefix`** (when uvicorn is configured with `proxy_headers=True`, which `start_server` enables under the gate). **When `public_url` is set, the OAuth callback URL becomes `<public_url>/auth/callback` verbatim — `X-Forwarded-Prefix` is ignored on that code path** because the operator has explicitly declared the public URL; **this is intentional: stacking the prefix on top would double-prefix the common case where the prefix is already baked into `public_url`.** **The hostname in `public_url` is also accepted as an exact HTTP `Host` and WebSocket `Origin` value**, supporting a reverse proxy that preserves the browser-facing hostname while forwarding to a loopback-bound dashboard.
- **Inputs / options:** `dashboard.public_url: "https://dashboard.example.com/hermes"`; `dashboard.trusted_proxies: ["172.20.0.5"]` (exact IP) or `["172.20.0.0/24"]` (a bounded CIDR for a dedicated proxy network). Env `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL`. Precedence table: `dashboard.public_url` in `config.yaml` (canonical for local dev / on-prem) → `HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL` env var (hosting-platform secrets / CI) → unset (reconstruct from `X-Forwarded-*`).
- **Outputs / side effects:** OAuth callback URL; accepted `Host`/`Origin`; trusted forwarding peers.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.public_url` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1810`), `dashboard.trusted_proxies` (`:1701`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Wildcards and suffix matches are not allowed**, so an attacker host such as `dashboard.example.com.evil.test` remains rejected by the DNS-rebinding guard. **Declaring a non-loopback `public_url` always engages the auth gate, even when the backend binds to loopback** — configure a provider first or Hermes fails closed at startup; **this prevents the local SPA session token from becoming a remote authentication mechanism through the proxy.** **Loopback proxies are trusted automatically**; if the TLS terminator connects from another container or host, add its exact IP (or a bounded CIDR). **Only listed peers may supply `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-For`. Hermes always preserves loopback trust and rejects `*`, `0.0.0.0/0`, and `::/0`.** "Trusting a network means every container or machine on that network can supply forwarding metadata, so prefer an exact proxy IP or a dedicated proxy-only network." **Validation rejects values without an `http://` / `https://` scheme, without a host, or containing quote / angle / whitespace / control characters; a malformed value silently falls through to header reconstruction so the login flow keeps working rather than dispatching the user to a hostile URL.** **`public_url` overrides the OAuth callback URL only** — the `Secure` cookie flag is still controlled by `request.url.scheme`, using `X-Forwarded-Proto` only when the connecting peer is loopback or listed in `trusted_proxies`. **Tailscale Serve** is one example of this shape: terminate tailnet-only HTTPS on `https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net` while proxying to the loopback dashboard, using that exact HTTPS origin as `public_url`; **it is still treated as a non-loopback browser-facing origin and therefore requires a dashboard auth provider — this does not require making the service reachable from the public internet.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Require exact host matches (never wildcards) for the rebinding guard, refuse unbounded CIDRs in the proxy allowlist, and fall through to header reconstruction on a malformed override rather than sending users to a bad URL. A better version would warn at startup when `public_url` is set but no `trusted_proxies` entry covers the connecting terminator.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `trusted_proxies: []` at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1701` and `public_url: ""` at `:1810`.

### Dashboard OAuth flow, cookies, logout, audit log  `id: docs-features.dash-oauth-flow`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** `/login`, `/auth/login`, `/auth/callback`, `/auth/logout`; `$HERMES_HOME/logs/dashboard-auth.log`
- **What it does:** Implements the Nous Portal OAuth contract v1 — authorization-code grant with PKCE (S256) — plus session cookies, logout, and an audit log.
- **How it works:** Six documented steps: (1) user hits `/` without a session cookie → gate redirects to `/login`; (2) login page shows a "Continue with Nous Research" button → `/auth/login?provider=nous`; (3) server stashes PKCE state in a short-lived cookie, redirects to `https://portal.nousresearch.com/oauth/authorize?…`; (4) user authenticates with Portal, lands at `/auth/callback?code=…&state=…`; (5) server exchanges the code for an access token at `POST /api/oauth/token`, **verifies the JWT signature against the Portal's JWKS (`/.well-known/jwks.json`)**, and sets the `hermes_session_at` cookie; (6) user is redirected to `/` (or the original deep-link path via the `next=` query parameter).
- **Inputs / options:** **Three cookies:** `hermes_session_at` — lifetime = token TTL (15 min), **HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure-when-HTTPS**; `hermes_session_pkce` — 10 min, HttpOnly, holds the PKCE verifier + provider hint during the round trip, **SameSite=None + Secure over HTTPS (must survive the cross-site IDP redirect chain — Chromium drops SameSite=Lax cookies set on a 302 in a cross-site chain), SameSite=Lax on loopback HTTP**; `hermes_session_rt` — **unused in v1**, reserved for forward-compat, **not written when `refresh_token` is empty**. All three are `Path=/`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** **Logout:** the sidebar widget shows `Logged in as <user_id…> via nous` with a logout icon; clicking it POSTs `/auth/logout`, which clears all dashboard-auth cookies and redirects back to `/login`. **Audit log:** every login start, success, failure, and session-verify failure is written as a JSON line to `$HERMES_HOME/logs/dashboard-auth.log`.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.oauth.client_id`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Access tokens have a 15-minute TTL. There is no refresh token in contract v1** — when the token expires, the SPA's fetch wrapper detects the 401 envelope and full-page-navigates back to `/login` to re-run the flow. **Sensitive fields (`access_token`, `refresh_token`, `code`, `code_verifier`, `state`, `Authorization` header) are redacted before logging.** The `Secure` flag is set when the dashboard is reached over HTTPS (detected via the request URL scheme, honouring `X-Forwarded-Proto` from an upstream TLS terminator under `proxy_headers=True`).
- **Rebuild notes:** Use `SameSite=None` only for the short-lived PKCE cookie that must survive a cross-site redirect chain, and redact every credential-bearing field before writing an audit line. A better version would implement refresh so a 15-minute session doesn't force a full re-login.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — contract reference is the public `nous-account-service` `agent-dashboard-oauth-contract.md`.

### Custom dashboard auth providers  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-custom`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** a plugin calling `ctx.register_dashboard_auth_provider(...)`
- **What it does:** Lets a plugin plug a non-Nous OAuth provider (Google, GitHub, custom OIDC) into the dashboard's auth gate.
- **How it works:** Documented skeleton at `~/.hermes/plugins/dashboard-auth-myidp/__init__.py`: subclass `DashboardAuthProvider` from `hermes_cli.dashboard_auth` with `name`, `display_name`, and five methods — `start_login(*, redirect_uri)`, `complete_login(*, code, state, code_verifier, redirect_uri)`, `verify_session(*, access_token)`, `refresh_session(*, refresh_token)`, `revoke_session(*, refresh_token)` — then `def register(ctx): ctx.register_dashboard_auth_provider(MyIdPProvider())`.
- **Inputs / options:** The five methods plus `name` / `display_name`; imports `DashboardAuthProvider`, `Session`, `LoginStart`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A new button on `/login`.
- **Config / env:** plugin system.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **The login page lists all registered providers; multiple providers can be stacked and the user picks one at `/login`.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Define the provider as a small ABC with a stable five-method contract so third-party IDPs need no core changes. A better version would ship a conformance test suite for provider authors.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — four bundled providers exist under `plugins/dashboard_auth/` (`basic`, `drain`, `nous`, `self_hosted`), demonstrating the extension point.

### Non-interactive bearer-token dashboard auth (drain provider)  `id: docs-features.dash-auth-token`
- **Surface:** Provider
- **Where:** `plugins/dashboard_auth/drain`; `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; `/api/gateway/drain`
- **What it does:** Adds a **non-interactive, service-to-service** auth capability alongside interactive human login.
- **How it works:** The `DashboardAuthProvider` ABC supports it via **`supports_token = True` + `verify_token(token=...)`**. When a provider opts in, **an inbound `Authorization: Bearer <token>` is verified and, on success, a `TokenPrincipal` is attached to the request (`request.state.token_principal`) for the endpoints that provider marks token-authable — no cookie, no redirect, no refresh.** **The bundled first consumer is the drain provider:** `nous-account-service` provisions a per-agent secret via `HERMES_DASHBOARD_DRAIN_SECRET`, and the provider **verifies inbound bearer tokens against it with a constant-time compare**, registering `/api/gateway/drain` as token-authable.
- **Inputs / options:** Env `HERMES_DASHBOARD_DRAIN_SECRET`; behavioural knobs `scope` and `min_secret_chars` under `dashboard.drain_auth` in `config.yaml`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A `TokenPrincipal` on the request; `/api/gateway/drain` reachable without a cookie.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.drain_auth` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1783`); env `HERMES_DASHBOARD_DRAIN_SECRET`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **It fails closed** — a weak/short secret (**< 256 bits**) is rejected at registration and the endpoint stays disabled; **it's a no-op when the env var is unset.** **Custom providers can implement `supports_token`/`verify_token` the same way to expose their own machine-authable endpoints.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Let a provider mark specific endpoints token-authable rather than making bearer auth global, and reject weak secrets at registration. A better version would rotate the drain secret automatically from the provisioning service.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `plugins/dashboard_auth/drain` exists; `dashboard.drain_auth` config block at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:1783`.

### Dashboard CORS policy  `id: docs-features.dash-cors`
