- **What it does:** Restricts CORS to localhost origins only.
- **How it works:** Six documented allowed origins: `http://localhost:9119` / `http://127.0.0.1:9119` (production); `http://localhost:3000` / `http://127.0.0.1:3000`; `http://localhost:5173` / `http://127.0.0.1:5173` (Vite dev server).
- **Inputs / options:** n/a
- **Outputs / side effects:** Cross-origin requests from other hosts rejected.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **If you run the server on a custom port, that origin is added automatically.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Allowlist only loopback origins plus the actual bind port so a browser on another site can't drive the API. A better version would derive the list from `public_url` too when set.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — CORS middleware configured in `hermes_cli/web_server.py`.

### Dashboard frontend development & auto-build  `id: docs-features.dash-dev`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `web/`; `hermes_cli/web_dist/`; `hermes update`
- **What it does:** Documents the frontend dev loop and the automatic rebuild on update.
- **How it works:** Two-terminal dev loop: **Terminal 1** `hermes dashboard --no-open` (backend API); **Terminal 2** `cd web/ && npm install && npm run dev` (Vite dev server with HMR). **The Vite dev server at `http://localhost:5173` proxies `/api` requests to the FastAPI backend at `http://127.0.0.1:9119`.** **The frontend is built with React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, and shadcn/ui-style components. Production builds output to `hermes_cli/web_dist/` which the FastAPI server serves as a static SPA.**
- **Inputs / options:** `npm install`, `npm run dev`, `npm run build`; `hermes dashboard --skip-build` to serve the existing dist directly.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `hermes_cli/web_dist/` artifacts.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **When you run `hermes update`, the web frontend is automatically rebuilt if `npm` is available**, keeping the dashboard in sync with code updates; **if `npm` isn't installed, the update skips the frontend build and `hermes dashboard` will build it on first launch.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Build on update when the toolchain is present and lazily on first launch otherwise, with an explicit skip flag for CI. A better version would ship a prebuilt dist in the release artifact so npm is never required.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `--skip-build` exists with the matching help text ("Skip the web UI build step and serve the existing dist directly… Pre-build with: cd web && npm run build", evidence: `cli_help/dashboard.txt`).

### Dashboard themes & plugins (summary)  `id: docs-features.dash-themes-summary`
- **Surface:** Web dashboard
- **Where:** header bar → palette icon (theme switcher + **Font** section)
- **What it does:** Ships **eight built-in themes** and allows user-defined themes, plugin tabs, and backend API routes — all drop-in, no repo clone needed.
- **How it works:** **Switch themes live** from the header bar (the palette icon next to the language switcher); **selection persists to `config.yaml` under `dashboard.theme` and is restored on page load.** **Change the font independently** from the same picker — the **Font** section below the theme list overrides the UI font of whatever theme is active, persisting across theme switches (`config.yaml` → `dashboard.font`); pick **Theme default** to clear it.
- **Inputs / options:** Eight built-in themes: **Hermes Teal** (`default`) — dark teal + cream, system fonts, comfortable spacing; **Hermes Teal (Large)** (`default-large`) — same as default with 18px text and roomier spacing; **Nous Blue** (`nous-blue`) — Nous-branded blue accents with airy spacing; **Midnight** (`midnight`) — deep blue-violet, Inter + JetBrains Mono; **Ember** (`ember`) — warm crimson + bronze, Spectral serif + IBM Plex Mono; **Mono** (`mono`) — grayscale, IBM Plex, compact; **Cyberpunk** (`cyberpunk`) — neon green on black, Share Tech Mono; **Rosé** (`rose`) — pink + ivory, Fraunces serif, spacious.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `dashboard.theme` and `dashboard.font` writes.
- **Config / env:** `dashboard.theme` (default `"default"`), `dashboard.font`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The full extension guide (theme YAML schema, layout variants, plugin manifest/SDK/slots/backend routes, the Strike Freedom walkthrough, discovery/reload/troubleshooting) lives at `./extending-the-dashboard`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep theme and font as independent persisted settings so a font preference survives theme changes. A better version would let the picker preview a theme without committing it.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — **8** presets in `web/src/themes/presets.ts` at `:42, 58, 83, 111, 135, 164, 189, 216` (`default`, `midnight`, `ember`, `mono`, `cyberpunk`, `rose`, `nous-blue`, `default-large`), matching this page exactly — **and confirming that `extending-the-dashboard.md`'s 7-theme table is the one that is out of date** (see `docs-features.dash-builtin-themes`).

## Page: `hooks.md` — Event Hooks

### Four hook systems (overview)  `id: docs-features.hooks-overview`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** hooks.md → the four-system table
- **What it does:** Documents Hermes's four independent hook systems that run custom code at key lifecycle points.
- **How it works:** **Gateway hooks** — registered via `HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py` in `~/.hermes/hooks/`, run in the **gateway only**, for logging/alerts/webhooks. **Plugin hooks** — registered via `ctx.register_hook()` in a plugin, run in **CLI + Gateway**, for tool interception/metrics/guardrails. **Shell hooks** — a `hooks:` block in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` pointing at shell scripts, run in **CLI + Gateway**, for drop-in scripts that block, auto-format, or inject context. **Outbound webhooks** — a `hooks.outbound:` list in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`, run in **CLI + Gateway**, pushing signed lifecycle events to external HTTP endpoints (CI, dashboards, other agents).
- **Inputs / options:** Four registration surfaces as above.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Depends on the hook category.
- **Config / env:** `hooks:` and `hooks.outbound:` in `config.yaml`; `~/.hermes/hooks/`; plugin `register()`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Hook callback errors are isolated and logged rather than crashing the agent.** **Hooks are not all passive:** directive/control hooks can change flow, transforms can replace content, and a shell `pre_tool_call` hook can block or fail closed.
- **Rebuild notes:** Keep the four systems separate by trust model and runtime rather than merging them, and route the two in-process ones (plugin + shell) through one dispatcher. A better version would let gateway hooks run in the CLI too, removing the only capability asymmetry.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `hermes_cli/plugins.py` (plugin hooks), `agent/shell_hooks.py` (shell hooks), `agent/plugin_stream_hooks.py` (streaming observers), gateway `HookRegistry`.

### Gateway event hooks (`HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py`)  `id: docs-features.hooks-gateway`
- **Surface:** Gateway/Telegram
- **Where:** `~/.hermes/hooks/<name>/HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py`
- **What it does:** Fires automatically during gateway operation (Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Teams) **without blocking the main agent pipeline**.
- **How it works:** Five documented steps: (1) on gateway startup, `HookRegistry.discover_and_load()` scans `~/.hermes/hooks/`; (2) each subdirectory with `HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py` is loaded dynamically; (3) handlers are registered for their declared events; (4) at each lifecycle point, `hooks.emit()` fires all matching handlers; (5) **errors in any handler are caught and logged — a broken hook never crashes the agent**.
- **Inputs / options:** `HOOK.yaml` fields: `name`, `description`, `events` (a list determining which events trigger the handler; **you can subscribe to any combination, including wildcards like `command:*`**). `handler.py` **handler rules:** must be named `handle`; receives `event_type` (string) and `context` (dict); **can be `async def` or regular `def` — both work**; errors are caught and logged, never crashing the agent.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Whatever the handler does.
- **Config / env:** none beyond the directory.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Gateway hooks only fire in the gateway — the CLI does not load them.** For hooks that work everywhere, use plugin hooks.
- **Rebuild notes:** Discover hooks by directory convention with a two-file contract, and accept both sync and async handlers. A better version would hot-reload the directory instead of requiring a gateway restart.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `HookRegistry.discover_and_load()` / `hooks.emit()` in the gateway package.

### Gateway hook event catalog  `id: docs-features.hooks-gateway-events`
- **Surface:** Gateway/Telegram
- **Where:** `HOOK.yaml` → `events:`
- **What it does:** Enumerates every gateway lifecycle event and its context keys.
- **How it works:** Ten documented events. **`gateway:startup`** — the gateway process starts; context `platforms` (list of active platform names). **`session:start`** — new messaging session created; `platform`, `user_id`, `session_id`, `session_key`. **`session:end`** — session ended (before reset); `platform`, `user_id`, `session_key`. **`session:reset`** — user ran `/new` or `/reset`; `platform`, `user_id`, `session_key`. **`session:compress`** — context compression completed; `platform`, `session_id`, `old_session_id` (**empty when compacted in place**), `in_place` (bool — `true` = transcript compacted on the same id, `false` = rotated from `old_session_id`), `compression_count`. **`agent:start`** — agent begins processing a message; `platform`, `user_id`, `chat_id`, `thread_id` (forum-topic / thread root id, **empty when not in a thread**), `chat_type` (`"dm"` | `"group"` | `"forum"`, **empty if unknown**), `session_id`, `message` (**truncated to 500 chars**). **`agent:step`** — each iteration of the tool-calling loop; `platform`, `user_id`, `session_id`, `iteration`, `tool_names`. **`agent:end`** — agent finishes processing; same keys as `agent:start` plus `response` (**truncated to 500 chars**). **`reaction:added`** — an emoji reaction was added to a message the bot can see (**Slack adapter currently**); requires the `reactions:read` scope + the `reaction_added` bot event subscription, **and the bot must be a member of the channel**; context `platform`, `reaction`, `user_id`, `item_user_id`, `item_type`, `channel_id`, `message_ts`, `team_id`, `event_ts`, `raw_event`. **`reaction:removed`** — same shape; requires the `reaction_removed` bot event subscription. **`command:*`** — any slash command executed; `platform`, `user_id`, `command`, `args`.
- **Inputs / options:** Any combination of the above in the `events:` list.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Handler invocations.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Wildcard matching** — handlers registered for `command:*` fire for any `command:` event (`command:model`, `command:reset`, etc.), so a single subscription monitors all slash commands. **Threaded replies tip:** a handler posting a follow-up message into the same Telegram forum topic should include `message_thread_id=int(thread_id)` when `chat_type == "forum"` and `thread_id` is non-empty.
- **Rebuild notes:** Truncate free text in event payloads (500 chars here) so a hook log can't become a transcript store, and expose thread identity so handlers can reply in place. A better version would document per-platform availability for every event, not just reactions.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — event names and context keys defined by the gateway's `hooks.emit()` call sites.

### Gateway hook examples (alert, logger, webhook)  `id: docs-features.hooks-gateway-examples`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** hooks.md → "Examples"
- **What it does:** Three copy-paste gateway hooks.
- **How it works:** **Telegram Alert on Long Tasks** (`~/.hermes/hooks/long-task-alert/`) — subscribes to `agent:step`, and when `iteration == THRESHOLD` (10) with `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` and `TELEGRAM_HOME_CHANNEL` set, POSTs `⚠️ Agent has been running for {iteration} steps. Last tools: {tools}` to `https://api.telegram.org/bot{BOT_TOKEN}/sendMessage` via `httpx.AsyncClient`. **Command Usage Logger** (`~/.hermes/hooks/command-logger/`) — subscribes to `command:*` and appends `{ts, command, args, platform, user}` JSON lines to `~/.hermes/logs/command_usage.jsonl` from a **synchronous** `def handle`. **Session Start Webhook** (`~/.hermes/hooks/session-webhook/`) — subscribes to `session:start` and `session:reset` and POSTs `{"event": event_type, **context}` to an external URL with `timeout=5`.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (illustrative)
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, `TELEGRAM_HOME_CHANNEL`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** The logger example demonstrates that a plain `def handle` works alongside `async def`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Ship one example per handler shape (async HTTP, sync file append, fan-out webhook) so authors see the whole contract. A better version would include a hook scaffolding command.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the examples use only the documented `handle(event_type, context)` contract.

### BOOT.md startup-checklist tutorial  `id: docs-features.hooks-bootmd`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** hooks.md → "Tutorial: BOOT.md"; `~/.hermes/BOOT.md`; `~/.hermes/hooks/boot-md/`
- **What it does:** Shows how to build a "run a Markdown checklist on every gateway boot" hook yourself. **Hermes does not ship a built-in BOOT.md hook.**
- **How it works:** Three pieces: (1) a file at `~/.hermes/BOOT.md` with natural-language startup instructions; (2) a gateway hook firing on `gateway:startup` that **spawns a one-shot agent with your gateway's resolved model/credentials** and runs the BOOT.md instructions; (3) a `[SILENT]` convention so the agent can opt out of sending a message when there's nothing to report. **The two key lines:** `_resolve_gateway_model()` reads the gateway's currently-configured model, and `_resolve_runtime_agent_kwargs()` resolves provider credentials the same way a normal gateway turn does — **including API keys, base URLs, OAuth tokens, and credential pools**. **Without these, a bare `AIAgent()` falls back to built-in defaults and will 401 against any non-default endpoint.** The handler builds the prompt, then starts a **daemon `threading.Thread` so gateway startup isn't blocked on a full agent turn**, constructing `AIAgent(model=_resolve_gateway_model(), **_resolve_runtime_agent_kwargs(), platform="gateway", quiet_mode=True, skip_context_files=True, skip_memory=True, max_iterations=20)` and calling `agent.run_conversation(...)`.
- **Inputs / options:** Silence tokens recognised by the example: `[SILENT]`, `SILENT`, `NO_REPLY`, `NO REPLY` (compared uppercased). Test with `hermes gateway restart` then `hermes logs --follow --level INFO | grep boot-md`, expecting `Running BOOT.md (N chars)` followed by `boot-md completed: …` or `boot-md completed (nothing to report)`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A one-shot agent turn per gateway boot; log lines.
- **Config / env:** the gateway's resolved model/credentials.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Delete `~/.hermes/BOOT.md` to disable the checklist** — the hook stays loaded but silently skips when the file isn't there (it also skips on an empty file). **Extending the pattern:** schedule-aware checklists keying off `datetime.now().weekday()` inside BOOT.md's instructions; multiple checklists by pointing separate hook directories at different files (`STARTUP.md`, `MORNING.md`); a **non-agent variant** that skips `AIAgent` entirely and posts a fixed notification via `httpx` (cheaper, faster, no provider dependency). **Why this isn't a built-in:** "An earlier version of Hermes shipped this as a built-in hook and silently spawned an agent with bare defaults on every gateway boot. That surprised users with custom endpoints and made the feature invisible to users who didn't know it was running." Keeping it a documented pattern means you see exactly what it does and opt in by writing the files.
- **Rebuild notes:** When a convenience feature would spawn inference on your behalf, ship it as a documented pattern rather than a silent built-in — invisible spend is worse than a tutorial. A better version would expose `_resolve_gateway_model` / `_resolve_runtime_agent_kwargs` as a supported public helper so the pattern doesn't depend on internals.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the tutorial imports `_resolve_gateway_model` and `_resolve_runtime_agent_kwargs` from `gateway.run`, and `AIAgent` from `run_agent`, all of which exist in the repo.

### Plugin hooks (`ctx.register_hook`)  `id: docs-features.hooks-plugin`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `ctx.register_hook("<event>", callback)` in a plugin's `register()`
- **What it does:** Registers hooks that fire in **both CLI and gateway** sessions.
- **How it works:** Registered programmatically in `register(ctx)`. Documented example registers `pre_tool_call`, `post_tool_call`, `pre_llm_call`, `post_llm_call`, `on_session_start`, `on_session_end`, and the three kanban board hooks with a note that **dependency-wait blocking may fire inside its transaction**, and that `kanban_task_claimed` runs in the **dispatcher process** while `kanban_task_completed` / `kanban_task_blocked` run in the **worker process**.
- **Inputs / options:** Any event in `VALID_HOOKS`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Depends on the hook category.
- **Config / env:** `plugins.hook_callback_timeout` (default 30, `0` disables, max 600); `plugins.stream_reasoning_deltas`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **General rules for all hooks:** callbacks receive **keyword arguments** — always accept `**kwargs` for forward compatibility; **callback exceptions are logged and skipped; later callbacks continue**; if a Python plugin callback on a **timeout-bounded** hook (hot-path observers such as `post_tool_call` / `pre_llm_call`, plus the policy hook `pre_tool_call`) blocks longer than `plugins.hook_callback_timeout`, **it is abandoned without joining the worker so the agent loop continues** — **timed-out or still-running `pre_tool_call` callbacks fail closed (block the tool); other bounded hooks fail open (skip)**; **hooks with a documented caller-thread contract (`subagent_stop`) are never moved onto a timeout worker**; **shell hooks keep their own per-entry `timeout`**. **The catalog is descriptive:** observers ignore returns, transforms accept the first valid string replacement, and directive/control hooks consume documented return shapes; **plugin middleware is a separate registry and surface, not another hook category**. **Correlation fields such as `turn_id`, `api_request_id`, `task_id`, `session_id`, and `api_call_count` are hook-specific and may be absent — treat IDs as opaque.** **Runtime event-name validity comes from `hermes_cli.plugins.VALID_HOOKS`**; `hermes hooks list` lists configured shell/outbound hooks, **not every available event**, and `hermes hooks test <event>` reports the valid set only when an invalid event is supplied.
- **Rebuild notes:** Bound hot-path callbacks with a timeout and pick the failure direction per hook (fail closed for policy, fail open for observers); exempt hooks with a caller-thread contract from the worker. A better version would expose `VALID_HOOKS` through a CLI subcommand so authors don't have to read the source.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `plugins.hook_callback_timeout: 30` at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:2635`; `VALID_HOOKS` at `hermes_cli/plugins.py:163`.

### Cache-safe plugin system-prompt sections  `id: docs-features.hooks-prompt-sections`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `ctx.register_system_prompt_section(id, value, position=…, max_chars=…)`
- **What it does:** Lets a plugin register durable, always-on system-prompt guidance **instead of injecting the same text through `pre_llm_call` on every turn** (which would break prompt caching).
- **How it works:** Documented example registers `"kanban-advanced.worker-rules"` with a callable returning a string, `position="after_memory"`, `max_chars=4000`. **A callable receives a read-only mapping with `session_id`, `model`, `provider`, `platform`, `profile_name`, and `cwd`. It runs once for a new session.** **Its rendered bytes are frozen on compression and recovered from the already-persisted full system prompt after a process restart/resume; plugin state is not re-read for an existing session.**
- **Inputs / options:** `id` — **global, stable, 1–128 character lowercase identifiers using only letters, numbers, `.`, `_`, and `-`; duplicate IDs are rejected**. `value` — a callable or a plain string. `position` — **`after_memory` is the only placement anchor**; sections are sorted by ID, rendered after memory/profile context and before session metadata; **plugins cannot reorder or replace core prompt content**. `max_chars` — **capped at 4,000 characters**.
- **Outputs / side effects:** A named section in the system prompt. **Every accepted section is named in the prompt and logged at session start with its plugin, position, and character count.**
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **All plugin sections together, including their audit headings, are capped at 8,000 characters and 32 sections.** **Empty, non-string, oversized, aggregate-over-budget, or raising sections are skipped with a warning; prompt construction continues.** **Use `pre_llm_call` for truly dynamic per-turn context.** **There is intentionally no plugin environment-hints hook in this contract:** changing cwd, branch, or other environment data **must not silently mutate a session's cached prompt** — such a hook needs a concrete consumer and the same frozen/resume-safe semantics before it can be added.
- **Rebuild notes:** Render plugin prompt sections once per session and freeze the bytes, so a cached prompt can never drift; cap per-section and aggregate size and skip (never fail) on violation. A better version would report the cache-hit impact of each registered section.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `register_system_prompt_section` on `PluginContext` in `hermes_cli/plugins.py`.

### Plugin-hook catalog (37 events)  `id: docs-features.hooks-catalog`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** hooks.md → "Shipped plugin-hook catalog"; `hermes_cli.plugins.VALID_HOOKS`
- **What it does:** The authoritative per-hook table of category, exact timing and return behaviour, explicit payload fields, and privacy sensitivity.
- **How it works:** Categories are **Directive/control**, **Observer**, and **Transform**. **For backward compatibility, `PluginManager` also adds `telemetry_schema_version="hermes.observer.v1"` to every plugin-hook callback** — "That legacy envelope marker does not mean all hook payloads share one semantic schema; new versioned contracts belong to their concrete event or capability family."
- **Inputs / options:** The 37 events, by category. **Directive/control (5):** `pre_tool_call` (first valid `block` or `approve` directive wins; `modify` returns are shallow-merged into the tool arguments); `pre_llm_call` (all valid string / `{"context": ...}` returns are joined and injected into the user message); `pre_verify` (first valid continue/block-stop directive keeps the turn going); `pre_gateway_dispatch` (first valid `skip`, `rewrite`, or `allow` controls flow). **Transforms (5):** `transform_tool_result` (after `post_tool_call`, before conversation append; first string replaces the result); `transform_terminal_output` (after bounded foreground process capture, before final output limiting); `transform_llm_output` (before `post_llm_call` and final delivery; first non-empty string replaces the response); `pre_transcription` (fired by the STT dispatcher after provider resolution and before any backend is invoked; **dict results are applied in registration order, last-writer-wins per field — `prompt`, `language`, `model`; `file_path` is read-only**); `transform_api_error_classification` (**run-all-then-pick-first**: all callbacks run, then the first dict with a valid `reason` wins, and skipped valid results log a runtime warning; **Python plugins only**). **Observers (27):** `post_tool_call`, `post_llm_call`, `pre_api_request`, `post_api_request`, `api_request_error`, `on_stream_start`, `on_stream_delta`, `on_stream_end`, `on_interim_message`, `on_session_start`, `on_session_end`, `on_session_finalize`, `on_session_reset`, `on_skill_lifecycle`, `subagent_start`, `subagent_stop`, `gateway_platform_event`, `pre_command`, `pre_approval_request`, `post_approval_response`, `kanban_task_claimed`, `kanban_task_completed`, `kanban_task_blocked`, `on_kanban_worker_spawned`, `on_kanban_worker_exited`, `on_kanban_worker_stale_claim`, `on_kanban_task_updated`, `on_kanban_dispatch_tick`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Per category — nothing (observers), a replacement string (transforms), or a flow decision (directive/control).
- **Config / env:** `plugins.hook_callback_timeout`, `plugins.stream_reasoning_deltas`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Privacy column highlights:** `pre_tool_call` / `post_tool_call` / `transform_tool_result` raw arguments and results may contain user content, paths, commands, or secrets; `pre_api_request` is flagged **high sensitivity** — "legacy `user_message`, `conversation_history`, and `request_messages` are intentionally raw; prefer sanitized `request`"; `transform_terminal_output` command/output may contain credentials; `pre_transcription`'s final prompt is uploaded to the STT provider with the audio, so "keep secrets out of hook returns"; `pre_gateway_dispatch` is **"extremely privileged in-process objects expose inbound user/routing data and host handles"**; `gateway_platform_event` exposes a **normalized plain-dict envelope only — raw SDK objects, adapter handles, and bot clients are never exposed**; `on_kanban_worker_spawned`'s `workspace_path` "may reveal project layout or usernames"; `on_kanban_task_updated`'s `changed_fields` "carries field names only, never values". **`pre_command` returns are ignored in v1** (directive-shaped dicts are logged at debug), and **gateway running-agent intercept commands (`/stop`, `/approve` during an active run) are deliberately excluded — "control-plane escape hatches must stay outside plugin reach"**. **`on_kanban_worker_spawned` runs inside the dispatch lock — keep callbacks fast.** **`on_kanban_dispatch_tick` fires once per tick strictly after the dispatch lock is released; idle and contended ticks fire too.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Publish a per-hook table with category, exact timing, payload fields and a privacy note, so a plugin author can reason about blast radius before writing code. A better version would generate the table from the call sites so it can't drift.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `VALID_HOOKS` at `hermes_cli/plugins.py:163` contains **exactly the 37 names** the catalog documents (`api_request_error`, `gateway_platform_event`, `kanban_task_blocked`, `kanban_task_claimed`, `kanban_task_completed`, `on_interim_message`, `on_kanban_dispatch_tick`, `on_kanban_task_updated`, `on_kanban_worker_exited`, `on_kanban_worker_spawned`, `on_kanban_worker_stale_claim`, `on_session_end`, `on_session_finalize`, `on_session_reset`, `on_session_start`, `on_skill_lifecycle`, `on_stream_delta`, `on_stream_end`, `on_stream_start`, `post_api_request`, `post_approval_response`, `post_llm_call`, `post_tool_call`, `pre_api_request`, `pre_approval_request`, `pre_command`, `pre_gateway_dispatch`, `pre_llm_call`, `pre_tool_call`, `pre_transcription`, `pre_verify`, `subagent_start`, `subagent_stop`, `transform_api_error_classification`, `transform_llm_output`, `transform_terminal_output`, `transform_tool_result`) — a complete, exact match, and the source of truth showing that `plugins.md`'s "26 hooks" claim is the inaccurate one.

### Streaming output hooks  `id: docs-features.hooks-streaming`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** `on_stream_start`, `on_stream_delta`, `on_stream_end`, `on_interim_message`
- **What it does:** Observer-only hooks letting plugins consume streaming LLM output for telemetry, live dashboards, or TTS pipelines **without changing the response**.
- **How it works:** **Delivered through host-owned bounded queues with one background worker per registered callback, so plugin callbacks never run inline on the token path.** **If one callback stalls, only that callback's queue can fill and drop its oldest pending observer event; other observers continue receiving events independently.** Implementation: `agent/plugin_stream_hooks.py`.
- **Inputs / options:** **Common fields for all four:** `turn_id` (str, opaque turn identifier when available); `iteration` (int, current API-call/tool-loop iteration); `session_id` (str); `model` (str); `provider` (str); `surface` (str — e.g. `cli`, `discord`, `telegram`). **Extra fields:** `on_stream_start` — none; `on_stream_delta` — `delta: str`, `kind: "text" | "reasoning"`; `on_stream_end` — `final_text: str`, `finished: bool`, `error: str | None`; `on_interim_message` — `text: str`, `already_streamed: bool`. Documented registration: `def on_delta(delta, kind, model, provider, **kwargs): ...` then `ctx.register_hook("on_stream_delta", on_delta)`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** **Return values are ignored.** "To keep the stream fast, callbacks should enqueue their own work and return quickly. Exceptions are logged and do not stop the stream."
- **Config / env:** **Reasoning deltas are not exposed to plugins by default** — opt in with `plugins: stream_reasoning_deltas: true`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **`on_interim_message` can also fire after a non-streaming response, so registering only that hook does not force a provider call onto streaming transport.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Never let a plugin callback run inline on the token path — use a bounded per-callback queue so one slow observer degrades only itself. A better version would expose queue-drop counts so a stalling observer is detectable.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `agent/plugin_stream_hooks.py` exists; all four names present in `VALID_HOOKS` with the source comment "Fired asynchronously off the token path by agent.plugin_stream_hooks; callbacks observe immutable normalized text/lifecycle payloads and cannot transform the stream" (`hermes_cli/plugins.py:174-181`).

### `pre_verify` hook contract  `id: docs-features.hooks-pre-verify`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** hook `pre_verify`
- **What it does:** Fires once per turn at the bounded edited-code verify gate, letting a callback keep the agent going — run a check, defer it, tidy the diff — instead of stopping.
- **How it works:** Fired **after the verify-on-stop guard**, when the agent has edited code and is about to verify/finish. A callback keeps the turn going by returning `{"action": "continue", "message": "<follow-up instruction>"}`; **the Claude-Code Stop shape `{"decision": "block", "reason": "..."}` (block the stop == keep going) is accepted too**. Anything else lets the turn finish.
- **Inputs / options:** Payload fields `session_id`, `platform`, `model`, `coding`, `attempt`, `final_response`, `changed_paths`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** The turn continues with the follow-up instruction, or finishes.
- **Config / env:** bounded by `agent.max_verify_nudges`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Privacy:** the payload carries the draft response and changed paths. **Hermes' shipped guidance lives in the evidence-based verification-stop nudge; this hook is for user/plugin policy.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Accept both the native and the Claude-Code return shape so existing hook scripts port unchanged, and bound the number of nudges. A better version would report the remaining nudge budget in the payload.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the `pre_verify` block comment at `hermes_cli/plugins.py:182-192` states the same two accepted shapes and the `agent.max_verify_nudges` bound verbatim.

### `transform_api_error_classification` hook contract  `id: docs-features.hooks-error-classification`
- **Surface:** Tool
- **Where:** hook `transform_api_error_classification`
- **What it does:** Lets a provider plugin own its provider's error quirks without core patches, by overriding the built-in API-error classification.
- **How it works:** Fired **once per failed API call at the top of `agent/error_classifier.classify_api_error()`, BEFORE the built-in pipeline**. Callbacks receive the parsed error context and **should self-scope on `provider`**. Return `None` to pass, or a dict with **required `reason` (a `FailoverReason` name)** plus optional `retryable` (bool), `should_compress` (bool), `should_rotate_credential` (bool), `should_fallback` (bool), `message` (str), `error_context` (dict).
- **Inputs / options:** Payload fields `provider`, `model`, `status_code`, `error_type`, `error_code`, `error_message`, `error_body`, `error`, `approx_tokens`, `context_length`, `num_messages`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** The chosen classification drives retry / compress / credential-rotate / fallback behaviour.
- **Config / env:** none. **Python plugins only.**
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Dispatch is run-all-then-pick-first:** every registered callback runs with its failures isolated (**an early answer never stops later callbacks**), then the first valid result in registration order wins — **on conflict the first-registered plugin is the tie-break, and every additional valid-but-losing result is reported with a runtime warning (the #64714 skipped-transform rule)**. **Invalid dicts and unknown reasons are skipped; a broken plugin can never break error classification.** **Cold path: fires only on API failure.** **Privacy:** `error_message` / `error_body` may carry an unredacted provider error dump.
- **Rebuild notes:** Run every callback before picking a winner so no plugin can short-circuit another's side effects, and warn on every valid-but-losing result so conflicts are visible. A better version would let a plugin declare which providers it handles so scoping isn't a convention.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — the full contract, including the run-all-then-pick-first rule, the #64714 skipped-transform warning, the optional keys, and the privacy note, appears verbatim in the source comment at `hermes_cli/plugins.py:196-215`.

### Shell hooks  `id: docs-features.hooks-shell`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `hooks:` block in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`; scripts under `~/.hermes/agent-hooks/` by convention
- **What it does:** Runs shell scripts as subprocesses whenever the corresponding plugin-hook event fires — in **both CLI and gateway sessions** — with **no Python plugin authoring required**.
- **How it works:** Registered by calling `agent.shell_hooks.register_from_config(cfg)` at both **CLI startup (`hermes_cli/main.py`)** and **gateway startup (`gateway/run.py`)**. **They compose naturally with Python plugin hooks — both flow through the same dispatcher.**
- **Inputs / options:** Four documented use cases: **block or modify a tool call** (reject dangerous `terminal` commands, enforce per-directory policies, require approval for destructive `write_file`/`patch`, or rewrite arguments — sanitize paths, inject defaults — before the tool runs); **run after a tool call** (auto-format Python or TypeScript files the agent just wrote, log API calls, trigger a CI workflow); **inject context into the next LLM turn** (prepend `git status` output, the current weekday, or retrieved documents); **observe lifecycle events** (write a log line on `subagent_stop` or `on_session_start`). Comparison table dimensions vs plugin/gateway hooks: **Declared in** (`hooks:` block vs `register()` vs `HOOK.yaml`+`handler.py`); **Lives under** (`~/.hermes/agent-hooks/` vs `~/.hermes/plugins/<name>/` vs `~/.hermes/hooks/<name>/`); **Language** (**Any — Bash, Python, Go binary** vs Python only vs Python only); **Runs in** (CLI + Gateway vs CLI + Gateway vs Gateway only); **Events** (`VALID_HOOKS` incl. `subagent_stop` vs `VALID_HOOKS` vs gateway lifecycle); **Can block a tool call** (Yes vs Yes vs **No**); **Can inject LLM context** (Yes vs Yes vs **No**); **Consent** (**first-use prompt per `(event, command)` pair** vs implicit Python plugin trust vs implicit dir trust); **Inter-process isolation** (**Yes — subprocess** vs No vs No).
- **Outputs / side effects:** One subprocess per matching hook per event.
- **Config / env:** `hooks:` and `hooks_auto_accept:` in `config.yaml`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Ordering and precedence:** both Python plugin hooks and shell hooks flow through the same `invoke_hook()` dispatcher; **Python plugins are registered first (`discover_and_load()`), shell hooks second (`register_from_config()`), so Python `pre_tool_call` block decisions take precedence in tie cases**; **the first valid block wins — the aggregator returns as soon as any callback produces `{"action": "block", "message": str}` with a non-empty message.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Let shell scripts subscribe to the same event set as Python plugins through one dispatcher, so there is a single ordering story. A better version would let a hook declare a priority instead of relying on registration order.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `agent/shell_hooks.py` exists with `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60` at `:166` and `MAX_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 300` at `:167`.

### Shell-hook configuration schema  `id: docs-features.hooks-shell-schema`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `hooks: <event_name>: - {matcher, command, timeout, fail_closed}`
- **What it does:** Declares which script runs on which event, with an optional tool-name matcher, a timeout, and a fail-closed flag.
- **How it works:** Each entry's `command` **runs via `shlex.split`, `shell=False`**.
- **Inputs / options:** Five keys. `<event_name>` — **must be in `VALID_HOOKS`**. `matcher` — optional regex, **used for `pre_tool_call` / `post_tool_call` only**. `command` — **required**; the shell command. `timeout` — optional seconds, **default 60, capped at 300**. `fail_closed` — optional bool, **default false, `pre_tool_call` only**; **`failClosed` is also accepted (Cursor/Claude Code compat)**. Plus top-level `hooks_auto_accept: false`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Subprocess spawns.
- **Config / env:** `hooks.*`, `hooks_auto_accept` (`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:2651`, default `False`).
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Typos produce a "Did you mean X?" warning and are skipped.** **Unknown keys inside a single entry are ignored; missing `command` is a skip-with-warning.** **`timeout > 300` is clamped with a warning.** **`fail_closed: true` on an event other than `pre_tool_call` warns and is ignored** (only blocking-capable events can fail closed).
- **Rebuild notes:** Validate event names against the canonical set with a did-you-mean suggestion, clamp rather than reject an over-large timeout, and warn on a flag that can't apply. A better version would validate the whole `hooks:` block with `hermes config` before startup.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60` and `MAX_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 300` at `agent/shell_hooks.py:166-167`; `hooks_auto_accept: False` at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:2651`.

### Shell-hook JSON wire protocol  `id: docs-features.hooks-shell-protocol`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** stdin/stdout of every shell-hook subprocess
- **What it does:** Defines exactly what a shell hook receives and what it may return.
- **How it works:** Each time the event fires, Hermes spawns a subprocess for every matching hook (matcher permitting), **pipes a JSON payload to stdin, and reads stdout back as JSON**.
- **Inputs / options:** **stdin payload keys:** `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `session_id`, `cwd`, `extra`. **`tool_name` and `tool_input` are `null` for non-tool events** (`pre_llm_call`, `subagent_stop`, session lifecycle). **The `extra` dict carries all event-specific kwargs** (`user_message`, `conversation_history`, `child_role`, `duration_ms`, …). **Unserialisable values are stringified rather than omitted.** **stdout response shapes (all optional):** block a `pre_tool_call` — `{"decision": "block", "reason": "…"}` (Claude-Code style) or `{"action": "block", "message": "…"}` (Hermes-canonical); modify a `pre_tool_call` — `{"action": "modify", "args": {…}}` (Hermes-canonical) or `{"decision": "modify", "tool_input": {…}}` (Claude-Code style); inject context for `pre_llm_call` — `{"context": "…"}`; keep the agent going at the verify gate — `{"action": "continue", "message": "…"}` or `{"decision": "block", "reason": "…"}`; **silent no-op — any empty / non-matching output is fine.**
- **Outputs / side effects:** Block / modify / inject / continue, or nothing.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Malformed JSON, non-zero exit codes, and timeouts log a warning but never abort the agent loop** (unless `fail_closed` is set). Both Claude-Code and Hermes-canonical shapes are **normalised internally**.
- **Rebuild notes:** Accept both your own and the ecosystem's response shapes and normalise internally, so existing scripts port with no edits; stringify unserialisable payload values rather than dropping them. A better version would publish a JSON Schema for both directions.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — protocol handling in `agent/shell_hooks.py`.

### Shell-hook exit code 2 = block  `id: docs-features.hooks-exit-2`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** a `pre_tool_call` shell hook exiting with code 2
- **What it does:** Blocks the tool call **even when stdout carries no block JSON** — Claude Code / Cursor compatible.
- **How it works:** The block message is resolved in **priority order**: (1) stdout block JSON (`reason` / `message`), when present; (2) **the first 400 characters of stderr**; (3) a generic `"Blocked by shell hook."` default. **The simplest possible blocking hook** is a two-line script that echoes to stderr and exits 2.
- **Inputs / options:** Exit code 2; optional stderr text.
- **Outputs / side effects:** The tool call is blocked with the resolved message.
- **Config / env:** none.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **For events whose block directive is not honored (everything except `pre_tool_call`), exit 2 is treated like any other non-zero exit:** a warning is logged and stdout is still parsed.
- **Rebuild notes:** Support the ecosystem's exit-code convention alongside structured JSON, with a documented three-step message fallback. A better version would surface which of the three sources produced the message in the log line.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — exit-code handling in `agent/shell_hooks.py`.

### Shell-hook fail-open vs fail-closed  `id: docs-features.hooks-fail-closed`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `fail_closed: true` (or `failClosed: true`) on a `pre_tool_call` entry
- **What it does:** Inverts the default so a crashed security gate blocks instead of silently allowing.
- **How it works:** **By default shell hooks fail open:** a spawn error, timeout, or unparseable stdout logs a warning and the action proceeds — "the right default for observability hooks — but wrong for security gates. A crashed secret-scanner must not silently allow the tool call it was supposed to vet." With `fail_closed: true` each failure **blocks** the tool call with `hook <command> failed closed: <reason>`.
- **Inputs / options:** Documented failure matrix — **Command not found / not executable:** fail-open warns and proceeds, `fail_closed` **blocks**; **Timeout:** warn+proceed vs **block**; **Non-JSON stdout (e.g. a stack trace):** warn+proceed vs **block**; **Clean exit, valid no-op JSON (`{}`):** proceed in both. Documented example: a `secret-scan.sh` on `matcher: "terminal|write_file|patch"` with `timeout: 10` and `fail_closed: true`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** The tool call blocked with a named reason.
- **Config / env:** `fail_closed` / `failClosed`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **`fail_closed` only applies to blocking-capable events (`pre_tool_call` today); setting it on any other event logs a warning at config-parse time and is ignored.** **`hermes hooks test` reflects these semantics — the `parsed` line shows exactly the block shape the dispatcher would receive.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Default to fail-open for observability and make fail-closed a per-entry opt-in restricted to blocking-capable events. A better version would let a hook declare itself a security gate so `fail_closed` is implied.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — fail-closed handling in `agent/shell_hooks.py`; `hermes hooks test` exists with a synthetic-payload contract (evidence: `cli_help/hooks__test.txt`).

### Shell-hook worked examples  `id: docs-features.hooks-shell-examples`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** hooks.md → "Worked examples"
- **What it does:** Four complete config-plus-script pairs.
- **How it works:** **1. Auto-format Python files after every write** — `post_tool_call` with `matcher: "write_file|patch"` running `auto-format.sh`, which reads the payload from stdin, extracts `.tool_input.path` with `jq`, runs `black` when the path ends in `.py` and `black` is on PATH, and prints `{}`. **2. Block destructive `terminal` commands** — `pre_tool_call` with `matcher: "terminal"`, `timeout: 5`, running `block-rm-rf.sh`, which greps `.tool_input.command` for `rm[[:space:]]+-rf?[[:space:]]+/` and prints `{"decision": "block", "reason": "blocked: rm -rf / is not permitted"}` or `{}`. **3. Inject `git status` into every turn** (the Claude-Code `UserPromptSubmit` equivalent) — `pre_llm_call` running `inject-cwd-context.sh`, which discards stdin, runs `git status --porcelain`, and emits `{context: ("Uncommitted changes in cwd:\n" + $s)}` via `jq --null-input --arg s`. **4. Log every subagent completion** — `subagent_stop` running `log-orchestration.sh`, which appends `{ts: now, parent: .session_id, extra: .extra}` to `~/.hermes/logs/orchestration.log` and prints `{}`.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (illustrative)
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** **In example 1, the agent's in-context view of the file is *not* re-read automatically — the reformat only affects the file on disk; subsequent `read_file` calls pick up the formatted version.** **Claude Code's `UserPromptSubmit` event is intentionally not a separate Hermes event — `pre_llm_call` fires at the same place and already supports context injection.**
- **Rebuild notes:** Map ecosystem event names onto your existing equivalents instead of adding aliases, and say so in the docs. A better version would ship these four as installable starter scripts.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — every example uses only the documented stdin/stdout protocol.

### Shell-hook consent model & allowlist  `id: docs-features.hooks-consent`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** first-use prompt; `~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json`
- **What it does:** Prompts for approval the first time Hermes sees each unique `(event, command)` pair, then persists the decision.
- **How it works:** Subsequent runs (CLI or gateway) skip the prompt. **Three escape hatches bypass the interactive prompt — any one is sufficient:** (1) `--accept-hooks` flag on the CLI (e.g. `hermes --accept-hooks chat`); (2) `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1` environment variable; (3) `hooks_auto_accept: true` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`.
- **Inputs / options:** The three escape hatches; **manual allowlisting** by writing `~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json` with an `approvals` array whose entries record the hook `event` and the **exact `command` string**, e.g. `{"approvals": [{"event": "post_llm_call", "command": "/home/hermes/.hermes/hooks/my-hook.py"}]}`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Allowlist entries persisted.
- **Config / env:** `hooks_auto_accept`; env `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Non-TTY runs (gateway, cron, CI) need one of the three escape hatches — otherwise any newly-added hook silently stays un-registered and logs a warning.** **Script edits are silently trusted:** the allowlist keys on the **exact command string, not the script's hash**, so editing the script on disk does not invalidate consent; **`hermes hooks doctor` flags mtime drift** so you can spot edits and decide whether to re-approve. **The command string must match the configured hook command exactly. A path-keyed object with a `sha256` field is not the expected format and will not approve the hook** — verify manual entries with `hermes hooks list`.
- **Rebuild notes:** Key consent on `(event, command)` and be explicit that edits are trusted, then give the operator a drift-detection command rather than pretending hashes are enforced. A better version would optionally pin a hash and re-prompt on drift.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `hooks_auto_accept: False` at `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py:2651`; `--accept-hooks` present as a group-level flag on `hermes mcp`, `hermes cron` and `hermes cron tick` with the exact text "(equivalent to HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1 / hooks_auto_accept: true)" (evidence: `cli_help/mcp.txt`, `cli_help/cron.txt`).

### `hermes hooks` CLI  `id: docs-features.hooks-cli`
- **Surface:** CLI
- **Where:** `hermes hooks <subcommand>`
- **What it does:** Inspects shell-script hooks declared in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`, tests them against synthetic payloads, and manages the first-use consent allowlist at `~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json`.
- **How it works:** Four subcommands (plus aliases).
- **Inputs / options:** **`hermes hooks list`** (alias `ls`) — "List configured hooks with matcher, timeout, and consent status"; no flags. **`hermes hooks test <event> [--for-tool FOR_TOOL] [--payload-file PAYLOAD_FILE]`** — "Fire every hook matching `<event>` against a synthetic payload"; `event` positional ("Hook event name (e.g. pre_tool_call, pre_llm_call, subagent_stop)"); `--for-tool` ("Only fire hooks whose matcher matches this tool name (used for pre_tool_call / post_tool_call)"); `--payload-file` ("Path to a JSON file whose contents are merged into the synthetic payload before execution"). **`hermes hooks revoke <command>`** (aliases `remove`, `rm`) — "Remove a command's allowlist entries (takes effect on next restart)"; positional `command` ("The exact command string to revoke (as declared in config.yaml)"). **`hermes hooks doctor`** — "Check each configured hook: exec bit, allowlist, mtime drift, JSON validity, and synthetic run timing"; no flags.
- **Outputs / side effects:** `test` runs the real scripts; `revoke` edits the allowlist.
- **Config / env:** reads `config.yaml` and the allowlist file.
- **Edge cases / guards:** `hermes hooks list` lists **configured shell/outbound hooks, not every available event**; `hermes hooks test <event>` reports the valid set **only when an invalid event is supplied**. Revocation **takes effect on next restart**.
- **Rebuild notes:** Ship a `doctor` that checks exec bit, consent, drift, output validity and timing in one pass — the five things that actually break a shell hook. A better version would let `list` also print the full `VALID_HOOKS` set on request.
- **Verification:** doc drift (minor) — the CLI's `revoke` has the documented aliases **`remove`** and **`rm`** and `list` has **`ls`**, none of which the page's CLI table mentions (evidence: `cli_help/hooks.txt`).

### Shell-hook security model  `id: docs-features.hooks-shell-security`
- **Surface:** Docs
- **Where:** hooks.md → "Security"
- **What it does:** States the trust boundary and four operating rules for shell hooks.
- **How it works:** **Shell hooks run with your full user credentials — the same trust boundary as a cron entry or a shell alias. Treat the `hooks:` block in `config.yaml` as privileged configuration.**
- **Inputs / options:** Four rules: **only reference scripts you wrote or fully reviewed**; **keep scripts inside `~/.hermes/agent-hooks/` so the path is easy to audit**; **re-run `hermes hooks doctor` after you pull a shared config to spot newly-added hooks before they register**; **if your `config.yaml` is version-controlled across a team, review PRs that change the `hooks:` section the same way you'd review CI config**.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** n/a
- **Edge cases / guards:** Inter-process isolation (subprocess) is the only isolation — not a sandbox.
- **Rebuild notes:** Name the equivalent trust boundary the reader already understands (cron entry / shell alias) rather than inventing a new one. A better version would offer an opt-in sandbox (namespace/seccomp) for hook subprocesses.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `command` runs via `shlex.split` with `shell=False`, which prevents shell metacharacter injection but grants full user credentials (`agent/shell_hooks.py`).

### Outbound webhooks  `id: docs-features.hooks-outbound`
- **Surface:** Config
- **Where:** `hooks.outbound:` list in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`
- **What it does:** POSTs a signed JSON payload to configured HTTP endpoints whenever a matching lifecycle event fires — **"the push-side mirror of the inbound webhook platform: inbound webhooks wake Hermes when the world changes; outbound webhooks tell the world when Hermes does something"** — with no polling on the receiving end.
- **How it works:** Configure a list of endpoints and the lifecycle events they care about. **Any event from the plugin-hook set is valid** (`pre_tool_call`, `post_tool_call`, `pre_llm_call`, `post_llm_call`, `on_session_start`, `on_session_end`, `subagent_start`, `subagent_stop`, …).
- **Inputs / options:** Six entry keys: `name` (optional label for logs); `url` (required); `events` (list); `secret_env` (**the name of an environment variable holding the HMAC secret, typically set in `~/.hermes/.env`**); `timeout` (**per-attempt seconds, 1–60**); `matcher` (regex, **tool-scoped events only**). Documented typical uses: notify a CI system or dashboard when an agent turn finishes (`on_session_end`); track subagent completions across a fleet (`subagent_stop`); feed tool activity into external monitoring (`post_tool_call` with a `matcher`); **wake another Hermes instance by pointing the URL at that instance's inbound webhook**.
- **Outputs / side effects:** Signed HTTP POSTs.
- **Config / env:** `hooks.outbound.*`; the env var named by `secret_env`.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Malformed entries warn and are skipped — a broken webhook never crashes the agent.** **Changes take effect on the next CLI session / gateway restart.** **Prefer `secret_env` over an inline `secret:` literal so the config file stays free of credentials.** **Entries without a secret are delivered unsigned (flagged as `UNSIGNED` by `hermes hooks list`).**
- **Rebuild notes:** Reference the secret by env-var name rather than inlining it, and mark unsigned targets loudly in the listing. A better version would refuse to register an unsigned non-loopback target without an explicit acknowledgement.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `hermes hooks list` "shows configured outbound targets alongside shell hooks, including whether each target is signed" per the page's own closing line.

### Outbound webhook wire format & signature  `id: docs-features.hooks-outbound-wire`
- **Surface:** API
- **Where:** the POST body and headers of every outbound delivery
- **What it does:** Defines the payload shape, headers, and HMAC verification.
- **How it works:** **Each firing POSTs a JSON body with the same top-level shape as shell hooks' stdin, plus delivery metadata** — `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `session_id`, `cwd`, `extra`, plus **`delivery_id`** and **`timestamp`**.
- **Inputs / options:** **Four headers:** `Content-Type: application/json`; `X-Hermes-Event` (the hook event name); `X-Hermes-Delivery` (unique id per delivery — **same value as `delivery_id` in the body**); `X-Hermes-Signature-256` (**`sha256=<hex>` — HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body, GitHub-style; only present when a secret is configured**). Documented verification helper: `expected = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()` compared with `hmac.compare_digest`.
- **Outputs / side effects:** n/a
- **Config / env:** the configured secret.
- **Edge cases / guards:** **Because `delivery_id` and `timestamp` live inside the signed body, a verified receiver also gets replay protection for free:** **dedupe** on `delivery_id` (or the matching `X-Hermes-Delivery` header) — remember recently seen ids and skip duplicates, since **Hermes retries failed deliveries once, so the same id can legitimately arrive twice**; **reject stale events** by checking `timestamp` against your clock with a tolerance window (**5 minutes is the common default**) — "An attacker replaying a captured request can't forge a fresh timestamp without the secret."
- **Rebuild notes:** Put the delivery id and timestamp **inside** the signed body so signature verification alone gives dedupe and replay protection. A better version would include the receiver's expected audience in the signed body to prevent cross-endpoint replay.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — GitHub-compatible `sha256=` HMAC scheme; the verification snippet on the page is the standard `hmac.compare_digest` pattern.

### Outbound webhook delivery semantics  `id: docs-features.hooks-outbound-delivery`
- **Surface:** Core
- **Where:** the outbound webhook dispatcher
- **What it does:** Defines six delivery properties.
- **How it works:** **Fire-and-forget, off the hot path** — events are serialized and queued instantly; **a single background thread performs the HTTP POSTs**, so a slow or dead endpoint can never stall a tool call or an agent turn. **Notify-only** — unlike shell hooks, outbound webhooks **cannot block tool calls or inject context; the response body is ignored. They observe, never steer.** **Bounded retries** — connection errors and 5xx responses are **retried once with backoff**; **4xx responses are not retried** (the receiver said the request itself is wrong); **failures are logged and dropped — delivery is best-effort, not guaranteed.** **Redirects are never followed** — a 3xx response is treated as a misconfiguration and logged, because "following a redirected POST would silently drop the signed payload"; point the `url` at the final endpoint. **Bounded queue** — if the queue backs up (dead endpoint, event storm), **new events are dropped with a warning rather than consuming unbounded memory**. **No consent prompt** — outbound targets execute no code on your machine, they receive data at a URL you configured.
- **Inputs / options:** n/a (automatic)
- **Outputs / side effects:** Best-effort HTTP deliveries.
- **Config / env:** **`HERMES_SAFE_MODE=1` still skips registration, same as plugins and shell hooks.**
- **Edge cases / guards:** **"payloads include tool inputs and event metadata, so only point targets at endpoints you trust, and prefer `https://`."**
- **Rebuild notes:** Never follow a redirect on a signed POST, retry only on transport/5xx, and bound the queue so an event storm degrades gracefully. A better version would expose delivery metrics (queued/dropped/retried) so a dead endpoint is detectable.
- **Verification:** implemented as documented — `HERMES_SAFE_MODE` gating is the same mechanism used for plugin and shell-hook registration.
